title: What To Do After You're Diagnosed With Prediabetes
content:
You can work with your healthcare team immediately after a prediabetes diagnosis to develop a care plan. The plan may focus on food choices, weight management, and exercise. They may also help you understand your blood sugars and any medications you may need.
The shocking health news came at a recent doctor’s visit: You have just been diagnosed with prediabetes.
You’ve had an initial conversation with your doctor, but much of that discussion is a fog that you don’t fully remember. Your doctor gave you handouts and information, but the reality is now just starting to set in.
So what’s next?
Your task of learning what prediabetes means for your life now begins, to make sure that your prediabetes doesn’t evolve into type 2 diabetes (T2D).
That means changing your life: the foods you eat, how physical activity you get, your mental health and support system, and whether you’ll need to take medications or learn about blood sugar management.
It can be overwhelming at first. But don’t worry, a prediabetes diagnosis doesn’t have to be stressful and life changing in stressful ways. You can take some simple actions in the days, weeks, and months after a new prediabetes diagnosis to make sure you’re living your best and healthiest life.
First off, you are not alone.
More than 1 in 3 adults in the United States live with it and 80% of people don’t know they have it.
You may have had prediabetes for years without knowing it, and not have experienced any symptoms to indicate prediabetes has been part of your life.
A prediabetes diagnosis means that your blood sugar levels are higher than normal, but not high enough to mean you have diabetes.
While prediabetes is a leading risk factor for T2D, it’s not a guarantee that you’ll eventually develop diabetes or even need medications to manage the condition. Some people may reverse their prediabetes. You may be one of those individuals.
However, this means that you will want to work closely with your healthcare team to make changes in your life.
You can learn more here about prediabetes, including its prevalence, what blood sugars mean and why they’re important, and what a prediabetes diagnosis may mean for your overall health.
No, prediabetes does not mean you will develop T2D.
But prediabetes is a major risk factor for T2D down the road, even with lifestyle changes or medications following your prediabetes diagnosis.
These are common symptoms of type 2 diabetes that you may keep in mind:
You can find more here about type 2 diabetes symptoms and what they mean.
A big part of managing prediabetes involves your eating patterns.
However, there is not a one-size-fits-all answer to the foods you must eat and how your eating habits need to change.
Generally, a lower-carbohydrate and calorie eating pattern with lower-glycemic foods could be beneficial. That includes:
You might also try certain meal plans and eating styles, including:
You may consider consulting your healthcare team, including a dietitian and diabetes care and education specialist (aka diabetes educator), to work with you on food and dietary changes.
Check out these 7 prediabetes-friendly foods, along with other eating tips that may help you with your new diagnosis.
Physical activity is another key part of managing your prediabetes.
The National Diabetes Prevention Program recommends 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week, such as brisk walking. Additionally, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends strength training 2 days a week on top of that moderate-intensity activity.
This also helped with weight loss, for which the DPP recommends at least a 7% weight loss goal during the first 6 months. The research found that lifestyle interventions, overall, could reduce the risk of T2D by 58% over the course of 3 years through the DPP.
Even if you don’t get that same amount of exercise, increase your daily physical activity.
This 2023 study found that for people with prediabetes who were not getting any physical activity, if they replaced that sedentary activity for just 30 minutes with light or moderate-to-vigorous activity, it helped reduce their risk of developing T2D and improved their health overall.
One way to increase your non-strenuous physical activity each week is to start aerobic exercise.
Research shows that this may help you achieve your weight management goals and lower your chances of developing T2D. The study found that this type of activity helped even more when it was continued for a year.
Try these exercises to help manage your prediabetes.
Obesity is a risk factor for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.
As mentioned above, the national DPP recommends a goal of at least 7% weight loss during the first 6 months to help lower the risk of developing T2D.
However, a prediabetes diagnosis does not necessarily mean you are overweight and need to lose any weight.
This personal point may vary for everyone, and it’s something to discuss openly and honestly with your healthcare team. Setting realistic goals can help you manage your prediabetes and overall health.
You may not need any medications at the time of your diabetes diagnosis.
At first, you may be able to put lifestyle changes into place to help manage your prediabetes and reverse it without any medications. That includes insulin, a hormone that many people eventually begin using to manage their type 2 diabetes.
However, this 2020 research review suggests that clinicians and professional medication associations shouldn’t shy away from prescribing medications or other treatments for prediabetes, beyond just lifestyle changes.
This is a personal discussion to have with your healthcare team, so that you can best understand what may be best for your life with prediabetes.
Your mental health is an important part of staying healthy and managing any type of diabetes, including prediabetes. It’s well known that stress, depression, and anxiety can make it more difficult to manage your diabetes and prediabetes.
In this 2024 study review, the authors cited an older study that found people with prediabetes who have depressive or anxiety symptoms are more likely to develop type 2 diabetes than those who don’t have those mental issues.
Always remember that you’re not alone in this prediabetes diagnosis.
Just as important is to avoid blaming or judging yourself. This diabetes stigma can be detrimental to your health and mindset.
You can find support in many places, from your family and friends to your healthcare team who can help you manage and cope with a prediabetes diagnosis.
Additionally, you may find support in the Diabetes Community, including those who live with prediabetes. Finding that support is helpful on its own in general, but can also improve your management habits and support when you feel more engaged and informed about your health.
American Diabetes Association: The ADA offers many resources for people with prediabetes and diabetes and their families and caregivers. This can include health information to discuss with your doctor, support resources, and ways to improve your eating and exercise routines.
National Diabetes Prevention Program: This program by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is a key resource for people with prediabetes trying to manage their health and prevent T2D. You can read more about prediabetes and diabetes, enter a lifestyle change program, and get other support resources to help you on your care journey.
Bezzy: This online forum, created by Healthline, connects people who live with prediabetes, type 2 diabetes, and other types of diabetes. You can ask questions, find helpful hints and tips, explore diabetes-friendly recipes, and share your own stories with the community.
Being diagnosed with prediabetes can be overwhelming. But this new diagnosis does not have to be overly stressful. You can make simple changes to your eating style, exercise routine, weight management, and overall health to help prevent prediabetes from becoming type 2 diabetes.
Your healthcare team can best guide you on how to manage prediabetes and if you need to consider any medications or blood sugar management.
What you do in the first weeks and months after a prediabetes diagnosis can help make sure you’re living your best and healthiest life.

title: Are Bipolar Disorder and PMS Related?
content:
Both conditions involve shifts in mood. However, premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is related to your menstrual cycle, and bipolar disorder episodes can operate independently of your cycle. 
Bipolar disorder and PMS may be connected, but their relationship is complex. 
Research suggests that some people with bipolar disorder may experience heightened symptoms of mood instability during the premenstrual phase, potentially due to hormonal fluctuations. 
However, having PMS does not cause bipolar disorder. The two conditions require distinct approaches to diagnosis and treatment.
There’s no evidence to suggest that bipolar disorder causes PMS or vice versa. 
However, the hormonal changes associated with PMS can worsen mood symptoms in people with bipolar disorder. A 2021 review found that premenstrual exacerbations (PME) of bipolar disorder symptoms are common.
In many cases, PME of bipolar disorder symptoms can look like the symptoms of PMS. Overlapping symptoms of bipolar disorder and PMS include: 
People with bipolar disorder may also be more likely to experience premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a mental health condition often described as “extreme PMS.” 
A 2021 systematic review found that people with bipolar disorder, especially bipolar II disorder, may be more likely to experience PMDD than the larger population.
This could be due to how hormone fluctuations affect mood regulation, particularly in those already predisposed to mood disorders. 
Still, PMS does not increase the risk of developing bipolar disorder. Instead, it may amplify existing mood-related symptoms in those who already have a diagnosis of bipolar disorder.
Research indicates that comorbidity between bipolar disorder and PMS is not uncommon. One 2014 study found that up to 65% of people with bipolar disorder experience worsening symptoms in the premenstrual phase.
A 2017 study included 158 women with bipolar disorder. Researchers found that hormonal changes caused by menstruation, after childbirth, and during menopause worsened bipolar disorder symptoms for most study participants.
This comorbidity can affect people’s overall treatment plan and outlook. For example: 
If you experience both bipolar disorder and PMS, it’s important to discuss this with the healthcare professional who treats your condition, whether it’s a primary care physician, psychiatrist, or therapist. 
The key differences between these conditions lie in the timing, duration, and intensity of symptoms:
If you think you may have PMS, bipolar disorder, or both, you might benefit from tracking your symptoms over several menstrual cycles. Keeping a symptom diary can provide valuable insights for you and your healthcare professional.
Bipolar disorder and PMS are distinct conditions, but they can overlap or interact. Understanding the relationship between these conditions can help guide treatment and improve quality of life.
If you’re experiencing significant mood changes or worsening bipolar disorder symptoms during your menstrual cycle, talk with a healthcare professional. They can help you identify patterns, adjust treatments, and develop a tailored management plan.
Sian Ferguson is a freelance health and cannabis writer based in Cape Town, South Africa. She’s passionate about empowering readers to take care of their mental and physical health through science-based, empathetically delivered information.

title: Holding Space for Someone
content:
Holding space for someone involves active listening and allowing them to process feelings at their own pace. Keep reading to learn more about how to hold space for others, as well as the potential benefits.
“Holding space” is a form of mindfulness, which is the practice of focusing your thoughts and being rooted in the present moment.
While mindfulness is associated with individual practice — such as meditation — it can also be extended to others. Holding space for someone else is one way to extend mindfulness to other people, and both parties can benefit.
Holding space for someone can involve:
Allow the other person to guide the conversation and broach topics when they are ready. Try to ask questions without judgement and let them reach conclusions on their own.
It is important to keep in mind that you are not trying to fix someone’s problems through holding space for them. Sometimes, instead of solutions, people want someone who can truly listen to what they are saying and empathize with their emotions.
If they express that they want solutions, then it is O.K. to share, but it is important to ask what they want first.
There isn’t a lot of research on the benefits of holding space specifically. However, having close friends you can hold space with can have some potential health benefits.
A 2018 review of studies found that being confided in has some benefits, such as increasing the feeling of intimacy between you and the person who confided in you. 
If you are holding space for someone, they may also be willing to reciprocate. Being able to confide in a friend can improve your well-being and help you feel socially supported.
A 2020 review of studies found that having friends — or, more broadly, people you can confide in — may make you less likely to suffer from depression.
A 2023 review of studies found that having friendships that provide support can decrease the likelihood of developing depression and anxiety.
When you are struggling, opening up to a friend can help you work through the issue. They are a shoulder for you to lean on and may be able to offer you advice, if you need it.
Holding space for someone and having them hold space for you may strengthen your relationship. 
While holding space for others may have benefits, doing so too frequently could lead to emotional burnout for both you and your friend. It is important to be honest with each other when it comes to how you are feeling and if you are able to engage in holding space.
Moreover, it is important that your friend can hold space for you, if you need it. 
If you are holding space for someone who will not hold space for you, it may be a sign of a one-sided friendship. Being in a friendship where all of the communication comes from you can be distressing.
If this is the case, you may consider having an open and honest conversation with your friend about how you feel. In turn, they can hold space for you so you can express your feelings.
Holding space is a form of mindfulness. When you hold space for someone, it can involve being fully present, active listening, and allowing them to reach their own conclusions without passing judgement.
The benefits of holding space for someone can include strengthening your relationship with that person, as well as a decreased risk of depression and anxiety.

title: What Is Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and Can You Prevent It?
content:
Relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) is a condition that develops when an athlete doesn’t get enough fuel to support their body’s energy demands. 
Relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) can affect athletes at every level, from recreational event competitors to Olympic medalists. If left unrecognized and untreated, REDs may drastically affect long-term athletic performance and overall quality of life.
When your body doesn’t get enough fuel from food, it gradually adapts by reducing functions that are not essential but have a high energy cost, such as hair growth and digestion.
REDs may lead to health challenges such as:
An athlete may develop REDs if they consistently do not consume enough calories to support their body’s energy demands.
Low calorie intake (consuming fewer calories than your body needs) over a period of time leads to low energy availability.
During periods of low energy availability, your body must prioritize certain functions over others. It typically prioritizes functions that are essential for life, such as breathing, heart function, and brain function.
Many nonessential but high energy functions may slow down, which can lead to health complications.
Examples of nonessential functions with a high energy demand include:
The term “REDs” was introduced in an International Olympic Committee consensus statement in 2014 to expand on an existing condition called “the female athlete triad.” The change was made to emphasize that REDs can affect anyone, even if it is more common in female athletes.
The female athlete triad involves three conditions that often occur together:
REDs can affect any athlete who isn’t getting enough energy through food, but it’s particularly common in:
The prevalence of low energy availability in female athletes has been reported to be as high as 44.8% in gymnasts and 33.3% in soccer players.
Overtraining syndrome can occur if you perform more physical activity within a certain time period than your body can recover from. It’s characterized by hormonal changes that can lead to many of the same symptoms as REDs, including:
According to a 2023 consensus statement from the International Olympic Committee, REDs and overtraining syndrome usually have overlapping symptoms, and healthcare professionals can’t use any single biomarker to diagnose either condition.
REDs develops when an athlete burns more calories than they take in over a period of time. This gradual energy imbalance may be accidental or intentional.
Some athletes, such as those competing in endurance sports, have energy demands that greatly exceed the needs of nonathletes. Undereating may be common among these athletes for many reasons, such as lack of appetite or challenges with meal planning.
Some psychological factors can also contribute to undereating. In some sports, such as those that emphasize weight or leanness, athletes may undereat to maintain a specific body shape and size that is required for competition. For other sports, the primary motivation may be to improve the strength-to-bodyweight ratio and performance. 
Athletes at risk of REDs may include those who:
REDs can cause many symptoms that affect multiple organ systems, including:
Preventing REDs starts with educating athletes and yourself about the potential harms of not consuming enough energy for a specific activity. It may also involve developing a plan to ensure adequate nutrition.
Educational programs should focus on increasing nutritional knowledge and recognizing disordered eating patterns.
You can help prevent REDs by:
A team of performance experts can potentially help you prevent REDs and improve your energy balance. You may benefit from working with experts such as:
Mild REDs may be treatable with dietary changes alone. However, athletes with prolonged or severe low energy availability or underlying eating disorders might need to take time off from training and get support from a mental health professional.
REDs is a condition that develops when an athlete’s energy intake is too low to meet their energy requirements. It can lead to health challenges such as frequent infections, depression, and intense fatigue.

title: Diovan Interactions: Alcohol, Medications, and Others
content:
Diovan (valsartan) has potential interactions with other medications and some supplements. These interactions could affect how well the drug works or cause harmful effects.
Diovan is used for the following:
The drug is also used in children ages 1 year and older for treating high blood pressure.
An interaction can occur because one substance causes another substance to have a different effect than expected. Interactions can also occur if you have certain health conditions.
Keep reading to learn about Diovan’s possible interactions. For a detailed overview, read this in-depth Diovan article.
Note about combination forms and interactions: The active ingredient in Diovan is valsartan, which is also available in combination with other drugs. Examples include Diovan HCT and Co-Diovan, both of which combine valsartan and hydrochlorothiazide. (Co-Diovan may not be available in the United States.) Interactions can occur with any of a medication’s active ingredients. When taking combination forms, be sure to check for interactions with each of the medication’s active ingredients. 
Learn more about hydrochlorothiazide and its interactions.
Before you start taking Diovan, tell your doctor and pharmacist about any prescription, over-the-counter, or other drugs you take. Sharing this information with them may help prevent possible interactions.
To learn whether Diovan interacts with herbs, vitamins, or supplements, see the “Are there other interactions with Diovan?” section.
If you have questions about drug interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
The following table lists drugs that may interact with Diovan. Keep in mind that this table does not include all drugs that may interact with Diovan. For more information about some of these interactions, see the “Drug interactions explained” section.
Certain health conditions or other factors could raise your risk of harm if you take Diovan. In such cases, your doctor may not prescribe Diovan for you. These are known as contraindications. Here are the contraindications of Diovan:
If you’re taking aliskiren (Tekturna) and have diabetes: Taking Diovan with aliskiren increases your risk of developing side effects from Diovan and aliskiren. These include:
Diabetes can raise the risk of developing some of these side effects, including kidney problems. Because of this, your doctor typically will not prescribe Diovan if you’re taking aliskiren and have diabetes.
Talk with your doctor before starting Diovan if you have diabetes and you’re taking aliskiren. They can prescribe an alternative medication for Diovan.
If you’ve had an allergic reaction: If you’ve ever had an allergic reaction to Diovan or any of its ingredients, your doctor likely won’t prescribe Diovan. This is because taking the drug could cause another allergic reaction. You can ask your doctor about other treatments that may be better options for you.
Before you start taking Diovan, talk with your doctor if any of the factors mentioned here apply to you. Your doctor can determine whether Diovan is safe for you to take.
Diovan is not known to interact with alcohol. Diovan and alcohol can both cause some similar side effects, such as:
Consuming alcohol can worsen the conditions that Diovan treats. For example, alcohol can cause high blood pressure and worsen heart failure.
Diovan’s side effects may worsen if you consume alcohol during Diovan treatment. And certain health conditions may not improve during Diovan treatment if you consume alcohol. Your doctor may recommend avoiding or limiting alcohol use during your Diovan treatment.
If you have questions about consuming alcohol while taking Diovan, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Learn more about certain drug interactions that can occur with Diovan.
Taking Diovan with NSAIDs may cause Diovan to be less effective at treating your blood pressure. NSAIDs treat pain and fever, but they can raise your blood pressure. Both NSAIDs and Diovan can increase your risk of developing kidney problems, including acute (sudden) kidney failure. Symptoms of sudden kidney failure can include:
You may be more likely to develop kidney problems if you take NSAIDs during your Diovan treatment.
Examples of NSAIDs that may interact with Diovan include:
Talk with your doctor about all the medications you take before starting treatment with Diovan. This includes prescriptions, over-the-counter medications, and supplements.
If you develop symptoms of possible kidney problems, including sudden kidney failure, talk with your doctor right away. They’ll likely have you complete certain tests to check your kidneys. They’ll also likely adjust your medications to reduce these side effects and manage your condition.
If you have questions about taking Diovan with NSAIDs, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Taking Diovan with ACE inhibitors may increase your risk of side effects from Diovan and the ACE inhibitors. ACE inhibitors treat high blood pressure. ACE inhibitors and Diovan cause similar side effects. If you take these medications together, you may be more likely to develop these side effects.
These side effects and their symptoms include:
Examples of ACE inhibitors that may interact with Diovan include:
Talk with your doctor about all the medications you take before starting Diovan treatment. This includes prescriptions, over-the-counter medications, and supplements.
Watch for symptoms of low blood pressure, high potassium level, or sudden kidney failure. If you develop symptoms, talk with your doctor right away. They’ll likely have you complete certain tests to check your kidneys and potassium levels. They also may have you check your blood pressure more frequently. Your doctor will likely adjust your medications as needed to reduce these side effects and manage your condition.
If you have questions about taking Diovan with ACE inhibitors, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Taking Diovan with pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) may cause Diovan to work less effectively in treating and lowering your blood pressure. Pseudoephedrine relieves nasal congestion, but it can cause high blood pressure.
High blood pressure typically doesn’t cause symptoms that someone may notice. But in severe cases of high blood pressure, symptoms are more common and can include:
Talk with your doctor about all the medications you take before starting Diovan treatment. This includes prescriptions, over-the-counter medications, and supplements.
Let your doctor know right away if your blood pressure isn’t improving or suddenly worsens, including the symptoms noted above. They may have you check your blood pressure more often than usual. They’ll likely adjust your medications as needed to reduce these side effects and manage your condition.
If the side effects seem life threatening or you think you’re having a medical emergency, immediately call 911 or your local emergency number.
If you have questions about taking Diovan with pseudoephedrine, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Diovan may have other interactions. They could occur with supplements, foods, vaccines, or lab tests. 
Here are additional interactions that may occur with Diovan. Note that this is not a full list of all other interactions possible with Diovan.
Before you start taking Diovan, talk with your doctor and pharmacist about any herbs, vitamins, or supplements you take. Sharing this information with them may help you avoid possible interactions.
If you’re taking potassium supplements, your doctor may check your potassium levels before and during your Diovan treatment. They may have you check your blood pressure more often than usual, especially if you’re taking high doses of fish oil. If needed, your doctor will adjust your medication and fish oil supplement to reduce your risk of side effects and manage your condition.
If you have questions about interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Diovan currently has no reports of interacting with herbs. But this doesn’t mean that interactions with herbs won’t be recognized in the future.
For this reason, it’s important to check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any of these products while taking Diovan.
Diovan currently has no reports of interacting with vitamins. But this doesn’t mean that interactions with vitamins won’t be recognized in the future.
For this reason, it’s important to check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any of these products while taking Diovan.
Certain salt substitutes may interact with Diovan. Salt substitutes may be used as an alternative to sodium (salt) in foods. Reducing the amount of salt in the foods you eat may help lower your blood pressure. One example of a salt substitute is NoSalt.
Instead of salt, some of these salt substitutes contain potassium. Both Diovan and these salt substitutes can increase potassium levels. So using these salt substitutes while taking Diovan may cause high potassium levels. But you may not notice or have any symptoms from high potassium levels since they are typically mild.
Talk with your doctor about any salt substitutes you use before starting Diovan. They may check your blood potassium levels before and during your Diovan treatment. This is to make sure your blood potassium levels are within the normal range while you’re taking Diovan and using salt substitutes. If needed, your doctor will adjust your medications to reduce high potassium levels and manage your condition.
Diovan currently has no reports of interacting with vaccines. If you have questions about getting certain vaccines during your Diovan treatment, talk with your doctor.
Diovan currently has no reports of interacting with lab tests. If you have questions about certain lab tests during your treatment with Diovan, talk with the healthcare professional ordering the test.
Diovan currently has no reports of interacting with cannabis (commonly called marijuana) or cannabis products such as cannabidiol (CBD). But as with any drug or supplement, talk with your doctor before using cannabis with Diovan.
Note: Cannabis is illegal at a federal level but is legal in many states to varying degrees.
Certain medical conditions or other health factors may raise the risk of interactions with Diovan. Before taking Diovan, talk with your doctor about your health history. They’ll determine whether Diovan is right for you.
Health conditions or other factors that might interact with Diovan include:
Kidney problems: Kidney problems may raise your risk of developing high potassium levels, especially if you’re taking Diovan. Diovan can worsen your kidney problems in certain situations, leading to sudden kidney failure. Your doctor will check your blood potassium levels and kidneys before and during your Diovan treatment, especially if you had or have kidney problems.
Liver problems: No studies have been conducted to determine the effects of taking Diovan in people who have severe liver problems. So it’s unknown whether Diovan is safe or works in people who have severe liver problems. Your doctor can further discuss your treatment options if you have or ever had liver problems.
Heart problems: The risk of developing certain Diovan side effects is higher if you have certain heart problems. For example, heart failure may raise your risk of developing low blood pressure, high potassium levels, and kidney problems. Your doctor will monitor your blood pressure, potassium levels, and kidneys more closely if you have or ever had heart problems.
Pregnancy: Diovan has a boxed warning for the risk of fetal harm if the drug is taken during pregnancy. Because of this, doctors typically won’t prescribe Diovan for you if you’re pregnant. If you’re pregnant or can become pregnant, talk with your doctor before starting treatment with Diovan. See the “Boxed warning: Risk of fetal harm” section near the beginning of this article to learn more.
Breastfeeding: Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with Diovan due to the possible risk of serious side effects. Research hasn’t been conducted to learn whether the drug passes into breast milk. It’s also not known whether Diovan causes side effects in a child who is breastfed. If you’re breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed, talk with your doctor about your options.
Allergic reaction: If you’ve ever had an allergic reaction to Diovan or any of its ingredients, your doctor likely won’t prescribe Diovan. This is because taking the drug could cause another allergic reaction. You can ask your doctor about other treatments that may be better for you.
Taking certain steps can help you avoid interactions with Diovan. Before starting treatment, talk with your doctor and pharmacist. Your discussion can include:
It’s also important to understand Diovan’s label and other paperwork that may come with the drug. Colored stickers that describe interactions may be on the label. The paperwork, sometimes called the patient package insert or medication guide, may have other details about interactions. 
If you did not get paperwork with Diovan, ask your pharmacist to print a copy for you. If you have difficulty reading or understanding this information, your doctor or pharmacist can help.
Taking Diovan exactly as prescribed can help prevent interactions.

title: Sublocade Interactions: Alcohol, Medications, and Others
content:
Sublocade (buprenorphine) is a prescription drug that helps treat opioid use disorder in adults. Sublocade can interact with alcohol, other drugs, and some supplements, including benzodiazepines and certain antifungals.
Sublocade contains the active ingredient buprenorphine. The drug is given as an injection under your skin by a doctor or another healthcare professional.
An interaction can occur because one substance causes another substance to have a different effect than expected. Interactions can also occur if you have certain health conditions.
Keep reading to learn about Sublocade’s possible interactions. And for more information about the drug, including details about its uses, see this in-depth Sublocade article.
Before you start receiving Sublocade injections, tell your doctor and pharmacist about any prescription, over-the-counter, or other drugs you take. Sharing this information with them may help prevent possible interactions. (To learn whether Sublocade interacts with herbs, vitamins, or supplements, see the “Are there other interactions with Sublocade?” section.)
If you have questions about drug interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
The table below lists drugs that may interact with Sublocade. Keep in mind that this table does not include all drugs that may interact with Sublocade. For more information about some of these interactions, see the “Drug interactions explained” section.
Certain health conditions or other factors could raise your risk of harm if you receive Sublocade. In such cases, your doctor may not prescribe Sublocade for you. These are known as contraindications.
Allergic reaction is the only contraindication of Sublocade.
If you’ve had an allergic reaction to Sublocade or any of its ingredients, your doctor likely won’t prescribe Sublocade for you. This is because receiving the drug could cause another allergic reaction. You can ask your doctor about other treatments that may be better options for you.
It’s not safe to drink alcohol during your Sublocade treatment.
Combining alcohol and Sublocade can raise your risk of respiratory depression (slow, shallow breathing) and central nervous system (CNS) depression (slowed brain function). These are serious side effects of Sublocade that can be life threatening. (To learn about Sublocade’s side effects, see this article.)
If you have other questions about alcohol and Sublocade, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Learn more about certain drug interactions that can occur with Sublocade.
Sublocade can interact with benzodiazepines, which are used to treat several conditions, including anxiety and seizures. 
Examples of benzodiazepine medications include:
Both Sublocade and benzodiazepines can cause respiratory depression and CNS depression. These are serious side effects that can lead to loss of consciousness, coma, or even death. Taking these drugs together can raise your risk of these side effects.
During your Sublocade treatment, your doctor will likely avoid prescribing benzodiazepines unless there are no suitable alternatives.
If you take a benzodiazepine during Sublocade treatment, your doctor will likely prescribe a lower dosage of the benzodiazepine for you. You should not take a higher dose than your doctor prescribes. 
If you take a benzodiazepine during your Sublocade treatment, tell your doctor right away if you have symptoms of respiratory depression or CNS depression. Symptoms may include confusion, dizziness, severe sleepiness, and slow or weak breathing. But if your symptoms seem severe or life threatening, call 911 or your local emergency number immediately.
If your doctor prescribes a benzodiazepine with Sublocade, they may recommend keeping naloxone nasal spray (Narcan, Kloxxado, others) on hand. Naloxone nasal spray is used for emergency treatment of an opioid overdose. It helps reverse respiratory or CNS depression caused by opioids such as Sublocade.
If you have questions about taking benzodiazepines with Sublocade, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Sublocade can interact with opioids, which are used to treat severe pain.
Sublocade is an opioid, but it’s prescribed to treat opioid use disorder, not pain. It reduces withdrawal symptoms and opioid cravings you may have after stopping the use of other opioids. It also reduces the effects of other opioids and can help keep you from misusing other opioids again.
Examples of other opioids include:
Sublocade can reduce the pain-relieving effect of other opioids you take. This could cause withdrawal symptoms and raise your risk of serotonin syndrome.
Sublocade and other opioids can both cause respiratory depression and CNS depression. Taking other opioids during Sublocade treatment can raise your risk of these side effects, which can also occur during an opioid overdose.
Respiratory depression and CNS depression can lead to loss of consciousness, coma, or even death. 
You should not take other opioids during your Sublocade treatment and for several months after your last Sublocade injection.
If you do take other opioids with Sublocade, tell your doctor right away if you have symptoms of respiratory depression or CNS depression. Examples may include confusion, dizziness, severe sleepiness, and slow or weak breathing. But if your symptoms seem severe or life threatening, call 911 or your local emergency number immediately.
While you’re receiving Sublocade for opioid use disorder, your doctor will likely recommend keeping naloxone nasal spray (Narcan, Kloxxado, others) on hand. Naloxone nasal spray is used for emergency treatment of opioid overdose. It helps reverse respiratory or CNS depression caused by taking other opioids with Sublocade.
If you need a pain reliever during your Sublocade treatment, you should not take one that contains an opioid. You can ask your doctor or pharmacist to recommend a safe medication for you. Be sure to tell them that you’re receiving Sublocade.
If you have questions about taking other opioids with Sublocade, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Sublocade can interact with certain antidepressants, which are used to treat mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety disorders.
Examples of antidepressant medications that interact with Sublocade include:
Sublocade and certain antidepressants can cause some of the same side effects, including sleepiness, low blood pressure, heart rhythm problems, and serotonin syndrome (a dangerous condition caused by high serotonin levels in your body). So taking these drugs together can raise your risk of these side effects.
If you take an antidepressant medication, talk with your doctor before starting treatment with Sublocade. In some cases, your doctor may recommend switching to a different antidepressant.
If you’re prescribed Sublocade and an antidepressant, your doctor will likely monitor you closely. Talk with your doctor about side effects you should watch for. These may include sleepiness, dizziness, tremor, restlessness, and changes in your heart rate.
If you have questions about Sublocade and antidepressants, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Sublocade may have other interactions. They could occur with supplements, foods, vaccines, or even lab tests. See below for details. Note that this information does not include all other possible interactions with Sublocade.
Before you start receiving Sublocade, talk with your doctor and pharmacist about any herbs, vitamins, or supplements you take. Sharing this information with them may help you avoid possible interactions.
If you have questions about interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Sublocade can interact with St. John’s wort, which is used to ease symptoms of depression and other conditions.
Taking St. John’s wort with Sublocade can cause your body to break down Sublocade faster than usual. This can make Sublocade less effective for treating opioid use disorder. It can also cause opioid withdrawal symptoms. Your doctor will likely recommend that you not take St. John’s wort during your Sublocade treatment.
If you have questions about taking other herbs with Sublocade, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
There are currently no reports of Sublocade interacting with vitamins. But this doesn’t mean that vitamin interactions won’t be recognized in the future.
For this reason, it’s still important to check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any of these products while receiving Sublocade.
Consuming grapefruit or grapefruit juice during Sublocade treatment could raise your risk of side effects from the drug. Your doctor may recommend that you avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice or limit the amount you consume during your Sublocade treatment.
If you have questions about consuming other foods or drinks during your Sublocade treatment, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
There are currently no reports of Sublocade interacting with vaccines. If you have questions about getting certain vaccines during your Sublocade treatment, talk with your doctor.
There are currently no reports of Sublocade interacting with lab tests. If you have questions about having certain lab tests done during your treatment with Sublocade, talk with the healthcare professional ordering the test.
Cannabis (commonly called marijuana) and cannabis products, such as cannabidiol (CBD), have been specifically reported to interact with Sublocade.
Using cannabis or cannabis products while receiving Sublocade may increase the risk of certain side effects of Sublocade and cannabis, such as sleepiness, dizziness, and confusion.
Before you start treatment with Sublocade, tell your doctor and pharmacist if you use cannabis. By sharing this information with them, you may help prevent possible interactions.
Note: Cannabis is illegal at a federal level but is legal in many states to varying degrees.
Certain medical conditions or other health factors may raise the risk of interactions with Sublocade. Before starting treatment with Sublocade, talk with your doctor about your health history. They’ll determine whether Sublocade is right for you.
Health conditions or other factors that might interact with Sublocade include:
Lung or breathing problems: Sublocade can cause respiratory depression. If you have lung or breathing problems, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), sleep apnea, or asthma, you may have a higher risk of this side effect. Talk with your doctor about whether Sublocade is right for you.
Adrenal gland problems: Sublocade may cause adrenal insufficiency. If you already have adrenal insufficiency or Addison’s disease, Sublocade could make your condition worse. Talk with your doctor about whether this drug is right for you.
Liver problems: Sublocade may cause liver problems. If you already have a liver problem, such as hepatitis B or C, Sublocade could make it worse. Talk with your doctor about whether Sublocade is right for you.
Certain heart problems: Sublocade can cause long QT syndrome (a type of abnormal heart rhythm) in some people. If you have heart failure or a slow or abnormal heartbeat, you may have a higher risk of this side effect. You may also have a higher risk if you have electrolyte imbalances, such as low levels of potassium or magnesium. Talk with your doctor about whether Sublocade is right for you.
Head injury or brain-related condition: Sublocade can increase the pressure of the fluid in your brain and spinal cord. This can be dangerous if you have an existing head injury or brain-related condition, such as a brain tumor. Before receiving Sublocade, tell your doctor if you’ve had a recent head injury or have a condition affecting your brain. Your doctor can determine whether it’s safe for you to receive Sublocade.
Gallbladder or bile duct problems: If you have a problem with your gallbladder or bile duct, Sublocade could make your condition worse. Talk with your doctor about whether this drug is right for you.
Pregnancy: If you receive Sublocade during pregnancy, your baby may have opioid withdrawal symptoms after birth. If you’re pregnant or planning a pregnancy, talk with your doctor before receiving Sublocade. Your doctor can discuss safe treatment options with you.
Breastfeeding: It’s not known whether it’s safe to receive Sublocade while breastfeeding. The drug passes into breast milk and may cause side effects in a child who is breastfed. If you’re breastfeeding or planning to do so, talk with your doctor about your options.
Allergic reaction: If you’ve had an allergic reaction to Sublocade or any of its ingredients, your doctor will likely not prescribe Sublocade for you. This is because receiving the drug could cause another allergic reaction. You can ask your doctor about other treatments that may be safer for you.
Taking certain steps can help you avoid interactions with Sublocade. Before starting treatment, talk with your doctor and pharmacist. Things to discuss with them include:

title: Can Birth Control Cause Seizures?
content:
Hormonal birth control does not cause seizure conditions. However, some research suggests it may increase seizure risk in people with epilepsy or other seizure disorders. 
This can happen due to hormonal changes or interactions with antiseizure medications. 
Not all birth control methods carry the same risk, so discussing your options with a healthcare professional can help you find the safest and most effective contraceptive method for your needs.
Although the research is mixed and inconclusive, hormonal birth control may affect how often people with seizure disorders experience symptoms. 
Hormones like estrogen and progesterone can affect brain activity and seizure thresholds, which determine how likely a seizure is to occur.
Estrogen can be proconvulsant, meaning it may increase seizure activity. High estrogen levels, like during ovulation, may make seizures more likely in some people.
Progesterone, on the other hand, may have anticonvulsant properties, meaning it can help reduce seizure risk.
The effects of hormonal birth control on seizure activity depend on the specific hormone levels and formulations.
A 2016 survey-based study recorded 2,712 contraceptive experiences reported by 1,144 people with epilepsy. Most participants said that they experienced no changes to seizure frequency while using birth control. 
However, 18.7% of hormonal birth control users reported an increase in seizures, and 9.5% of nonhormonal users reported a decrease. 
It’s worth noting that 17.5% of depo medroxyprogesterone (Depo-Povera) users reported a decrease, but 19% reported an increase. Depo-Provera is a progestin-only shot given in the arm or upper buttocks.
This study is flawed in some ways — it’s small and based on self-reporting, which leaves room for error — but it’s one of the largest studies on the topic. More research is needed on seizure risk and contraception. 
People with epilepsy or a seizure disorder can safely use many birth control methods, but some may be better options than others.
If you’re interested in hormonal birth control, your healthcare professional may recommend a progestin-only method. This includes: 
These options may be safer for people at risk of seizures because they avoid the potential proconvulsant effects of estrogen. 
You might also consider nonhormonal birth control. These methods do not affect hormone levels, making them a reliable option for avoiding hormonal triggers.
This includes:
Birth control and emergency contraception containing estrogen and progestin — the combination pill, certain “morning after” pills, skin patch, and vaginal ring — may decrease the effectiveness of lamotrigine (Lamictal). 
However, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists says that there’s no conclusive evidence that combined hormonal contraception increases epileptic seizures. 
Lamotrigine (Lamictal) and other enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs can also decrease the effectiveness of birth control and emergency contraception containing estrogen and progestin.
This includes:
These drugs increase the rate at which the liver metabolizes hormones, reducing hormone levels in the bloodstream.
If you’re taking one of these medications, your healthcare professional may recommend a higher dose hormonal contraceptive or a nonhormonal option, like a copper IUD, to ensure reliable pregnancy prevention.
Hormonal birth control does not directly cause seizures but can influence seizure activity in people with epilepsy or other seizure disorders. Progestin-only and nonhormonal methods are often safer options.
If you take antiseizure medications, it’s important to discuss potential interactions with a healthcare professional. They can help you find a birth control method that works for your body and lifestyle while minimizing the risk of seizures or unplanned pregnancy.

title: We Tried It: 6-6-6 Walking Challenge
content:
The 6-6-6 walking challenge involves a 60 minute walk at either 6 a.m or 6 p.m with an additional 6 minutes each for warmup and cooldown.
The 6-6-6 walking trend is a new, low-impact exercise trend.
It comes after the 12-3-30 trend, which involves walking at a 12 percent incline for 30 minutes at a 3 mile per hour pace on a treadmill.
I tried the 6-6-6 workout for a week. Keep reading for my honest thoughts on the workout below.
As on optional step, you may consider stretching before your warmup and after your cooldown.
I thought it would be important to share my circumstances before I dive into my review.
Where I live, the sun has not yet risen at 6 a.m. and has already set by 6 p.m. Temperatures routinely dip below freezing when the sun is down. To avoid freezing to death, I completed this challenge on a walking pad.
However, you don’t have to use a walking pad to complete this workout — it can be done virtually anywhere. Some places you may consider are:
I also attend a Pilates class most mornings, so for consistency’s sake, I chose 6 p.m. as my workout time.
As I was only able to do this trend for one week, I did not notice any significant changes in my weight.
Weight can fluctuate day-to-day and even week-to-week for a number of reasons, and everybody is different. While this may not have had any particular effect on me, it could lead to different results for you.
If you are trying to lose weight, losing one to two pounds per week is generally considered safe. It is important to talk to your doctor about your weight loss goals before making any drastic changes to your diet and exercise habits.
If you are new to exercising, you do not have to complete the entire 60 minutes the first time. You can start out with 30 minutes, or however much time you can complete, and work your way up from there.
I felt that this challenge had a positive effect on my mood.
Since my start time was at 6 p.m., it gave me time to decompress from work. I could catch up with friends, hang out with my cat, and otherwise separate myself from my working mindset before I started.
I find that I am usually tired after work, so I had to motivate myself a little to actually get up and start the workout. However, once I started walking, I enjoyed it.
After the walk, I felt a little happier and less tired. I could jump into making dinner and other evening household tasks in a better mood compared to my usual post-work routine of sitting on the couch and doom scrolling.
During my workout, I watched shows that nobody else wants to watch with me (specifically The Legend of Korra, if anyone is interested.)
One of the reasons I looked forward to the workout was because I could watch my show. I did not watch it at any other point in my day — even if the last episode ended on a cliffhanger — reserving it specifically for the workout.
I’m not saying you have to watch a show to do this workout, but pairing the walking with another habit helped. To me, an hour is a long time to focus on one thing.
If you are like me and need another form of stimulation, you may consider pairing your walk with a:
You could also ask a friend or family member to do this challenge with you. That way, you can hold each other accountable and keep each other company during your walk.
Yes!
The 6-6-6 walking trend is an exercise routine that is easy to incorporate into your daily routine. Since it can be done at either 6 a.m. or 6 p.m., you can fit the workout in before things get busy during the day.
After doing this challenge for a week, I can say that my mood and energy levels have improved. However, for me personally, I did not notice a change in weight.

title: What Is the Difference Between Dermatomyositis and Lupus?
content:
Dermatomyositis and lupus are autoimmune conditions that may share symptoms like skin rashes, muscle weakness, and chronic inflammation. Dermatomyositis may involve lung complications and skin ulcers, while lupus causes a butterfly-shaped facial rash.
Dermatomyositis and lupus are separate diagnoses that may require a comprehensive medical exam and some testing to detect differences.
Dermatomyositis often leads to muscle weakness and reddish or purplish skin rashes. Lupus usually involves inflammation in the joints, skin, and internal organs. 
The symptoms of dermatomyositis and lupus can sometimes overlap, making it challenging to differentiate the two conditions. 
Both are autoimmune diseases that affect multiple organs and involve some degree of fatigue, muscle weakness, and skin irritation. “Autoimmunity” means the immune system fights the body’s own tissues because it mistakes them for harmful invaders.
Common symptoms of dermatomyositis include:
Common symptoms of lupus include:
Yes, it’s possible to have both lupus and dermatomyositis, though this is relatively uncommon. 
If you have both conditions, you may notice specific rashes associated with dermatomyositis, like Gottron papules, along with symptoms of lupus, such as a butterfly-shaped rash across the face.
In a 2023 case series including eight individuals with both lupus and dermatomyositis, seven of them initially received a lupus diagnosis (mostly cutaneous lupus erythematosus) and later developed dermatomyositis. 
The eighth person had dermatomyositis first and then developed lupus after receiving a specific immune-modulating therapy for a separate condition.
In a 2016 case study, a person with dermatomyositis later developed systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). 
Dermatomyositis symptoms included skin ulcers and pustules on the palms and soles along with lung involvement. Within a year, lupus signs emerged, and diagnostic tests, along with kidney issues, confirmed lupus nephritis. 
Researchers concluded that this suggests immune dysfunction in dermatomyositis may have contributed to the development of lupus.
Research is very limited and nonconclusive regarding the link between COVID-19 and lupus and dermatomyositis. 
However, some studies suggest that COVID-19 can potentially trigger the onset or worsening of autoimmune diseases, including dermatomyositis and lupus. 
In a 2021 case study, a 58-year-old woman developed both dermatomyositis and lupus after having COVID-19. This is known as overlap syndrome. It refers to a condition in which a person has core symptoms of two or more autoimmune diseases simultaneously. 
The woman experienced muscle weakness, characteristic skin changes such as rashes, and cardiac complications, including myopathy. 
Overlap syndrome poses diagnostic challenges, as symptoms of dermatomyositis and lupus may be worsened or mistaken for COVID-19-related complications.

Treatment options for dermatomyositis and lupus typically involve the management of chronic inflammation and decreasing the immune response.
