Dermatomyositis and lupus can sometimes occur at the same time, creating what’s known as overlap syndrome. This means symptoms may be similar or may happen in the same areas. For example, skin rashes, muscle weakness, and joint pain can occur in either condition.

title: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome: What Is the Life Expectancy?
content:
The life expectancy of people with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome depends on the location of a person’s gastric tumors and whether or not they have metastasized (spread) to the liver.
Keep reading to learn about average life expectancy with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and the different factors that can affect it.
People with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome that has not spread to the liver typically have a greater life expectancy than those with liver metastases. About one-third of people have liver metastases at diagnosis.
About 60% to 90% of gastrinomas are cancerous and spread to the:
People whose gastrinomas do not spread to the liver have an average 20-year survival rate of 95%. This means that 95% of people without liver metastases are alive 20 years later.
People with liver metastases have a 15% 10-year average survival rate after surgery to remove the tumors. This means that only 15% of people with liver metastases are alive 10 years after the tumor removal surgery.
Learn more about liver metastases.
Where a tumor starts can affect the likelihood of its spreading to different parts of the body.
Duodenal gastrinomas start in the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.
Pancreatic gastrinomas start in the pancreas. Pancreatic gastrinomas are more likely to spread to the liver than duodenal gastrinomas.
Learn more about pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.
Each person is different. Other factors can affect your individual life expectancy with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
These can include:
Innovations in treatment are improving for gastrinomas and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. It’s possible that the life expectancy of people being diagnosed today with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome may have a better life expectancy compared with people in the past.

title: Descovy vs. Truvada: What You Should Know
content:
Descovy and Truvada are prescription drugs used to treat and help prevent HIV. Both drugs come as oral tablets that are taken once per day. Truvada is available as a generic drug, while Descovy is not. 
This article explains the main ways that Descovy and Truvada are alike and different. For more information about these drugs, including details about their uses, see this Descovy article and this Truvada article.
See the following list to find out whether Descovy or Truvada is available as a generic. (A generic drug contains an exact copy of the active ingredient in a brand-name medication.)
If you’ve been prescribed Truvada and are interested in taking the generic version instead, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
See the following table for details on the uses of each drug in adults.
For treating HIV, Descovy and Truvada are taken with other HIV medications.
To learn more about using Descovy or Truvada to treat your condition, talk with your doctor. You can also see this Descovy for PrEP article.
Descovy and Truvada are used to treat HIV in children. Descovy is approved for children weighing at least 14 kilograms (kg), which is about 30 pounds (lb). Truvada is used for children who weigh at least 17 kg (about 37 lb).
Descovy and Truvada are also used as PrEP to help prevent HIV in children who weigh at least 35 kg (about 77 lb).
For more information about the use of either drug in children, talk with your child’s doctor.
Here’s an overview of the dosage and how you’ll take Descovy and Truvada.
To learn more about the dosages for each drug, see the Descovy dosage article and Truvada dosage article.
Below are the dosages of Descovy and Truvada for treating or helping prevent HIV in adults. Strengths of Descovy are listed in milligrams (mg) of emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. Strengths of Truvada are listed in mg of emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. 
Your doctor will prescribe the right dosage of Descovy or Truvada for you.
Descovy and Truvada are used to treat and help prevent HIV in certain children.
Below are the dosages of Descovy and Truvada for treating or helping prevent HIV in children. Strengths of Descovy are listed in mg of emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. Strengths of Truvada are listed in mg of emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate.
Your child’s doctor will determine the right dosage of Descovy or Truvada for your child.
Some people taking Descovy or Truvada may experience mild to serious side effects.
For more information about possible side effects, see the Descovy side effects article and Truvada side effects article. 
Descovy and Truvada may cause mild side effects. The following table lists examples of mild side effects that have been reported with these drugs.
This table may not include all mild side effects of these drugs. For more information on mild side effects of the two drugs, see the Descovy prescribing information and Truvada prescribing information.
Serious side effects may also occur in people taking Descovy or Truvada. See the following table for a list of side effects that have been reported with these drugs.
To learn about your specific risk for serious side effects from Descovy or Truvada, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
* Descovy and Truvada have boxed warnings for these side effects. A boxed warning is the most serious warning from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). To learn more, see the “What are the warnings of Descovy and Truvada?” section.
For some people, Descovy or Truvada can cause an allergic reaction. But this side effect wasn’t reported in studies of Descovy or Truvada.
In general, symptoms of allergic reaction can be mild or serious.
What might help
If you have mild symptoms of an allergic reaction, such as a mild rash, call your doctor right away. They may suggest a treatment to manage your symptoms and can determine whether you should keep taking Descovy or Truvada. 
If you have symptoms of a severe allergic reaction, such as swelling or trouble breathing, call 911 or your local emergency number right away. These symptoms could be life threatening and require immediate medical care.
If your doctor confirms you’ve had a serious allergic reaction to Descovy or Truvada, they may have you switch to a different treatment.
Get answers to some frequently asked questions about Descovy and Truvada.
Not typically. Weight gain wasn’t reported as a side effect in studies of Descovy or Truvada. In fact, weight loss was a common side effect in studies of Truvada for PrEP.
A recent review of studies suggests that long-term treatment with HIV medications may lead to weight gain. However, it’s unclear if this is related to the body recovering from HIV or to a specific medication.
If you’re concerned about how Descovy or Truvada might affect your weight, talk with your doctor.
One drug isn’t necessarily safer than the other for people with kidney problems. Both Descovy and Truvada can cause new or worsened kidney problems. And doctors typically will not prescribe either drug for people with severe kidney problems.
If you have a kidney problem, talk with your doctor before starting Descovy or Truvada treatment. They can help you determine whether either medication is a safe option for you.
You may wonder whether Descovy or Truvada is effective for your condition.
Descovy and Truvada are both used to treat and help prevent HIV. Studies of Descovy and Truvada have shown that both drugs are effective for this use. 
In addition, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services includes both drugs in its treatment recommendations for HIV. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also includes both drugs in its guidelines for HIV prevention.
It’s important to note that your results from Descovy or Truvada may differ from those seen in studies. Talk with your doctor about whether one of these drugs is right for you.
If you’d like to read more about how each drug performed in studies, see the prescribing information for Descovy and Truvada.
Whether you have health insurance or not, cost may be a factor when you’re considering these drugs. Visit Optum Perks to get price estimates for Descovy and Truvada when you use coupons from the site. (Note: Optum Perks is a sister site of Healthline.) It’s important to note that Optum Perks coupons cannot be used with any insurance copays or benefits.
Keep in mind that what you’ll pay for either drug will depend on your treatment plan, your health insurance, and the pharmacy you use.
Descovy and Truvada are both brand-name drugs. Truvada also has a generic form. You’ll usually pay more for brand-name drugs than for generics. If you’re interested in taking the generic form of Truvada, talk with your doctor.
For other resources that might help you save on the price of these drugs, see the Descovy cost article and Truvada cost article.
Descovy or Truvada may not be right for you if you have certain medical conditions or other factors that affect your health. These may be referred to as warnings.
The two drugs have some of the same warnings, but they also have different ones. Some of these warnings are mentioned in the following sections. Before you start taking Descovy or Truvada, be sure to talk with your doctor to see whether these warnings apply to you.
Descovy and Truvada have boxed warnings. A boxed warning is the most serious warning from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). It alerts doctors and patients about drug effects that may be dangerous.
Risk of worsened hepatitis B: Stopping Descovy or Truvada treatment may worsen hepatitis B in people who have both HIV and the hepatitis B virus (HBV). Worsening of hepatitis B could lead to serious liver problems, including liver failure.
Your doctor will test you for HBV before starting your Descovy or Truvada treatment. If you develop hepatitis B while taking Truvada or Descovy, talk with your doctor before stopping either drug.
If they tell you it’s safe to stop Descovy or Truvada, your doctor will give you tests to check how well your liver is working. They may continue checking your liver for several months after your final dose of Descovy or Truvada.
If you have worsened hepatitis B after stopping Descovy or Truvada treatment, your doctor may prescribe a treatment for this condition.
Risk of HIV resistance: Descovy and Truvada can be used as PrEP to help prevent HIV in people at risk of contracting the virus. When used as PrEP, neither drug should be prescribed for people who have HIV.
If a person with HIV uses Descovy or Truvada as PrEP, the virus can become resistant to the drug. This means Descovy or Truvada may be less effective at treating HIV.
Due to this risk, doctors will test for HIV before prescribing Descovy or Truvada for PrEP. They’ll continue testing for HIV every 3 months during your treatment. If a positive HIV test result occurs while you’re taking either drug as PrEP, your doctor will prescribe a different medication for HIV treatment.
For more information about these warnings, talk with your doctor.
In addition to boxed warnings, Descovy and Truvada have other warnings.
Before taking Descovy or Truvada, talk with your doctor if any of the following conditions or health factors apply to you.
To learn more about these drugs, see this Descovy article and this Truvada article. 
The short answer: It’s possible, if your doctor recommends it.
Details: Both Descovy and Truvada are used to treat and help prevent HIV. It may be possible to switch from one drug to the other for these purposes. Your doctor can provide more information.
Reminder: You should not switch drugs or stop your current treatment unless your doctor recommends it.

title: How Much Does Vascepa Cost on Medicare?
content:
Vascepa is an omega-3 fatty acid also known as icosapent ethyl. Doctors prescribe it to adults with certain conditions to lower their blood triglyceride levels and help reduce the risk of heart problems.
Prescription drugs like Vascepa are generally covered by Medicare Part D, but whether your specific plan covers this drug or its generic version depends on your specific plan in your area. This is because private insurers manage Part D plans.
That said, according to Vascepa’s manufacturer’s data, the drug is covered without restrictions for more than 90% of people enrolled in Medicare Part D. If your plan covers this drug, your cost will depend on how it’s classified under your plan.
According to Optum Perks, 30 capsules of Vascepa can cost between $91 and $99 without insurance, depending on the pharmacy you get them from. Generic versions tend to cost between $21 and $44 for the same number of capsules.
However, how much you might pay out of pocket under Medicare Part D can vary depending on the tier your plan places the drug within its formulary. Tier 1 drugs tend to have the lowest copayments.
Your cost may also depend on the amount of medication your doctor prescribes. If you opt for a Medicare Advantage plan that includes prescription drug coverage, your cost will similarly depend on your specific plan. Generic versions of the drug are likely to cost less in most cases.
You have some additional options to consider for additional savings:
Learn more: Vascepa and cost.
The cost of your Medicare drug coverage can include a monthly premium and deductible that varies by plan. Some plans have no deductible. You may also have to pay copayments or coinsurance.
Enrollment in Part D is voluntary. Typically, you can choose between a Part D plan and Original Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan with prescription drug coverage.

title: Signs and Symptoms of Scleroderma on the Face
content:
Scleroderma on the face can cause symptoms that may affect your appearance, including the texture, discoloration, and elasticity of your skin. Medications, facial exercises, and dermatological procedures may help.
Scleroderma affects connective tissues like your skin, blood vessels, muscles, and tendons. It’s an autoimmune condition that occurs when your body’s immune system attacks its own cells, resulting in inflammation that triggers an overproduction of collagen and other proteins.
Collagen is a protein that provides structure, strength, and elasticity to your connective tissues. But when you produce too much collagen, it may cause tissue to thicken or harden.
Scleroderma symptoms may be localized, primarily affecting the skin and underlying tissues. It may also be systemic, affecting your skin as well as the blood vessels and tissues of major organ systems. Both types of scleroderma can cause changes to the tissues of your face.
Changes to your facial tissue from scleroderma can contribute to a variety of cosmetic and functional effects. 
As skin tightens and hardens, depending on its location, it may alter the shape or symmetry of your face. Scleroderma may also prevent you from effectively using your mouth or jaw, and it may cause wrinkles and dimpling as it pulls on sections of your skin.
How scleroderma presents on the face may vary depending on the type of scleroderma and its severity.
Localized scleroderma on the face typically develops in two patterns:
Systemic scleroderma involves more widespread areas of tissue change but may begin as patches of hardened or tightened skin, especially in cutaneous systemic sclerosis, a subtype of systemic scleroderma.
Scleroderma face symptoms primarily seen in systemic scleroderma include:
In both local and systemic scleroderma, you may also notice:
The development of calcium deposits, functional impairment, and the appearance of blood vessels are more common in forms of systemic scleroderma.
Facial scleroderma can feel differently to each person, depending on individual sensitivities, the extent of the affected area, and the severity of symptoms.
You may notice:
Scleroderma on the face can be painful. Not only can tight, hardened skin pull on sensitive areas around your eyes and mouth, but changes in circulation, like in Raynaud’s phenomenon, can heighten skin sensitivity to touch, temperature, and blood flow.
A study from 2021 notes that Raynaud’s phenomenon is one of the most commonly reported causes of pain in systemic scleroderma.
There’s no cure for scleroderma yet, but treatment may slow the condition’s progression and help you manage symptoms. Your treatment plan may be based on individual diagnosis and symptoms.
Common components in a scleroderma treatment plan include:
Hydrating facial lotions and creams help combat skin dryness and itching. A doctor may also recommend switching to gentle, fragrance-free products and using daily sun protection to help reduce irritation overall.
Topical medications can help reduce inflammation and autoimmune processes in localized areas.
For more widespread symptoms, a doctor may prescribe oral immunosuppressants, antifibrotic medications to limit collagen production, or targeted medications such as vasodilators and calcium channel blockers for Raynaud’s phenomenon.
Stretching, massage, and facial exercises may help improve function when scleroderma face symptoms affect movement in your mouth or jaw.
Laser therapy, dermabrasion, and microneedling are examples of procedures that may help improve skin texture and discoloration, though they are not indicated for everyone with scleroderma.
No treatment is available for calcinosis yet. Surgery is a rare option if the mobility of your mouth or jaw is severely limited or in severe cases of calcinosis. 
Working with a mental health professional may help you manage challenges like depression or anxiety, which are a common experience due to scleroderma’s chronic nature and effects on appearance and self-esteem.
The type of scleroderma impacts the likelihood of specific facial symptoms, but all forms can cause tight, hard areas of skin, texture changes, discoloration, the appearance of blood vessels, and feature asymmetry.

title: Fluzone Interactions: Alcohol, Medications, and Others
content:
Fluzone (influenza vaccine) has potential interactions with other medications. These interactions could affect how well the drug works or cause harmful effects.
Fluzone is used in people ages 6 months and older to help prevent influenza (flu). Specifically, it works in helping to prevent influenza types A and B.
An interaction can occur because one substance causes another substance to have a different effect than expected. Interactions also can occur if you have certain health conditions.
Keep reading to learn about Fluzone’s possible interactions. For a detailed overview of this drug, check out this in-depth Fluzone article.
Before you receive Fluzone, tell your doctor and pharmacist about any prescription, over-the-counter, or other drugs you take. Sharing this information with them may help prevent possible interactions.
Immunosuppressants are drugs that weaken the immune system. These drugs may interact with Fluzone and can make Fluzone less effective. Examples of immunosuppressants are:
For more information about interactions with immunosuppressants, see the “Drug interactions explained” section.
Keep in mind that other drugs also might interact with Fluzone. If you have questions about drug interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
To learn whether Fluzone interacts with herbs, vitamins, or supplements, see the “Are there other interactions with Fluzone?” section.
Certain health conditions or other factors could raise your risk of harm if you receive Fluzone. In such cases, your doctor may not prescribe Fluzone for you. These are known as contraindications. A contraindication of Fluzone is:
Before you receive Fluzone, talk with your doctor if the factor above applies to you. Your doctor can determine whether Fluzone is safe for you.
Fluzone isn’t known to interact with alcohol. But both Fluzone and alcohol can cause headache. So consuming alcohol may worsen a headache caused by receiving Fluzone.
If you have questions about consuming alcohol after receiving your Fluzone vaccine, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Learn more about certain drug interactions that can occur with Fluzone.
Fluzone can interact with immunosuppressant drugs. These are used to treat various health conditions, including multiple sclerosis and Crohn’s disease. Immunosuppressants weaken (suppress) your immune system, which is a network of body parts that defends against disease and infection.
Your body needs to develop a strong immune response to the flu vaccine. This helps prevent you from getting flu later. But having a weakened immune system may not allow your body to build the needed immune response to the influenza (flu) vaccine. So Fluzone may not work as well in helping prevent flu in people who also take immunosuppressants.
Some immunosuppressants that may interact with Fluzone are:
Be sure to tell your doctor about all the medications you take before receiving Fluzone. This includes prescriptions, over-the-counter medications, and supplements. Typically, it’s recommended that you receive any vaccines needed, including Fluzone, a couple of weeks before starting immunosuppressants if possible. 
If you’ve already started immunosuppressants, your doctor can recommend the best time to receive Fluzone. Based on your medical condition and the immunosuppressants you take, it’s possible they may recommend a different flu vaccine instead of Fluzone.
If you have questions about receiving Fluzone while taking immunosuppressants, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Fluzone may have other interactions. They could occur with supplements, foods, vaccines, or even lab tests.
Before you receive Fluzone, talk with your doctor and pharmacist about any herbs, vitamins, or supplements you take. Sharing this information with them may help you avoid possible interactions.
If you have questions about interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Fluzone currently has no reports of interacting with herbs. But this doesn’t mean that interactions with herbs won’t be recognized in the future. For this reason, it’s important to check with your doctor or pharmacist if you use any herbs before receiving Fluzone.
Fluzone currently has no reports of interacting with vitamins. But this doesn’t mean that interactions with vitamins won’t be recognized in the future. For this reason, it’s important to check with your doctor or pharmacist if you take any vitamins before receiving Fluzone.
Fluzone currently has no reports of interacting with food. If you have questions about certain foods interacting with Fluzone, talk with your doctor.
Currently, Fluzone has no reports of interacting with other vaccines. If you have questions about getting certain vaccines before or after Fluzone, talk with your doctor.
Fluzone currently has no reports of interacting with lab tests. If you have questions about whether certain lab tests interact with Fluzone, talk with the healthcare professional ordering the test.
Fluzone currently has no reports of interacting with cannabis (commonly called marijuana) or cannabis products such as cannabidiol (CBD). But before receiving Fluzone, let your doctor know if you use cannabis products.
Note: Cannabis is illegal at a federal level but is legal in many states to varying degrees.
Certain medical conditions or other health factors may raise the risk of interactions with Fluzone. Before receiving Fluzone, talk with your doctor about your health history. They’ll determine whether Fluzone is right for you.
Health conditions or other factors that might interact with Fluzone include:
Guillain-Barré syndrome: The influenza (flu) vaccine from 1976 was reported to increase the risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). This is a rare condition that affects your nerves and results in muscle weakness and numbness. It’s not clear whether other flu vaccines, including Fluzone, cause GBS. Be sure to tell your doctor or pharmacist if you’ve ever had GBS within 6 weeks of receiving any flu vaccine. They’ll help determine whether Fluzone is safe for you.
Weakened immune system: Fluzone may not work as well in people who have a weakened immune system. They are typically immunocompromised and unable to fight infection as well as usual. This can be caused by autoimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis. It also can be caused by immunosuppressant drugs that reduce your immune system’s strength. Be sure to tell your doctor or pharmacist if you have any immune system problems before receiving Fluzone.
Age: Fluzone is not recommended for use in children younger than age 6 months. Studies also report a lower immune response to the influenza (flu) vaccine in older adults (ages 65 years and older). A strong immune response to the flu vaccine is important in helping prevent flu later. So in older adults, Fluzone may not work as well in helping prevent flu. Let your doctor or your child’s doctor know if either factor applies to you or your child. They can discuss other options for preventing flu.
Pregnancy: Too little information is available to determine whether Fluzone is safe to receive during pregnancy. Animal studies showed no harmful effects when Fluzone Quadrivalent, a vaccine similar to Fluzone, was given to pregnant rabbits. It’s important to know that animal studies don’t always predict what may happen in humans.
But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) considers Fluzone and certain other influenza (flu) vaccines safe during pregnancy. Typically, it’s recommended for pregnant people to receive the flu vaccine by injection (shot) but not by nasal spray. This is because the flu vaccine nasal spray, including FluMist, may increase the risk of infection if you’re pregnant.
The CDC recommends that pregnant people receive the flu vaccine, such as Fluzone, yearly. It considers the protective benefits greater than the potential harm. Talk with your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions about receiving a flu vaccine during pregnancy. 
If you do receive Fluzone while pregnant, consider enrolling in the drug’s pregnancy registry. This registry collects details about pregnancy issues reported with Fluzone. To learn more, call 800-822-2463 or talk with your doctor.
Breastfeeding: It’s not known whether Fluzone passes into breast milk. And information also isn’t known about how the drug affects milk production or side effects it might cause in a child who is breastfed.
But the CDC considers influenza (flu) vaccines, including Fluzone, safe for people who breastfeed. Also, the number of influenza antibodies in breast milk increases after flu vaccination. Antibodies are proteins that help your body fight infection. So this leads to additional protection from flu for a child who’s breastfed.
 Talk with your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions about breastfeeding and receiving Fluzone. 
Allergic reaction: If you’ve ever had an allergic reaction to Fluzone or any of its ingredients, your doctor likely will not prescribe Fluzone. This includes having an egg allergy, as Fluzone contains eggs. Receiving this vaccine could cause another allergic reaction. You can ask your doctor about other vaccines that may be better options for you.
Taking certain steps can help you avoid interactions with Fluzone. Before starting treatment, talk with your doctor and pharmacist. Things to discuss with them include:
It’s also important to understand Fluzone’s label and other paperwork that may come with the drug. Colored stickers that describe interactions may be on the label. The paperwork, sometimes called the patient package insert or medication guide, may have other details about interactions. 
If you did not get paperwork with Fluzone, ask your pharmacist to print a copy for you. If you have difficulty reading or understanding this information, your doctor or pharmacist can help.
Receiving Fluzone exactly as prescribed also can help prevent interactions.

title: Travatan Z Dosing Schedule
content:
The typical Travatan Z (travoprost) dosage is one drop in the affected eye once daily. Specific dosages may vary depending on factors like your individual symptoms and other medications you may be taking. It’s important to follow the Travatan Z dosage your doctor prescribes.
Travatan Z (travoprost) is a prescription drug used to lower eye pressure in people with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension. The drug comes as an eyedrop solution. It’s usually given once per day.
This article describes the dosage of Travatan Z, its strength, and how to use it. To learn more about Travatan Z, including its side effects and uses, read this in-depth Travatan Z article.
Your doctor will likely start you on a low dosage and adjust it over time to reach the right amount for you. They’ll ultimately prescribe the smallest dosage that provides the desired effect.
The following information describes dosages commonly used or recommended for Travatan Z. But be sure to follow the dosage your doctor prescribes for you. They’ll determine the best dosage to fit your needs. In some cases, doctors may adjust your dosage from those mentioned here.
Travatan Z is available as an eyedrop solution.
Travatan Z comes in one strength of 0.004%, which is 0.04 milligrams (mg) of travoprost per milliliter (mL) of solution (0.04 mg/mL).
Travatan Z is approved to lower eye pressure in adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension. The typical Travatan Z dosage for adults is one drop in the affected eye once daily, in the evening.
Always follow your doctor’s instructions. Notify them if you experience any side effects that may prevent you from taking your medication.
Travatan Z is used to lower eye pressure in children ages 16 years and older with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension. The dosage for children is the same as for adults: one drop in the affected eye once daily, in the evening.
For more information about Travatan Z’s dosage for children, talk with your child’s doctor or a pharmacist.
Your doctor or pharmacist will give you specific instructions for using Travatan Z. Typically, recommendations for using Travatan Z include:
Travatan Z is usually a long-term treatment. If you and your doctor determine that it’s safe and effective for your condition, you’ll likely use it long term once you reach your maintenance dose.
Do not use more Travatan Z than your doctor prescribes, as this can lead to harmful effects.
Call your doctor right away if you think you’ve used too much Travatan Z. You can also call 800-222-1222 to reach America’s Poison Centers or use its online resource. But if you have severe symptoms, immediately call 911 (or your local emergency number) or go to the nearest emergency room.

title: NovoSeven RT Interactions: Alcohol, Medications, and Others
content:
NovoSeven RT is a prescription drug that’s used to help prevent and treat bleeding episodes in certain situations. This drug can interact with other medications. For example, NovoSeven RT can interact with Autoplex and Corifact.
An interaction can occur because one substance causes another substance to have a different effect than expected. Interactions can also occur if you have certain health conditions.
The active ingredient in NovoSeven RT is coagulation factor VIIa (recombinant). Keep reading to learn about NovoSeven RT’s possible interactions. For a detailed overview of this drug, check out this in-depth NovoSeven RT article.
Before you start using NovoSeven RT, tell your doctor and pharmacist about any prescription, over-the-counter, or other drugs you take. Sharing this information with them may help prevent possible interactions. To learn whether NovoSeven RT interacts with herbs, vitamins, or supplements, see the “Are there other interactions with NovoSeven RT?” section.
If you have questions about drug interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
The table below lists drugs that may interact with NovoSeven RT. Keep in mind that this table does not include all drugs that may interact with NovoSeven RT. For more information about some of these interactions, see the “Drug interactions explained” section.
NovoSeven RT is not known to interact with alcohol. However, consuming alcohol can make it harder for your blood to form clots. This raises your risk of bleeding. If you have a bleeding disorder, your doctor may advise you to avoid alcohol or limit the amount you drink.
If you have other questions about drinking alcohol while using NovoSeven RT, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Learn more about certain drug interactions that can occur with NovoSeven RT.
NovoSeven RT can interact with aPCC, which is used to treat certain blood clotting disorders.
Examples of aPCC medications include anti-inhibitor coagulant complex, available as brand names, such as Feiba and Autoplex.
NovoSeven RT and aPCC can both cause blood clots. So, taking these drugs together can raise your risk of this side effect.
Both NovoSeven RT and aPCC have a boxed warning about the risk of blood clots. See the “Boxed warning” section at the top of the article to learn more about NovoSeven RT and this risk.
Due to the risk of blood clots, doctors do not prescribe NovoSeven RT and aPCC together. They’ll recommend using one or the other to manage bleeding, but they won’t prescribe both at the same time.
NovoSeven RT can interact with coagulation factor XIII, which is used to treat certain blood clotting disorders.
Examples of coagulation factor XIII medications include Corifact and Tretten.
Coagulation factor XIII and NovoSeven RT can both cause blood clots. So, using these drugs together can raise your risk of this side effect.
NovoSeven RT has a boxed warning about the risk of blood clots. See the “Boxed warning” section to learn more.
Because of the risk of blood clots, doctors typically won’t prescribe NovoSeven RT and coagulation factor XIII together. Instead, they’ll prescribe one medication or the other to manage bleeding specific to your condition.
NovoSeven RT may have other interactions. They could occur with supplements, foods, vaccines, or even lab tests. See below for details. Note that this information does not include all other possible interactions with NovoSeven RT.
Before you start using NovoSeven RT, talk with your doctor and pharmacist about any herbs, vitamins, or supplements you take. Sharing this information with them may help you avoid possible interactions.
If you have questions about interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
There are currently no reports of NovoSeven RT interacting with herbs. But this doesn’t mean that interactions with herbs won’t be recognized in the future.
For this reason, it’s still important to check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any of these products while using NovoSeven RT.
There are currently no reports of NovoSeven RT interacting with vitamins. But this doesn’t mean that such interactions won’t be recognized in the future.
For this reason, it’s still important to check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any of these products while using NovoSeven RT.
There are currently no reports of NovoSeven RT interacting with food. If you have questions about eating certain foods during your treatment with NovoSeven RT, talk with your doctor.
There are currently no reports of NovoSeven RT interacting with vaccines or lab tests. If you have questions about receiving certain vaccines or having lab tests done during your NovoSeven RT treatment, talk with your doctor.
There are currently no reports of NovoSeven RT interacting with cannabis (commonly called marijuana) or cannabis products such as cannabidiol (CBD). But as with any drug or supplement, talk with your doctor before using cannabis with NovoSeven RT.
Note: Cannabis is illegal at a federal level but is legal in many states to varying degrees.
Certain medical conditions or other health factors may raise the risk of interactions with NovoSeven RT. Before using NovoSeven RT, talk with your doctor about your health history. They’ll determine whether NovoSeven RT is right for you.
Health conditions or other factors that might interact with NovoSeven RT include:
Heart or vascular (blood vessel) disease: If you have heart or vascular disease, you may already have an increased risk of developing blood clots. NovoSeven RT works by helping your blood form clots to stop bleeding. Because of this, using NovoSeven RT if you have one of these conditions can further raise your risk of dangerous blood clots. 
NovoSeven RT has a boxed warning about the risk of blood clots as a side effect. (See the “Boxed warning” section at the top of the article to learn more.)
Pregnancy: It’s not known whether NovoSeven RT is safe to use during pregnancy. If you’re pregnant or planning a pregnancy, talk with your doctor before using NovoSeven RT. 
Breastfeeding: It’s not known whether it’s safe to use NovoSeven RT while breastfeeding. It isn’t known whether the drug passes into breast milk or if it may cause side effects in a child who’s breastfed. If you’re breastfeeding or planning to do so, talk with your doctor about your options.
Allergic reaction, including allergy to bovine (cattle), hamster, or mouse proteins: If you’ve had an allergic reaction to NovoSeven RT or any of its ingredients, your doctor will likely not prescribe NovoSeven RT for you. They also likely won’t prescribe NovoSeven RT if you have an allergy to bovine, hamster, or mouse proteins, as using NovoSeven RT could trigger an allergic reaction. You can ask your doctor about other treatments that may be better choices for you.
Taking certain steps can help avoid interactions with NovoSeven R. It will also help your doctor prescribe the safest and most effective treatment plan for you. Before starting treatment, talk with your doctor or pharmacist about the following:
It’s also important to understand NovoSeven RT’s label and other paperwork that may come with the drug. Colored stickers that describe interactions may be on the label. And the paperwork (sometimes called the patient package insert or medication guide) may have other details about interactions. (If you did not get paperwork with NovoSeven RT, ask your pharmacist to print a copy for you.)
If you have difficulty reading or understanding this information, your doctor or pharmacist can help.
Using NovoSeven RT exactly as prescribed can also help prevent interactions.

title: A 2025 Review of PlushCare: Costs, Services, and More
content:
PlushCare is a membership-based telehealth platform. If you’re wondering whether the membership is worth it, take a look at our PlushCare review as we dive into what it has to offer.
PlushCare is a telehealth platform that offers a range of healthcare services, including mental health, prescription refills, and weight loss programs. In this review, we break down what the service has to offer and the cost of it all. Plus, we have a tester share their experiences with PlushCare’s platform.
Like most telehealth platforms, PlushCare offers preventive care and urgent care for people 3 years and up.
PlushCare identifies urgent care as nonemergency health concerns like colds or flu, tooth infections, UTI treatments, blood tests, and more.
During these visits, a healthcare professional assesses your symptoms and provides the best course of action for you, whether it’s prescription medication, referrals for testing, over-the-counter medications, etc. You can also schedule a follow-up with this healthcare professional after your treatment course to make sure your recovery is on track and you’re feeling better.
PlushCare also offers preventive healthcare services like annual virtual wellness checkups. While they won’t be able to conduct physical exams, your healthcare professional can provide referrals as necessary for in-person exams, blood tests, and anything else you may need.
PlushCare also offers services and can help develop treatment plans for smoking cessation, high blood pressure, allergies, diabetes, back pain, and more.
PlushCare physicians can help you determine your hair loss diagnosis. After an online consultation, your treatment plan can include any of the following:
PlushCare touts a straightforward three-step plan for getting hormone therapy:
Hormone therapy may have side effects and risks based on your medical history, so it’s important to meet with your healthcare professional and be transparent about your health history. After you discuss your symptoms with your healthcare professional, they will help you decide on the best treatment plan for you.
PlushCare offers a multitude of sexual health services for all genders. For those services that do require in-person consultations or tests, your healthcare professional will recommend STI testing centers to you based on your location.
STI testing and treatments
Birth control
PrEP & PEP treatment
HIV/AIDS treatment
PlushCare offers seven types of erectile dysfunction (ED) medications, including:
ED medications are known for being very expensive, especially the brand names. PlushCare offers both the brand and the generic versions of Viagra, Cialis, and Levitra. PlushCare’s membership includes a prescription discount card that can help you save up to 80% on medications.
When you meet with your healthcare professional, you will go over your health history with them, including any heart conditions, to make sure you’re eligible for ED medications. If they believe you can safely take the medication, your healthcare professional will send a prescription to your local pharmacy.
PlushCare offers doctor-led weight loss programs. You’re paired with a health coach, who you can communicate with via a smartphone app. PlushCare offers Ozempic and other weight loss prescription medications to those who are deemed eligible.
When you sign up for PlushCare’s membership and weight loss program, you’ll have access to:
Based on your initial visit and lab work, your healthcare professional will determine whether Ozempic or another weight loss medication is appropriate.
Total turnaround time from your initial visit to your prescription being processed is typically 7 to 14 business days. Once ready, prescriptions are sent to your local pharmacy.
PlushCare accepts most major insurance providers, but coverage of GLP-1 medications isn’t guaranteed.
PlushCare offers online therapy to help treat depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and more.
After you fill out a questionnaire, PlushCare will give you a list of therapist to choose from. From there, you can schedule an appointment and begin talk therapy.
Note that the price for therapy is $169 per session without insurance, compared with $129 without insurance for other telehealth services PlushCare offers.
Psychiatrists are not available online at PlushCare. If you and your therapist decide medication is something that could benefit your treatment, they will refer you to a medication management professional at PlushCare who can prescribe the medication, or to an online psychiatrist.
Our tester, Parisa Syed, set up a sample profile to go through the process of setting up an account with PlushCare.
Syed’s initial impression of the home page was that it was calming, clean, and uncluttered. It’s made clear right away that PlushCare accepts insurance. There are appointments at the top and throughout the home page to get an account started.
The home page is pretty straightforward, but Syed mentions the tabs are pretty general. 
“There’s no dropdown for the types of online prescriptions they offer, which can feel a bit intimidating for some, especially when you’re feeling hesitant about going online for a prescription,” she said. 
PlushCare also has a list of some health conditions it treats in the middle of the home page after a bit of scrolling.
The pricing is pretty transparent throughout the platform. For the medications themselves, it was not very clear for any condition, though. 
“The closest they got to product pricing was in the middle of each condition page, where they have the FAQ ‘how much does this medication typically cost?'” Syed said.
There are three questionnaire interfaces you come across when creating a profile. If you go from a general health page or online prescription page, you are taken straight to whether you’ll be paying with or without insurance.
From there, you either select your insurance or select the state you’re in. Then, you’re given a list of doctors in your state. No filters or anything, just their names, their profile, picture, and reviews. Once you choose a doctor, you can then choose a time that works for you and create a profile.
If you go to PlushCare’s mental health or weight loss tabs, you’re given different screens.
The mental health screen asks whether you’re wanting to meet with a therapist or talk with a physician. Then, it asks if the appointment is for you or someone else. It asks for your state, and then will show you available therapists in your area. Once you find a therapist you like, you can select a time that works for you, and then create your profile.
For weight loss, you click the “Next” button a few times before you get to the questionnaire. The first question is about your medical history. There’s a progress bar at the top of the page so you can see how much you have left to answer. 
Afterward, you’re asked whether you’ll be paying with or without insurance, and then about the state you’re in so you can choose your healthcare professional.
After you’ve created your profile and selected your appointment date, you’re brought to the confirmation page where you can double-check all of your information and see the total cost of your appointment. 
Here, PlushCare will remind you of the membership fee, which will be charged to your payment method after your 30-day free trial.
After your appointment, if your healthcare professional has prescribed any medication, it will be sent to the pharmacy of your choice.
PlushCare has board certified doctors who can prescribe medications for mental health, general health, sexual health, and more.
To get a prescription, or a refill of a previous prescription, PlushCare requires an online evaluation before the prescription is filled. The appointment should take about 15 minutes. Afterward, the prescription is sent to a local pharmacy of your choice, where you can pick it up usually on the same day.
PlushCare, like most telehealth and online therapy platforms, does not prescribe controlled substances like Adderall, morphine, Xanax, Ambien, and more.
Included in PlushCare’s membership is its discount card. This card can help you save up to 80% on eligible prescriptions at more than 50,000 pharmacies nationwide.
PlushCare does charge a membership fee for anyone who uses its services. There are two payment options: You can pay $19.99 per month or $99 per year.
Both PlushCare memberships include: 
PlushCare does offer a free 30-day trial when you first sign up. You can cancel at any time if you feel like this platform isn’t for you.
If you decide not to pay the subscription fee, PlushCare says you need to call to schedule appointments with them. It mentions its membership covers costs that add value to its platform, including its services, technology, wellness offerings, ongoing support, and more.
An additional perk of the PlushCare membership is the family plan. If you do subscribe to PlushCare, annually or monthly, you can share your membership with up to five adult family members at no extra cost.
Each party is responsible for their own visit and copay fees, and they can create their own, private PlushCare profiles.
The cost of most of PlushCare’s services are the same. 
PlushCare accepts a majority of insurance plans, so the only payments users have to make are the copay and the membership fee. Insurance does not cover this fee.
If you choose to pay out of pocket, you must pay the membership fee and $129 per appointment. If you’re using PlushCare’s online therapy services, you must pay $169 per appointment and the membership fee.
At this time, PlushCare does not accept Medicare or Medicaid, but it does accept health savings account (HSA) and flexible spending account (FSA) payments.
PlushCare also has a refund policy. It offers a full refund for the appointment (not including the membership fee). It does not accept returns of any prescriptions.
At the time of publishing, PlushCare has a B rating from the Better Business Bureau (BBB). There are 369 complaints on its BBB page, and it has a 2.09 out of 5-star customer rating. 
Keep in mind, though, that sites like BBB are meant so users can share their complaints on a public platform so their issues can be resolved.
On the Google Play store, PlushCare has 4.7 stars based on 7,130 reviews. Most of the reviews are positive, citing they loved the care they received from their doctor and that wait times were very low. 
However, some reviewers mention the app has some technical issues and bugs that need to be resolved. Some also mention they were still charged a membership fee after they canceled their auto-renewal.
PlushCare has a 4.9-star rating based on 123,800 reviews on the Apple Store. Reviews are mostly positive, but some users explained they had issues with getting ahold of customer service or support. They also reported technical issues while connecting to a session.
Because PlushCare’s membership offers a variety of support tools, PlushCare may be best for people who need ongoing care with regular check-ins. Its weight loss programs, for example, have ongoing support even after reaching the desired goals.
PlushCare may also be beneficial for people with insurance, since the copay is likely cheaper than the service without insurance. People who also need access to medication refills without going to the doctor in person could see PlushCare as an alternative option. The prescription drug discount card that PlushCare offers could be a huge help in this area.
For any urgent care needs, like a flu or cold, or just a checkup, PlushCare may be beneficial and convenient since you can do it in the comfort of your home instead of heading to the doctor’s office.
While PlushCare does have good services, it cannot help in the case of emergencies. If you or someone you know needs immediate assistance, call your local emergency services or dial 911.
For folks who need controlled substances, like Adderall or Ambien, it’s better to go in person for these checkups so your healthcare professional can monitor your treatment and adjust the dosage as necessary.
PlushCare does offer care to anyone over 3 years old when it comes to general health, but for online therapy, users need to be at least 18 years old for treatment. There are other online therapy options for teens, though, and some also take insurance.
PlushCare is a subscription-based telehealth platform that can assist with a variety of services. For people who don’t need immediate assistance but need ongoing assistance or convenient care, PlushCare could be for you.

title: Does Hyperthyroidism Lead to Heart Disease?
content:
Hyperthyroidism may affect the function of multiple organs throughout the body, including the heart. Rapid heart rate, irregular heart rhythm, and widened pulse pressure are potential heart complications related to hyperthyroidism.
Hyperthyroidism or an overactive thyroid refers to the thyroid gland producing more hormones than the body requires or needs. High levels of thyroid hormones may lead to significant changes in your heart function. 
Thyroid hormones, particularly thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), have direct and indirect regulatory effects on your heart cells and vascular tissues.
Some cases of untreated severe hyperthyroidism may increase the risk of heart disease and heart failure by keeping your heart in a high-output state that stretches and weakens the muscle over time. In some instances, untreated hyperthyroidism may be life threatening.
Thyroid hormones affect every organ in your body. When it comes to your heart, these hormones directly regulate the genetic expression and chemical sensitivity of the heart cells and vascular tissues. They also regulate metabolic processes throughout the body that influence the overall demand on your heart.
When elevated thyroid hormones cause symptoms, this is known as thyrotoxicosis, a clinical state of high levels of circulating thyroid hormones.
Thyrotoxicosis promotes changes in the body that affect heart health, such as:
Over time, hyperthyroidism-related heart symptoms and complications may include:
Hyperthyroidism doesn’t always cause dramatic or alarming heart symptoms, particularly if treated. But common warning signs may include:
Untreated hyperthyroidism may lead to thyroid storm in rare cases. This is a medical emergency, and symptoms often include:
Not everyone with hyperthyroidism experiences heart disease. Hyperthyroidism occurs across a spectrum of severity, and people with mild or well-managed hyperthyroidism, for example, may not develop any long-term cardiac effects.
Your age, overall heart health, type of hyperthyroidism, and underlying medical conditions can all affect your individual risk.
Untreated hyperthyroidism is one potential cause of thyrotoxicosis. When thyroid hormones remain elevated without management, any heart symptoms you’re experiencing can worsen, and some may become irreversible or life threatening.
Approximately 1% of people experiencing thyrotoxicosis progress to thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy, a severe form of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) in which the heart muscle (primarily the left ventricle) stretches, becomes thinner and weakens.
DCM is often progressive and prevents your heart from effectively circulating blood. It can create body-wide challenges with blood clots, fluid retention, and organ failure. For many people, it can lead to life threatening arrhythmias by impairing the heart’s ability to contract.
Hyperthyroidism treatment, when indicated, helps reduce the chance of related heart conditions. Treating hyperthyroidism may also reverse some cardiac symptoms before damage is permanent.
Hyperthyroidism can be treated with medications that help regulate thyroid hormone production. Some people with Graves’ disease, an autoimmune condition that causes hyperthyroidism, receive radioactive iodine (RAI) treatment or surgery to remove part or all of the thyroid gland.
In addition to medical management of hyperthyroidism, heart-healthy lifestyle changes may help and include:
Elevated thyroid hormone levels in hyperthyroidism can affect heart health in various ways. Blood pressure changes, irregular heart rhythm, rapid heart rate, and increased risk for blood clots are a few examples of possible heart effects of hyperthyroidism.
If left untreated, hyperthyroidism could lead to irreversible damage to your heart and might become life threatening. Depending on your specific case, managing hyperthyroidism may involve medications, RAI, or surgery. These also reduce the chance of heart-related complications.

title: Dosage Details for Xadago (Safinamide)
content:
The usual Xadago (safinamide) dosage for Parkinson’s disease is one 50-mg or 100-mg oral tablet taken once daily. Specific dosages may vary depending on various factors. Always take the Xadago dosage your doctor prescribes.
Xadago is a prescription drug used to help treat Parkinson’s disease in adults. It’s prescribed for use during “off periods.” This term refers to the sudden return of Parkinson’s disease symptoms between doses of carbidopa/levodopa (another drug often prescribed for Parkinson’s disease). Xadago helps decrease the symptoms and duration of off periods.
Xadago belongs to a group of drugs called monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B) inhibitors. It contains the active ingredient safinamide.
This article describes the dosages of Xadago, as well as its strengths and how to take it. To learn more about this medication, including its side effects and uses, read this in-depth Xadago article.
Your doctor will likely start you on a low dose of Xadago and adjust it over time to reach the right amount for you. They’ll ultimately prescribe the smallest dose that provides the desired effect.
The following information describes Xadago dosages that are commonly used or recommended. But be sure to take the dosage your doctor prescribes. They’ll determine the best dosage to fit your needs — which, in some cases, may be different than what’s shown here.
Xadago comes as an oral tablet.
Xadago is available in two strengths: 50 milligrams (mg) and 100 mg.
The typical starting dosage of Xadago for adults with Parkinson’s disease is one 50-mg tablet per day. If, after 2 weeks, you aren’t experiencing bothersome side effects, your doctor may recommend increasing your dosage to 100 mg per day. This is the maximum recommended dosage of Xadago.
Always follow your doctor’s instructions. Notify them if you experience any side effects that may prevent you from taking your medication.
Here are some typical recommendations for taking Xadago. Your doctor or pharmacist will give you specific instructions for taking this drug.
You should swallow Xadago tablets whole. Do not cut, crush, chew, or dissolve them. If you have trouble swallowing tablets, check out these tips to help swallow pills, or talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
You can take Xadago with or without food, but try to take it around the same time each day. This helps keep a steady level of the drug in your system, which helps it to work effectively. 
Xadago is usually a long-term treatment. If you and your doctor determine that it’s safe and effective for your condition, you’ll likely take it long term once you’ve reached your maintenance dose.
Do not take more Xadago than your doctor prescribes, as this could potentially lead to harmful effects.
Call your doctor right away if you think you’ve taken too much Xadago. You can also call 800-222-1222 to reach America’s Poison Centers or use its online resource. But if you have severe symptoms, immediately call 911 (or your local emergency number) or go to the nearest emergency room.

title: 6 Strategies to Help You Stay Social with Ulcerative Colitis
content:
When you have ulcerative colitis (UC), planning ahead can make it easier to socialize and stay connected with friends and family. 
UC is a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Symptoms include abdominal pain, bowel frequency and urgency, and rectal bleeding. 
Unpredictable and exhausting symptoms can make it challenging to stay social. It might feel easier to cancel your plans, but staying connected with others is good for your health. People with IBD have higher rates of anxiety and depression. A lack of social connections can make this worse.
There are times when staying home is an important part of taking care of yourself. Other times, being social can boost your physical and mental health.
Here’s how to make it work.
Dr. Amber Cohen is a clinical psychologist and CEO of The Cohen Clinic. The Cohen Clinic is an Ontario-based holistic therapy practice focused on integrating the mind-body connection to promote mental wellness.
“Living with ulcerative colitis can make it difficult to stay social due to the unpredictable nature of the condition,” explained Cohen. “Symptoms like frequent bathroom urgency, abdominal pain, fatigue, and bloating can create anxiety and embarrassment, making social plans feel stressful or overwhelming.”
Cohen validated how several things can make socializing feel complicated. “Individuals may worry about finding restroom access, managing symptoms in public, or having to cancel plans at the last minute, leading them to avoid social interactions altogether,” she said. “Additionally, the emotional toll of living with a chronic illness, such as low energy or feelings of being different, can further reduce motivation to engage socially.”
Being social might feel like the last thing you want to do, but there are health benefits to doing so.
“Maintaining social connections is important for individuals with ulcerative colitis or other chronic conditions,” explained Cohen. “Chronic illnesses have so many nuanced difficulties to contend with, which can leave people feeling very alone with their unique challenges.”
Isolation and loneliness are common in people with UC. A 2024 study of 218 people with IBD showed that over half reported loneliness and 72% were socially isolated. This can have many effects on health. People who experience social isolation and loneliness are more likely to develop depression, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease.
“Isolation can significantly impact [your] health,” said Cohen. “It often leads to heightened levels of anxiety, depression, and feelings of loneliness, which can worsen overall emotional well-being.”
Isolation can also affect your physical health. “[It’s] associated with elevated stress levels, disrupted sleep, and a weakened immune system,” said Cohen.
We all need community. Researchers have found a link between a lack of social connections and a lower quality of life in people with IBD.
“The lack of social connection can make it harder to cope effectively, highlighting the importance of human connection to overall health,” said Cohen. “Social interactions encourage positive health behaviors and coping strategies, contributing to improved overall health outcomes.”
It may feel like too much work to gather with others. There are things you can do to make it a little more manageable. Here are things to consider, whether you’re meeting with a group or team or joining friends for a meal.
Make sure to scope out where the bathrooms are. Knowing that bathrooms are available, unlocked, and clean can put your mind at ease. Bathroom access can also be a factor in deciding where to go. Call ahead if you’re not sure about the bathroom situation.
You might consider keeping a card that says you have a medical condition and may need urgent bathroom access. This can allow you to use a bathroom when no public one is available. 
The Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation has a mobile app that helps you find available public restrooms in your area.
It’s always smart to have backup supplies. This can be comforting if you’re worried about managing unpredictable symptoms.
Keep flushable wipes, toilet paper, any medications you may need, and extra underwear and pants with you. Bring disposable zipper storage bags to hold anything that needs cleaning.
While it’s always your decision to disclose your health history, there are benefits to having loved ones who know what is going on with your condition. 
“Being open with trusted friends or family about your condition can reduce stress and help them offer support,” recommended Cohen. “Emotional support from friends, family, or support groups provides a sense of belonging and understanding, enhancing mental well-being.”
People who care about you will want to know how to support you and what they can do to help make socializing more accessible. They will understand if you need to cancel or modify your plans to make it work for you.
You won’t always have control over the details of social gatherings. If you do, great. Otherwise, you’ll need to figure out if you can make it work for you.
“Planning ahead is key,” said Cohen. “Choose locations with accessible restrooms and bring along items that provide comfort, like extra supplies or snacks. This can help ease anxiety.”
Remember that you don’t have to attend everything. Don’t feel bad about skipping things that aren’t a good fit. Save your energy to attend the events that matter to you.
Cohen also reminded folks that there are different ways to stay connected. “If in-person plans currently feel overwhelming, start small with shorter outings close to home or one-on-one meetups. This can make socializing feel more manageable. You can build on these successes to larger social goals.”
She’s also a believer in the power of peer support. “Joining support groups, whether online or in-person can provide understanding and connection [for those with UC],” said Cohen. “This is a reminder that you’re not alone in this experience.”
Consider hosting gatherings at your place. This way, you can be comfortable in your own space, plus you can decide the activities and dress code. Hosting doesn’t mean you have to do all the work. Ask guests to bring food, games, or activities or if they can help with some of the prep work.
If hosting isn’t an option for you, ask a good friend or family member if they can host so you’ll still be in a familiar space.
If you’re not feeling great but want to make an appearance, remember that you can just do a short visit. If you feel comfortable, you can give the host a heads-up of your plan. Then, you can leave quietly when you’re ready.
Joining a club can be a great way to get out and meet new people or learn new things. Think about the types of groups you’re interested in and then find out more details. 
Are meetups in a place with bathrooms nearby? Are you likely to still be able to attend even if you’re feeling worn down? Some activities might not be a good fit when you’re experiencing pain or exhaustion. 
You can also consider virtual options such as painting classes, learning a new language, or attending a book club. Virtual groups can allow you to connect with others from the comfort of your home.
Symptoms of UC can make it hard to socialize. You may feel like avoiding social gatherings, but staying connected is good for your health.

The COVID-19 vaccine helps prevent severe illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19.
You may experience mild side effects from the vaccine. Whether or not you’ve received a COVID-19 vaccine in the past, it’s best to go into your appointment knowing what to expect.

title: Should You Take Strattera at Night?
content:
Strattera is a prescription drug used to treat ADHD. It is usually taken once per day in the morning, but it can be taken twice per day (once in the morning and once in the evening).
Strattera (atomoxetine) is used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults and children ages 6 years and older.
It comes as an oral capsule. The typical dosing schedule for Strattera is once per day in the morning. Learn more about whether there are benefits to taking Strattera at night and when the drug reaches peak levels in your body.
Strattera’s prescribing information recommends taking the dose in the morning if you have a daily dosing schedule. If the dose is divided into twice-per-day dosing, then one dose should be taken in the morning and another in the late afternoon or early evening.
A 2009 trial that compared taking doses of Strattera in the morning versus the evening found that taking the drug at either time decreased ADHD symptoms. Morning dosing was found to be more effective in certain ways, but people could tolerate evening dosing better.
Taking Strattera at night might help you better manage the side effects of the drug. Strattera can cause sedation or sleepiness, so taking the drug in the evening could result in fewer noticeable side effects.
Strattera is not a stimulant medication like some other ADHD medications, such as amphetamine/dextroamphetamine (Adderall, Adderall XR). Stimulant medications can increase alertness and energy levels, which can make it difficult to sleep at night. 
That’s why Strattera can be taken at night if that works better for you.
That said, it may take some time to figure out what dosing schedule works best for you. It may also depend on how Strattera makes you feel. But taking Strattera at night can be helpful in certain situations.
Talk with your doctor or pharmacist if you have questions about your dosing schedule for Strattera.
Strattera starts working right away after you take your first dose. Strattera’s peak time, or maximum concentration in the body, is 1 to 2 hours after the dose. Even though Strattera starts working right away, it may take 2 to 4 weeks for you to notice a decrease in ADHD symptoms.
The half-life of Strattera is 5 hours. It typically takes about 4 to 5 half-lives for a drug to be cleared from your body. This means a dose of Strattera will stay in your system for about 20 to 25 hours. So the drug shouldn’t wear off during the day, even if you take your dose of Strattera at night.
If you have questions about how long it takes for Strattera to work, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Strattera is a prescription drug used to treat ADHD in adults and certain children. The typical dosing schedule is once daily in the morning, but the dose may be divided into two doses taken in the morning and late afternoon or early evening.
If you are experiencing side effects, such as sleepiness, from Strattera, it may be helpful to take your dose in the evening. Since Strattera is not a stimulant medication, it can be taken at whatever time works best for you.

title: 6 Mental Health Benefits of Socializing for Aging Adults
content:
One powerful action you can take to improve your mental health at any age is strengthening your social connectedness.
Yet, certain life events can leave older adults feeling isolated and lonely, like adult kids moving away, retirement, illness, and the death of a spouse. 
Isolation and loneliness can have negative effects on your mental health because social connectedness can be essential to well-being. When social connectedness improves, better well-being often follows.
We’ve partnered with Home Instead to learn more about how socializing can improve mental health in older adults.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), social connectedness is feeling like you belong and are valued and supported in your relationships.
One 2021 research review found that being involved in community groups gave older adult participants a sense of belonging. 
Activities that helped them feel greater belonging included volunteer teaching, physical activity groups, and other activities where they were part of a group of people with shared interests, hobbies, or cultural backgrounds.
The CDC says that people who socialize more tend to have a greater quality of life.
The benefit people receive from social interactions depends strongly on their subjective experience and interpretation of the situation.
People benefit most when they feel cared for, feel that they care for others, and when they feel genuinely connected.
Older people tend to especially benefit from participating in physical activities they find fun rather than doing them just because they’re “healthy.”
The better our social connectedness, the better we sleep, a different 2021 review shared.
For example, one 2023 review found that older adults with strong social support systems — friends, family, and spouses — had higher quality sleep than those with less social support.
People may regulate their own emotions and calm themselves down better in the presence of caring friends and loved ones.
People who socialize more tend to better process their stress in their minds and decrease their levels of the stress hormone cortisol.
Socializing is a great exercise for your brain.
One review from 2024 showed that executive function — higher level thinking and reasoning — improved in older people without dementia who had regular social interactions.
In one 2023 study, older people who had longer structured video conversations with researchers several times per week for a year had higher scores in their abilities to think, remember, and reason than those who spoke with researchers for a single short check-in call each week.
MRI scans of the participants’ brains showed greater neural connectivity in attention-related areas, suggesting the video conversations helped reinforce their attentional abilities.
A small 2018 study found that older people who socialized tended to perform better on theory of mind tests than those who didn’t socialize as much.
In other words, socializing may help you retain and develop your knowledge of how others think, understanding that it may differ from your own.
Loneliness clearly links to an increased risk of depression in older people.
On the flip side, social connection seems to have a protective effect against depression.
There’s no one way to socialize. Face-to-face interactions are great, but virtual interactions can help, too.
The interactions don’t have to be deep or prolonged, either. Simply exchanging a few words every day with shopkeepers, classmates, or neighbors may improve well-being. 
The World Health Organization and the CDC share that many ways of socializing can improve older people’s well-being. Consider taking part in activities like:
Socializing can help improve your mental well-being, and you can do it in many ways.
It’s important to remember that your social connectedness doesn’t just depend on how frequently you engage with other people. It’s also about how connected you feel. That’s why it’s possible to still feel lonely in a room full of people.
As you look for more ways to engage with others, consider participating in activities you can do regularly and that you like doing for their own sake.

title: Side Effects of Fintepla: What You Need to Know
content:
Fintepla (fenfluramine) is a prescription drug used to treat seizures from certain epilepsy conditions. Fintepla can cause side effects that range from mild to serious. Examples include diarrhea and sleepiness.
Specifically, Fintepla is used in adults and certain children to treat seizures from some types of epilepsy, including:
The active ingredient in Fintepla is fenfluramine. The drug comes as a liquid solution you swallow.
Keep reading to learn about common, mild, and serious side effects Fintepla can cause. And for a detailed overview of this drug, check out this in-depth Fintepla article.
Fintepla has a boxed warning. This is the most serious warning from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). For details, see the “Side effects explained” section.
Some people may experience mild to serious side effects during Fintepla treatment. Examples of the drug’s commonly reported side effects include:
* To learn more about this side effect, see the “Side effects explained” section.
Mild side effects can vary slightly depending on the condition Fintepla is being used to treat. 
People taking Fintepla for Dravet syndrome reported mild side effects, including:
People taking Fintepla for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome reported mild side effects, including:
In most cases, these side effects should be temporary. And some may be easily managed. But if you have symptoms that are ongoing or bothersome, talk with your doctor or pharmacist. And do not stop Fintepla treatment unless your doctor recommends it. 
Fintepla may cause mild side effects other than those listed above. See the drug’s prescribing information for details.
* To learn more about this side effect, see the “Side effects explained” section.
 Serious side effects have been reported with Fintepla. These include:
If you develop serious side effects while taking Fintepla, call your doctor right away. If the side effects seem life threatening or you think you’re having a medical emergency, immediately call 911 or your local emergency number.
* To learn more about this side effect, see the “Side effects explained” section.
Note: After the FDA approves a drug, it tracks and reviews side effects of the medication. If you’d like to notify the FDA about a side effect you’ve had with Fintepla, visit MedWatch.
For some people, Fintepla can cause an allergic reaction, but it’s not clear whether this side effect occurred in the drug’s studies.
In general, symptoms of allergic reaction can be mild or serious.
What might help
If you have mild symptoms of an allergic reaction, such as a mild rash, call your doctor right away. They may suggest a treatment to manage your symptoms and can determine whether you should continue Fintepla treatment. 
If you have symptoms of a severe allergic reaction, such as swelling or difficulty breathing, call 911 or your local emergency number right away. These symptoms could be life threatening and require immediate medical care.
If your doctor confirms you’ve had a serious allergic reaction to Fintepla, they may have you switch to a different treatment.
Learn more about some of the side effects Fintepla may cause.
Fintepla has aboxed warning. This is the most serious warning from the FDA. It alerts doctors and patients about drug effects that may be dangerous.
Taking Fintepla may increase your risk for valvular heart disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).
Valvular heart disease is when you have damage to at least one of the valves of your heart. PAH is a type of high blood pressure in the vessels of your lungs. These are rare potential side effects of Fintepla. In studies of the drug, no one developed these side effects. But these side effects have happened with drugs that work similarly to Fintepla.
Symptoms of these conditions include:
Fintepla is only available through the Fintepla REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) program due to these serious risks. Before prescribing Fintepla for you, your doctor will order an echocardiogram. This test will check the health of your heart and the pressure in your lung’s arteries. Your doctor will test you every 6 months during your Fintepla treatment, as well as 3 months and 6 months after your treatment ends.
In studies of Fintepla, abnormal echocardiograms were common. However, there were no reports of valvular heart disease or PAH with Fintepla treatment. (These side effects have happened with drugs that work similarly to Fintepla, though.)
If you have symptoms of valvular heart disease or PAH during Fintepla treatment, call your doctor right away. They’ll check whether you have these conditions and determine whether you should stop taking this medication.
Talk with your doctor if you have questions about these risks from Fintepla.
Treatment with Fintepla may cause sleepiness or drowsiness. This was a common side effect reported in studies of the drug. In most cases, this eases with continued treatment. But sleepiness, drowsiness, or lethargy may be serious in some cases.
If you experience sleepiness with Fintepla, do not perform tasks that require alertness (such as driving or operating machinery) until you know how the medication affects you. Do not drink alcohol or take other central nervous system (CNS) depressants (also called sedatives) during Fintepla treatment. These substances can increase your risk of excessive sleepiness, drowsiness, or lethargy.
Talk with your doctor if you have questions about this side effect of Fintepla.
