title: What Medical Procedures Are Used for Cystic Fibrosis (CF)?
content:
People with CF may undergo multiple medical procedures to manage lung infections, digestive issues, and other complications.
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic condition that leads to the production of thick, sticky mucus, which can cause complications in multiple organs, including the sinuses, lungs, intestines, and liver. 
As a result, people with CF often undergo a variety of medical procedures to manage symptoms, prevent complications, and maintain quality of life. 
Endoscopy is a minimally invasive procedure that allows doctors to visualize the interior of the body using a flexible tube with a camera and light source. In CF, doctors commonly use an endoscopy for:
Lavage refers to the washing out of a body cavity, typically performed during an endoscopic procedure to remove mucus or debris and improve function.
Nasal and sinus surgery, typically performed through endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS), is used to treat chronic sinus infections and nasal blockages common in people with CF. 
The thick mucus buildup associated with CF can lead to recurring sinus infections, inflammation, and nasal polyps. When medications such as antibiotics, nasal rinses, and steroids are no longer effective, a medical professional may recommend surgery.
ESS helps clear blocked sinuses, remove polyps, and improve drainage, providing relief from symptoms like congestion and sinus pain. 
A small 2021 study analyzed data from 119 endoscopic sinus surgeries performed on 88 people over 6 years. The researchers focused on changes in sinus scores and lung function before and 3 to 6 months after surgery.
The results showed that, on average, participants had a significant improvement in their sinus symptoms after surgery. However, those with a certain type of bacteria (pseudomonas) in their sinus culture showed less improvement. 
People with CF often experience reduced appetite, malabsorption, and higher energy demands due to lung infections and damage, making it challenging to meet their nutritional needs. 
When regular meals and oral supplements are insufficient, enteral tube feeding becomes necessary.
This method delivers high calorie nutrition either through a nasogastric tube (inserted through the nose) or a gastrostomy tube (surgically placed into the stomach). A medical professional will frequently administer tube feeding overnight to promote growth and maintain overall health.
Research shows that feeding tube insertion can lead to the following benefits:
However, tube feeding can be expensive and may affect self-esteem or cause minor complications like tube dislodgement, nausea, or site infections. 
Bowel surgical interventions help address blockages, cancer risks, and other complications related to CF’s impact on the digestive system. 
Here are several reasons why people with CF may need bowel surgery:
CF causes thick mucus buildup, infections, and scarring in the lungs, which can eventually lead to end stage lung disease.
Doctors may consider transplants when treatments are no longer effective, lung function drops to about 30%, and the disease progresses to an advanced stage — but before it reaches end stage.
About 17% of all lung transplants are for people with CF.
Delaying the transplant too long can reduce options, increase the risk of complications, or lead to death while waiting for a donor.
CF can affect bile flow, resulting in conditions such as cirrhosis (advanced liver scarring) and portal hypertension (high blood pressure in the liver’s veins). 
Liver disease affects about 5% to 10% of people with CF, typically manifesting around the age of 10 or 11. CF-related liver disease (CFLD) is recognized as the third leading cause of death among people with CF.
When CFLD progresses to severe complications — such as cirrhosis, portal hypertension, or life threatening issues like variceal bleeding — a liver transplant may be necessary to save the person’s life. 
Healthcare professionals often consider transplants when liver function deteriorates significantly and other treatment options can no longer manage the complications. 
CF is a complex condition that affects multiple organs, including the lungs, intestines, and liver. 
To manage complications, people with CF may undergo airway clearance therapies, gastrointestinal surgeries, and transplants (like liver or lung).

title: Can Ovarian Cysts Cause Abnormal Pap Smears?

title: Understanding How Hepatitis C Is Diagnosed
content:
Hepatitis C is a viral infection that affects your liver. You may not have symptoms.
Hepatitis C is a viral infection caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV) that affects the liver. It can be acute or chronic and is primarily spread through blood-to-blood contact. Diagnosis involves a series of blood tests.
Read on for more information about how hepatitis C is diagnosed, where you can get these tests, and what to do next.
You may need more than one blood test to diagnose hepatitis C. The tests that diagnose hepatitis C include:
The first test is called a HCV antibody test (anti-HCV test). It checks for the presence of antibodies to the virus. 
A negative result means you do not have hepatitis C. A positive result means you have been exposed to the hepatitis C virus at some point, but it does not confirm that you have an active infection. 
After a positive antibody result, your doctor will recommend a nucleic acid test (NAT), such as an HCV ribonucleic acid (RNA) test, to detect the presence or levels of HCV RNA in your blood. 
If HCV RNA is detected, this confirms that the virus is active and currently circulating in your blood. If RNA is not detected, it means you are not currently infected.
Additional testing for hepatitis C may include:
Make an appointment with your doctor, healthcare professional, or local clinic to discuss testing if you’re concerned that you’ve been exposed to hepatitis C or if you have certain risk factors that increase your chance of exposure.
It’s important to note that there is a hepatitis C window period of 8 to 11 weeks between exposure to the virus and when the antibodies can be detected in your blood. Testing too early in this period may result in a false negative result.
Your doctor may order either traditional lab testing or rapid testing. The main difference is in the time it takes to get the results. Rapid testing results may be ready in just 30 minutes. Results from traditional lab tests may take much longer. 
Other testing options include:
In all cases, follow-up with a healthcare professional is essential to help interpret your results and make a treatment plan, if needed.
Knowing your hepatitis C status is an important first step to managing the disease. If your results come back positive, it means that the virus is currently circulating in your blood and that you need treatment to clear the virus and avoid complications. 
What you need to know:
Hepatitis C is primarily spread through blood-to-blood contact, such as sharing needles or receiving blood products containing the virus. 
While it’s uncommon to contract the virus through sexual contact, and it’s not classified as a sexually transmitted infection (STI), it’s possible to contract the virus through sex.
Related factors that increase the risk of hepatitis C include:
You may lower your risk of contracting the hepatitis C virus by wearing condoms and avoiding sharing personal care items that can have blood on them, such as razors, needles, toothbrushes, and other items.
Hepatitis C typically causes no symptoms until the virus leads to significant liver injury. For this reason, it’s sometimes referred to as a “silent” killer. 
One in 3 people with hepatitis C does not know they have it, and 65% to 75% of people with the virus don’t have any symptoms. It’s possible to have the virus for years before it causes severe liver injury and notable health effects.
An estimated 2.4 million people in the United States are living with hepatitis C, and half of them don’t know they have the virus. 
Doctors recommend that everyone over 18 years old get tested, as well as at-risk pregnant people (during each pregnancy), and others who have additional risk factors.

title: Inderal: How It’s Used for Treating Anxiety
content:
Inderal LA and Inderal XL (propranolol) are brand-name prescription drugs that may be used off-label to treat anxiety. Inderal is also available as a generic drug. 
Inderal LA and Inderal XL come as extended-release oral capsules. (Extended-release capsules release the medication slowly into your body over a period of time to give a long-acting effect.) In general, this article will use the term “Inderal” to refer to both forms of the drug unless otherwise noted.
The active ingredient in Inderal is propranolol. Inderal belongs to a group of drugs called beta-blockers. To learn more about the drug, see this in-depth Inderal article.
Note: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Inderal LA and Inderal XL to treat high blood pressure. Inderal LA is also approved to treat certain heart conditions and help prevent migraine. In some cases, your doctor may prescribe Inderal off-label for anxiety. (With off-label use, a drug is prescribed for a purpose other than what it’s approved for.)
Anxiety is a feeling of worry, fear, dread, or unease. It can cause physical symptoms and affect your behaviors.
Anxiety can be a natural and expected response to stressful or frightening situations. But if you have anxiety that’s excessive, out of proportion, or affects your daily life, it can become a medical problem.
Symptoms of anxiety can include:
Anxiety can also cause physical symptoms. These can include:
Some people with anxiety may also have panic attacks. A panic attack is a sudden and overwhelming feeling of intense fear that causes physical symptoms such as those listed. Other symptoms can include nausea, chest pain, trouble breathing, and feeling detached from reality.
Doctors may prescribe Inderal off-label for people who have physical symptoms of anxiety or panic attacks. (With off-label use, a drug is prescribed for a purpose other than what it’s approved for.)
The FDA has approved Inderal for other conditions, including high blood pressure, certain heart conditions, and migraine. To learn more about the drug’s approved uses, see this in-depth Inderal article.
Inderal treats anxiety by reducing some of the physical symptoms that happen when you’re anxious. These include increased heart rate, shaking, sweating, and tense muscles. Reducing these physical symptoms can help you feel physically calmer. And this may help reduce anxious feelings and thoughts. 
Physical symptoms of anxiety occur when your body releases a hormone called epinephrine, also known as adrenaline. This hormone causes the fight, flight, or freeze response. It speeds up your heart rate and increases blood flow to your muscles.
Inderal works by blocking the action of epinephrine on your heart and blood vessels. This slows your heart rate, reduces your blood pressure, and helps reduce sweating, shaking, and muscle tension.
How long does Inderal take to work?
How quickly Inderal works to treat anxiety may depend on the form of Inderal you take (Inderal LA or Inderal XL).
Inderal LA and Inderal XL both come as extended-release oral capsules. (Extended-release capsules release the medication slowly into your body over a period of time to give a long-acting effect.)
Both forms start to reduce physical symptoms of anxiety soon after you take a dose. But Inderal XL releases the medication into your body more slowly than Inderal LA, so it takes longer to produce its maximum effect. Inderal XL is meant to be taken at bedtime to produce its maximum effect in the morning.
The FDA has not approved Inderal LA or Inderal XL for use in anyone under age 18 years. It’s not known if these drugs are safe or effective in children.
Doctors are unlikely to prescribe Inderal LA or Inderal XL for anxiety in children. However, doctors may prescribe other forms of propranolol (the active ingredient in Inderal) for anxiety in children.
To learn more about using propranolol for anxiety in children, talk with your doctor.
It’s not known how effective Inderal is for anxiety. The drug manufacturer hasn’t studied the drug for this use.
Propranolol, the active ingredient in Inderal, has been widely used for treating anxiety for many years. But there haven’t been many reliable studies that looked at the drug’s effectiveness for anxiety.
In fact, a recent review of studies concluded there wasn’t enough evidence to prove propanolol’s effectiveness in treating anxiety. More research is needed to find out how effective this drug is for anxiety.
If you have questions about Inderal’s effectiveness for anxiety, talk with your doctor.
Inderal LA and Inderal XL come as extended-release capsules that you swallow. Extended-release capsules release the medication slowly into your body over a period of time. They have a long-acting effect. 
There isn’t a recommended dosage or maximum dose of Inderal for treating anxiety. This is because anxiety is an off-label use of the drug, and the manufacturer hasn’t given dosage recommendations for off-label uses.
If your doctor prescribes Inderal to treat anxiety, they’ll prescribe a dosage that’s right for you.
Note: Besides being prescribed off-label for anxiety, Inderal is FDA approved for certain other uses. When used off-label, the drug’s dosage may differ from the dosage of these approved uses. To learn more, talk with your doctor.
Inderal LA and Inderal XL capsules should be swallowed whole. This may be easier if you take the capsules with a drink. You should not open, split, crush, or chew the capsules.
You should take Inderal LA without food. The manufacturer hasn’t studied whether taking the drug with food can affect its action.
You can take Inderal XL either with or without food. However, you should always take it the same way (with or without food).
You should take Inderal once per day. 
The best time to take Inderal for anxiety depends on the form your doctor prescribes. You can take Inderal LA at any time of day, but you should take it around the same time each day. You should take Inderal XL at bedtime. This helps it produce its maximum effect in the morning.
Using Inderal off-label for anxiety may cause side effects in some people. (With off-label use, a drug is prescribed for a purpose other than what it’s approved for.)

For information about other possible side effects of this medication, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
You can also learn more from the side effects article on Inderal or from Inderal’s prescribing information.

In many cases, mild side effects from the drug can be temporary. Some side effects may be easy to manage, too. But if side effects last longer, bother you, or become severe, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Taking Inderal may lead to rare but serious side effects. Examples include:
Call your doctor right away if you have any serious side effects while using Inderal. If the side effects seem life threatening or if you think you’re having a medical emergency, call 911 or your local emergency number immediately.
For some people, Inderal can cause an allergic reaction. In general, symptoms of allergic reaction can be mild or serious.
What might help

If you have symptoms of a severe allergic reaction, such as swelling or trouble breathing, call 911 or your local emergency number right away. These symptoms could be life threatening and require immediate medical care.
If your doctor confirms you’ve had a serious allergic reaction to Inderal, they may have you switch to a different treatment.

Some of these are mentioned here. If any of these apply to you, talk with your doctor before taking Inderal:
It’s also important to note that suddenly stopping Inderal treatment could cause serious heart issues, such as chest pain or heart attack. You should not stop taking Inderal unless your doctor recommends it. If you want to end your treatment, they’ll likely reduce your dosage gradually before you completely stop taking the drug. To learn more, talk with your doctor.
The price of Inderal depends on several factors. These can include your treatment plan, your insurance plan, the pharmacy you use, and your location.

title: Auvi-Q Interactions: Alcohol, Medications, and Others
content:
Auvi-Q (epinephrine) is a prescription drug that’s used to treat emergency allergic reactions. This drug can interact with other medications and some supplements. For example, Auvi-Q can interact with beta-blockers and ergot alkaloids.
Auvi-Q is used in adults and children to treat emergency allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis (a life threatening allergic reaction). It comes as a single-dose auto-injector for injection into your thigh. The active drug in Auvi-Q is epinephrine.
An interaction can occur because one substance causes another substance to have a different effect than expected. Interactions can also occur if you have certain health conditions.
Keep reading to learn about Auvi-Q’s possible interactions. For a detailed overview of this drug, check out this in-depth Auvi-Q article.
Before you start using Auvi-Q, tell your doctor and pharmacist about any prescription, over-the-counter, or other drugs you take. Sharing this information with them may help prevent possible interactions. (To learn whether Auvi-Q interacts with herbs, vitamins, or supplements, see the “Are there other interactions with Auvi-Q?” section.)
If you have questions about drug interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
The table below lists drugs that may interact with Auvi-Q. Keep in mind that this table does not include all drugs that may interact with Auvi-Q. For more information about some of these interactions, see the “Drug interactions explained” section.
Auvi-Q is not known to interact with alcohol. You can use Auvi-Q if you’ve recently had alcohol. 
You should not drink alcohol after using Auvi-Q. The drug is for emergency treatment of a serious allergic reaction. Anytime you use a dose of Auvi-Q, you should get immediate medical care.
If you have questions about consuming alcohol while using Auvi-Q, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Learn more about certain drug interactions that can occur with Auvi-Q.
Auvi-Q can interact with antihistamines, which are used to treat the symptoms of allergies, colds, and flu. 
Examples of antihistamine medications include:
Taking Auvi-Q with an antihistamine can increase the effect of Auvi-Q. This can raise the risk of side effects, including serious side effects. Antihistamines have many of the same effects in the body as Auvi-Q. This includes raising your heart rate and blood pressure. Together, Auvi-Q and antihistamines can cause very high blood pressure and other side effects that can lead to serious problems.
If you take an antihistamine and have concerns about using Auvi-Q, talk with your doctor. They can provide more information about the interaction. They’ll also likely advise you to use Auvi-Q even if you take an antihistamine. This is because Auvi-Q is an emergency treatment for severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis. Potential interactions should not be a reason to avoid using Auvi-Q in an emergency.
If you have questions about taking Auvi-Q with an antihistamine, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Beta-blockers are prescribed for several medical conditions, including high blood pressure, heart problems, and migraine headaches.
Examples of beta-blocker medications:
Taking Auvi-Q with a beta-blocker can make Auvi-Q less effective. This is because beta-blockers have the opposite effects of Auvi-Q in the body.
For example, Auvi-Q works to increase blood pressure, while beta-blockers work to reduce it. Quickly raising blood pressure is an important part of treating a severe allergic reaction. This is because your blood pressure can drop suddenly during a severe allergic reaction. Taking a beta-blocker may make it harder for Auvi-Q to treat this symptom.
Talk with your doctor if you take a beta-blocker and have a prescription for Auvi-Q. They can tell you more about this interaction. They’ll also likely recommend using Auvi-Q anyway if you have a severe allergic reaction. This interaction should not be a reason to avoid using Auvi-Q in an emergency.
If you have questions or concerns about taking Auvi-Q with a beta-blocker, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Diuretics help treat several medical conditions, including high blood pressure, heart failure, and kidney problems 
Examples of diuretic medications:
Taking Auvi-Q with a diuretic can increase the risk of irregular heart rhythms. Irregular heart rhythms can feel like a fluttering, pounding, or skipping heartbeat. The risk is also higher if you have heart problems, such as coronary artery disease (CAD), or high blood pressure.
If you take a diuretic, talk with your doctor about using Auvi-Q. They’ll give you more information about the interaction. They’ll also likely advise you to use Auvi-Q even if you take a diuretic. Auvi-Q is an emergency treatment for severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis. Because of this, interactions should not be a reason to avoid using Auvi-Q in an emergency.
Talk with your doctor or pharmacist if you have questions or concerns about taking Auvi-Q.

If you have questions about interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.

For this reason, it’s still important to check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any of these products while using Auvi-Q.
Auvi-Q may interact with caffeine. Caffeine can increase the effect of Auvi-Q. This may raise the risk of irregular heart rhythms and very high blood pressure. Examples of foods and beverages that contain caffeine include coffee, tea, and chocolate.
You can use Auvi-Q if you’ve recently had caffeine, but don’t consume caffeine after using Auvi-Q. The drug is for emergency treatment of a serious allergic reaction. Anytime you use a dose of Auvi-Q, you should get immediate medical care.
There are currently no reports of Auvi-Q interacting with vaccines. If you have questions about getting certain vaccines during your Auvi-Q treatment, talk with your doctor.
There are currently no reports of Auvi-Q interacting with lab tests. If you have questions about having certain lab tests done during your treatment with Auvi-Q, talk with the healthcare professional ordering the test.

Certain medical conditions or other health factors may raise the risk of interactions with Auvi-Q. Before using Auvi-Q, talk with your doctor about your health history. They’ll determine whether Auvi-Q is right for you.
Health conditions or other factors that might interact with Auvi-Q include:
Diabetes: Using Auvi-Q may increase your blood sugar levels for a period of time. Get immediate medical care after using Auvi-Q. Your care team will monitor your blood sugar levels and help you make adjustments to your diabetes treatment if necessary.
Heart problems or high blood pressure: Having heart problems or high blood pressure can increase the risk of irregular heart rhythms, chest pain, or high blood pressure with Auvi-Q. Your doctor will likely recommend using Auvi-Q anyway. Always see a doctor immediately after using Auvi-Q.
Parkinson’s disease: Using Auvi-Q can cause a temporary worsening of Parkinson’s disease symptoms. Your doctor will likely recommend using Auvi-Q anyway if you’re having a severe allergic reaction.
Thyroid problems: If you have hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid), using Auvi-Q may make your symptoms worse for a period of time. Because Auvi-Q is an emergency treatment, your doctor will likely advise you to use it anyway.
Pregnancy: If you’re pregnant or planning a pregnancy, talk with your doctor about using Auvi-Q. They’ll likely advise you to use it if you have a severe allergic reaction.
Breastfeeding: It’s not known whether it’s safe to use Auvi-Q while breastfeeding. If you’re breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed, talk with your doctor about your options. They’re likely to recommend using Auvi-Q anyway because it’s an emergency treatment.
Taking certain steps can help you avoid interactions with Auvi-Q. Before starting treatment, talk with your doctor and pharmacist. Things to discuss with them include:
It’s also important to understand Auvi-Q’s label and other paperwork that may come with the drug. Colored stickers that describe interactions may be on the label. And the paperwork (sometimes called the patient package insert or medication guide) may have other details about interactions. title: Uveal Melanoma: Causes, Symptoms, and Treatment Options

Uveal melanoma is a type of cancer that develops in the middle layer of your eye called the uvea. It can cause symptoms like blurry vision, floaters, or loss of vision.
Melanoma is a type of cancer that grows in cells called melanocytes that give your skin and tissues their pigment.

The outlook for uveal melanoma is often best when the cancer starts in your iris. This is because tumors in this location are often identified and treated early. 
Uveal melanoma that is diagnosed before it spreads to other tissues and body parts responds well to treatment. However, the outlook tends to worsen if the cancer spreads to your liver or other organs.
Eye melanoma is an extremely rare cancer, but it’s the most common type of primary eye cancer in adults. Primary eye cancer means it starts in your eye instead of spreading from other tissues to the eye.
Eye melanoma develops in about 1 in 200,000 adults. It’s much less common than skin melanoma, which is the fifth most common cancer in the United States for men and women.
Melanoma that starts in your uvea is called uveal melanoma. Uveal melanoma starts in the choroid in about 90% of cases. The other 10% of cases start in your iris or ciliary body.
Eye melanoma can also start in the thin, clear layer that covers your eye white, called the conjunctiva. Melanoma that starts here is called conjunctival melanoma.
About 30% of people with uveal melanoma don’t have any symptoms in the early stages. When symptoms do appear, they often include:
The signs and symptoms you develop can depend on the size of the melanoma tumor and where it’s located. For example, people with melanoma on the iris may develop a growing dark spot.
It’s important to see an eye doctor any time you notice changes in your vision. The doctor may order many tests to determine the cause of your symptoms. If they suspect cancer, you may go through diagnostics tests such as:

It’s not clear if ultraviolet (UV) light exposure increases the risk of uveal melanoma. If it does, its role is thought to be less significant than for skin melanoma.
According to research, about 98% of cases of uveal melanoma develop in Caucasian people. Eye melanoma is diagnosed in Caucasians around 8 to 10 times more often than in people of African descent.
No cure has been found for cancer. However, doctors consider cancer cured if you go into complete remission for 5 years. Remission means that you no longer have symptoms of the disease. 
Many people who receive treatment for uveal melanoma achieve complete remission, especially if their cancer has not spread to other tissues.

Many of the risk factors of uveal melanoma, like family history, cannot be managed or prevented. 
It’s not clear if UV light exposure is linked to an increased risk of uveal melanoma, but it’s still a good idea to UV protection for your eyes when out in the sun to support your overall eye health.
Uveal melanoma has the best outlook when it’s diagnosed and treated before it spreads.

The outlook for uvea melanoma is usually best when the tumor develops in your iris. Melanoma in the iris rarely spreads to other body parts because it’s usually detected earlier.

title: Will Medicare Pay for Nephrocaps?
content:
Nephrocaps, a dietary supplement often marketed to support kidney health, is not typically covered by Medicare.
Original Medicare (parts A and B) generally does not cover over-the-counter or prescription supplements like Nephrocaps. Part A covers inpatient hospital care, and Part B covers outpatient services and medically necessary treatments.
However, Part B excludes most dietary supplements unless prescribed for a specific medical condition as part of a treatment plan. Even then, coverage is rare and only applies if the supplement is considered medically necessary.
Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans, offered by private insurers, combine parts A and B with additional coverage.
Some Part C plans may offer additional health services or wellness benefits, but they typically exclude coverage for supplements unless they’re part of a broader medically necessary treatment plan.
Part D, which covers prescription drugs, generally does not cover OTC supplements unless they’re prescribed for a specific therapeutic purpose and are FDA approved for that use.

title: How to Recognize and Cope With ADHD Burnout
content:
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) burnout refers to a state of mental and physical exhaustion occurring from ADHD-related stress and coping.
Burnout is a mental and physical state of exhaustion. It may occur when the constant demands on your mind and body overwhelm your ability to cope effectively. People experience burnout for various reasons, but all of those reasons have a common underlying feature: chronic stress.
When you push your mind and body to the limit for long periods of time, your stress reaction stays engaged and starts to negatively affect your body.
Your stress reaction refers to the physiological responses that happen when you perceive a threat or adversity. These changes do everything from raising your heart rate and respiration to releasing hormones and altering neurotransmitters. When this reaction stays engaged for long periods of time, it’s known as chronic stress.
ADHD burnout is an informal term for the kind of chronic stress that comes from managing ADHD symptoms. 
Here’s a closer look at why it happens and how to manage it. 
In ADHD, people often associate burnout with the chronic stress of managing ADHD symptoms and adapting to unsupportive environments.
Many people with ADHD “mask” or suppress ADHD behaviors to fit in with social groups, which can take a lot of energy.
In addition, symptoms related to time management, attention, and emotional regulation can lead to stress about spending more time on projects, organization, or being “less than” compared to neurotypical people.
Sensitivity to rejection, hyperfocus, and traits of perfectionism or self-criticism in ADHD can also add to the persistent stress associated with ADHD burnout.
Symptoms of burnout tend to look similar, regardless of the cause.
Burnout can look like:
If you live with ADHD, burnout may make your symptoms feel more severe because it strains your ability to cope effectively. If you experience challenges with attention, for example, you may notice your focus and concentration get worse when you reach a stage of burnout.
The ADHD burnout cycle refers to a pattern of overexertion, burnout, and recovery experienced in ADHD.
While many people can find balance in daily life with the right support and symptom management, ADHD is a lifelong condition. If you’re under high levels of persistent stress related to ADHD symptoms like inattention, hyperfocus, or masking, it can be difficult to avoid burnout.
When burnout happens, you realize you need to make a change and allow yourself space to recover. However, if you don’t address the underlying stressors, burnout is likely to occur again once you return to the original situation.
Not everyone living with ADHD will cycle through a pattern of burnout. It’s possible for burnout to be specific to certain circumstances or one-time experiences.
If you’re in a stage of burnout, the first step is to remove yourself from the source of chronic stress, if possible. You need to recover, and recovery is difficult when you’re still exposed to stressors.
Removing stressors in ADHD often involves effectively managing ADHD symptoms through medication, lifestyle changes, and environmental support. When you’re able to manage your symptoms, and you have support in place to help you succeed each day, the pressure to conform or “make up” for ADHD diminishes.
Tips to help you recover from burnout include:
You don’t have to face this alone. Speaking with a mental health professional can help you prevent and overcome ADHD burnout. Not only will a therapist work with you to develop a comprehensive management plan for ADHD symptoms, but they can also help you build more effective coping strategies for chronic stress.
ADHD burnout is a state of physical and mental exhaustion brought on by the chronic stress of challenges in ADHD. While not everyone living with ADHD will experience burnout, many people face ongoing stress as they manage symptoms and strive to meet expectations in unsupportive environments.

title: Does Epidiolex Contain THC?

No, Epidiolex isn’t currently a controlled substance. (This means a drug has an approved medical use but may be misused for other purposes. It also means government agencies, doctors, and pharmacists pay close attention to how the drug is prescribed and used.)
However, be sure to keep the prescription label on your bottle of Epidiolex, especially when traveling. It’s legal to have prescription Epidiolex in the United States, but in some states, it’s illegal to use CBD without a prescription.

If you live in a state where medical cannabis or CBD products haven’t been legalized or are unavailable, you can still benefit from products containing industrial hemp-derived CBD. Before you start receiving Ocrevus, talk with your doctor and pharmacist about any herbs, vitamins, or supplements you take. Sharing this information with them may help you avoid possible interactions.

Live vaccines are made from weakened versions of the bacteria or virus they’re meant to protect against. Examples of live vaccines include chickenpox, measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), and the nasal spray flu vaccine.
Getting a live vaccine during Ocrevus treatment may increase your risk of getting the infection it’s meant to protect against.

Non-live vaccines are made from similar or inactivated parts of the bacteria or virus they’re meant to protect against. Examples of non-live vaccines include shingles, tetanus, and the injectable flu vaccine.
It’s possible that non-live vaccines may not work as well if you receive them during Ocrevus treatment. Your doctor may advise you to delay the start of Ocrevus treatment for at least 2 weeks after receiving a non-live vaccine.

title: Vision Impairment: From Mild to Severe Forms of Vision Loss
content:
Cataracts, glaucoma, and refractive errors are just a few examples of conditions that cause visual impairment, a decline in your ability to see that’s significant enough to affect daily life.
“Visual impairment” is a broad term describing vision loss from conditions that alter the systems, structures, or functions of the eye. It includes low vision, where some sight remains, as well as conditions of blindness.
Visual impairment can involve changes to the clarity or acuity of your vision and losses to your field of view, eye coordination, depth perception, light sensitivity, and color contrast.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 2.2 billion people around the world live with some form of visual impairment.
Almost everyone’s vision changes naturally with age. The older you are, the more likely you’ll develop at least one form of visual impairment.
Globally, the leading causes of vision impairment are:
A global prevalence study from 2021 examining visual impairment in people over the age of 50 years found that cataracts was the most prominent condition reported, followed by glaucoma, refractive errors, age-related macular degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy.
A cataract occurs when the natural lens of your eye becomes cloudy, limiting how well light passes into the retina. Most cataracts develop slowly, as degenerative processes cause proteins to clump within the eye’s lens.
You can develop a cataract in one eye or both eyes. If you have cataracts in both eyes, they may progress at different rates and affect your vision with different severity.
Cataracts are known for causing blurred or cloudy vision, faded color perception, low night vision, and seeing “halos” around lights.
Glaucoma occurs when damage to the optic nerve affects how your eyes transmit visual signals to your brain. Most cases of glaucoma are caused by increased intraocular pressure (IOP), a measurement of the force exerted within your eye by clear fluid called the aqueous humor.
Several types of glaucoma exist, including:
Glaucoma affects your peripheral vision or your side vision. It’s often subtle, with no obvious signs or symptoms until its advanced stages. Angle-closure glaucoma, a form of glaucoma that requires urgent medical attention, may cause sudden pain, nausea, blurred vision, or a headache.
When the shape of your eye alters how light is focused on your retina, it causes a refractive error. If the light isn’t focused on the retina accurately, it distorts or blurs vision at different distances or makes it difficult to focus your eyes.
Types of refractive errors include:
There are many reasons why you might develop refractive errors, including changes to eye lens flexibility, varied eyeball length, and irregularity in your cornea, the clear layer on the front of your eye.
Age-related macular degeneration (ARMD) is a progressive condition that affects the macula of your eye, the part of your retina responsible for detailed vision.
ARMD is divided into two subtypes based on the underlying processes affecting the macula.
In dry ARMD, yellowish deposits called drusen form between your retina and the layers of the eye that supply it with blood. Comprised of fats, proteins, and other cellular waste products, drusen contribute to damage in the retina and photoreceptor cells, which affects central vision.
In wet ARMD, also known as neovascular ARMD, abnormal blood vessels form beneath your macula. They promote fluid leakage that can lead to inflammation and permanent scarring.
ARMD doesn’t always feature symptoms in its early stages. As it progresses, you may notice blurred vision, difficulty seeing in low light, trouble seeing details, or seeing straight lines as wavy.
Diabetic retinopathy is a complication of diabetes. It develops when prolonged, elevated blood sugar levels (hyperglycemia) put stress on your retinal cells, trigger inflammation, and promote the development of new, leaky blood vessels on the surface of the retina or in the vitreous, the gel-like substance filling the eye.
Blood from abnormal, leaky vessels can cloud the vitreous, leading to sudden vision impairment or loss. New vessels on the surface of the eye can pull your retina away from its natural position, resulting in retinal detachment.
Diabetic retinopathy doesn’t always present with symptoms in its early stages. As it progresses, you may notice sudden vision changes, floaters or spots in your eyes, blurry vision, or difficulty seeing in low light.
Visual impairment describes a spectrum of vision loss across a variety of eye conditions. Below are answers to some commonly asked questions:
“Vision impairment” is an umbrella term that describes different severities of vision loss affecting daily life. Total blindness, the absence of any light perception, is considered a severe form of visual impairment.
In the United States, the Social Security Administration considers you eligible for disability benefits if you’re “legally blind.” There are two qualifications for legal blindness:
Even if you don’t meet these criteria, you may be eligible for disability benefits if vision challenges prevent you from maintaining employment.
Visual impairment is primarily treated by ophthalmologists and optometrists, though your eye care team may involve other specialists depending on the cause of vision impairment.
If you need help covering the cost of eye care, consider contacting:
“Visual impairment” is a broad term that describes vision loss across a spectrum of severity and conditions. It includes legal or total blindness, which are complete or near-complete states of vision loss.

title: What Are Metal Levels in Marketplace Insurance?
content:
The Health Insurance Marketplace categorizes plans into four levels that have names based on metals, plus a fifth “catastrophic” level for younger people or individuals with a lower income. These tiers reflect how healthcare costs are shared between you and the insurer.
The Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare, established the Health Insurance Marketplace to help people get affordable health coverage.
If you lack private insurance through your employer and don’t meet the eligibility criteria for Medicare or Medicaid, you can purchase a plan from the Marketplace.
The plans available on the Marketplace are categorized into levels based on metal types.
On the Marketplace, insurance plan metal levels are Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum.
It’s important to know that health insurance providers in the Marketplace don’t organize their plans into these metal tiers according to the benefits offered to individuals. 
Rather, they classify them based on how healthcare expenses are divided between you and the insurance company.
Marketplace health insurance plans are required to cover essential outpatient care, hospitalizations, and emergency room visits. 
In addition, plans typically also cover the following:
Although your specific out-of-pocket expenses may vary between different plans, the general distribution of costs between you and the health insurance company typically remains consistent.
The following chart summarizes the typical difference in this distribution and coverage:
You might be eligible for reduced costs related to deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance. This is exclusively available with the Silver plan, which offers an extra savings option.
If you choose the Silver plan, it will cover between 73% and 96% of your expenses, while you’ll be responsible for paying between 6% and 27%, based on the level of savings you qualify for. 
In addition to the four metal levels, a fifth category of Marketplace plans is known as the “catastrophic” category. You’re eligible for this if you’re under age 30 years or if your income is limited. These plans typically come with low premiums but high deductibles.
But if you qualify for premium tax credits or cost-sharing reductions, a Bronze or Silver plan might offer better value, so it’s best to compare your options.
If you’re thinking about choosing a Marketplace plan, here are a few tips to keep in mind:
Under the Affordable Care Act, if you aren’t eligible for Medicare or Medicaid and don’t have private insurance through your job, you can buy a plan from the Health Insurance Marketplace.
The Marketplace sorts available plans into metal levels: Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum. In addition, there is a fifth “catastrophic” level for younger people or those with lower economic means.

title: Seizure Medications That Cause Weight Gain
content:
Valproate and gabapentin are seizure medications commonly linked to weight gain. Other ASMs, like topiramate or lamotrigine, may lead to weight loss. Some may not affect weight.
Certain medications used to treat seizures, also known as antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) or antiseizure medications (ASMs), may cause weight gain for some people. Other people may experience no weight change or weight loss.
Discuss your concerns about weight gain and other side effects of seizure medications as you work with a healthcare professional to find the most effective treatment plan for you.
Do not stop taking your seizure medication before speaking with your neurologist or other healthcare professional, even if you’re seeing weight gain. Stopping without approval may cause more severe or frequent seizures.
Many medications, including those used to treat seizures, may cause weight gain by slowing your metabolism so you burn fewer calories or changing your brain’s chemistry. This change may disrupt when your brain signals that you’re hungry.
Because of the disruption in signaling, you may feel hungrier more often, leading you to eat more and gain a modest amount of weight.
Not all seizure medications will cause weight gain. Sometimes, these medications may cause your brain to signal hunger less (suppress hunger), potentially leading to weight loss.
A few ASMs or mood-stabilizing medications that may have the potential for weight loss include:
Even the seizure medications most frequently associated with weight gain won’t always cause it. Everyone’s response will vary.
But several ASMs or mood-stabilizing agents associated with weight gain may include:
Valproate, in particular, has a main side effect of weight gain. A 2017 randomized study of 66 females with newly diagnosed or untreated epilepsy took either valproate or lamotrigine.
At the end of 1 year, the group that took valproate had a significantly higher body weight than the lamotrigine group.
Research also indicates that valproate and carbamazepine may cause weight gain in 71% and 43%, respectively, of people who take them.
The benefits of taking seizure medication often outweigh the risks. If you’re worried about weight gain, speak with your doctor. They may recommend combination therapy or lifestyle modifications to minimize or prevent weight gain.
While several seizure medications are associated with weight gain and a few with weight loss, some may be neutral to weight gain and loss. This means they’re not associated with any weight changes.
Seizure medications potentially neutral to weight changes are:
But remember, everyone will respond to treatment differently. Just because these medications may be weight neutral doesn’t mean they’ll be weight neutral for everybody.
Because obesity is a risk factor for epilepsy, according to a 2022 observational study, your doctor will consider this when prescribing a seizure medication and dosage.
Your doctor knows dosage is important because it’s typically related to the degree of the side effects. They might have to adjust your dosage or change your medication depending on how you respond to the ASM.
Besides keeping track of any side effects you experience to manage weight gain from your medication, you might also try (or keep up, if you already do these):
While some seizure medications may cause weight gain, other ASMs or AEDs are neutral or have weight loss potential. Speak with your doctor about potential side effects, including weight changes, from seizure medications.
You can manage your weight while taking seizure medication by tracking any changes and side effects, maintaining a balanced diet, and exercising regularly. You should also consider speaking with your doctor about weight loss drugs.

title: Vascepa Interactions: Alcohol, Medications, and Others
content:
Vascepa (icosapent ethyl) is a prescription drug used to treat high triglycerides and lower certain heart-related risks. Vascepa can interact with alcohol, other drugs, and some supplements. For example, it can interact with anticoagulants and thiazide diuretics.
An interaction can occur because one substance causes another substance to have a different effect than expected. Interactions can also occur if you have certain health conditions.
Before you start taking Vascepa, tell your doctor and pharmacist about any prescription, over-the-counter, or other drugs you take. Sharing this information with them may help prevent possible interactions. (To learn whether Vascepa interacts with herbs, vitamins, or supplements, see the “Are there other interactions with Vascepa?” section.)
If you have questions about drug interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
The following table lists drugs that may interact with Vascepa. Keep in mind that this table does not include all drugs that may interact with Vascepa. For more information about some of these interactions, see the “Drug interactions explained” section.
Certain health conditions or other factors could raise your risk of harm if you take Vascepa. In such cases, your doctor may not prescribe Vascepa for you. These are known as contraindications. Vascepa has one contraindication, which is listed below.
If you’ve had an allergic reaction: If you’ve had an allergic reaction to Vascepa or any of its ingredients, your doctor likely won’t prescribe Vascepa for you. This is because taking the drug could cause another allergic reaction. You can ask your doctor about other treatments that may be better options for you.
Vascepa is not known to interact with alcohol. But excessive alcohol use can increase your triglyceride level, and Vascepa is prescribed to lower high triglycerides. Because of this, your doctor may suggest that you avoid alcohol or limit the amount you consume if you’re taking Vascepa.
If you have questions about consuming alcohol while taking Vascepa, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Learn more about certain drug interactions that can occur with Vascepa.
Vascepa can interact with anticoagulants, which are used to treat and help prevent blood clots. 
Examples of anticoagulant medications include:
Vascepa and anticoagulants can both increase your risk of bleeding. Taking these drugs together can further raise your risk of this side effect.
If you take Vascepa with an anticoagulant, your doctor may prescribe a lower dosage of Vascepa for you. You should not take a higher dose of either medication than your doctor prescribes. Your doctor may also suggest an alternative to Vascepa instead.
If you take Vascepa and an anticoagulant together, tell your doctor right away if you have symptoms of bleeding. Examples of these symptoms include excessive bleeding from minor cuts (such as a paper cut), coughing up blood, or blood in your stool.
If you have questions about taking Vascepa with anticoagulants, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Vascepa can interact with thiazide diuretics. These medications are prescribed to treat high blood pressure and edema (fluid buildup) related to conditions such as heart failure.
Examples of thiazide diuretic medications include:
Taking Vascepa and a thiazide diuretic together can make Vascepa less effective. Thiazide diuretics can increase the level of triglycerides in your blood, and Vascepa is prescribed to treat high triglycerides.
Although there is an interaction between Vascepa and thiazide diuretics, doctors sometimes prescribe them together. The risk for serious side effects or other harm from this interaction is considered low compared with the benefit these medications may have.
If you take Vascepa with a thiazide diuretic, your doctor may prescribe a lower dosage of the thiazide diuretic for you. Or they may prescribe a higher Vascepa dosage for you. You should not take a higher dose of either medication than your doctor prescribes.
Vascepa can interact with beta-blockers. These medications are prescribed to treat high blood pressure and certain other heart conditions, including arrhythmia.
Examples of beta-blocker medications include:
Taking Vascepa and a beta-blocker together can make Vascepa less effective. Beta-blockers can increase triglyceride levels in your blood, and Vascepa is prescribed to treat high triglycerides.
Although there is an interaction between Vascepa and beta-blockers, doctors sometimes prescribe them together. Compared with the benefits these medications may have for treating your condition, the risk of serious side effects or other harm from this interaction is considered low.
If you take Vascepa with a thiazide diuretic, your doctor may prescribe a higher dosage of Vascepa for you. Or they may prescribe a lower dose of the beta-blocker. You should not take a higher dose of either medication than your doctor prescribes.
Vascepa may have other interactions. They could occur with supplements, foods, vaccines, or lab tests. Note that the following information does not include all possible interactions with Vascepa.
Before you start taking Vascepa, talk with your doctor and pharmacist about any herbs, vitamins, or supplements you take. Sharing this information with them may help you avoid possible interactions.
If you have questions about interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Vascepa can interact with the following herbal supplements:
These supplements are reported to increase the risk of bleeding. Vascepa also increases this risk. So combining Vascepa and one or more of these supplements can further raise your risk of bleeding.
In addition, fish oil supplements may be unnecessary if you’re prescribed Vascepa. Vascepa contains a form of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) as its active ingredient. And EPA is a key ingredient in many fish oil supplements.
For this reason, it’s important to check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any of these products with Vascepa. Your doctor can advise on whether you should stop taking the supplement if you’re prescribed Vascepa.
There are currently no reports of Vascepa interacting with vitamins. But this doesn’t mean that vitamin interactions won’t be recognized in the future.
For this reason, it’s still important to check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any of these products while taking Vascepa.
If you drink green tea, talk with your doctor before consuming it while taking Vascepa. As noted above, supplements that contain green tea extract may interact with Vascepa by increasing your risk of bleeding. (Vascepa also increases this risk.)
Drinking green tea can also increase your risk of bleeding if you’re taking Vascepa. However, whether or not your doctor advises you to avoid green tea will likely depend on other risk factors you may have for bleeding. You and your doctor can discuss the risks and benefits of consuming green tea while taking Vascepa.
Learn more about the health benefits of green tea.
If you have questions about eating certain foods during your treatment with Vascepa, talk with your doctor.
There are currently no reports of Vascepa interacting with vaccines. If you have questions about getting certain vaccines during your Vascepa treatment, talk with your doctor.
There are currently no reports of Vascepa interacting with lab tests. If you have questions about having certain lab tests during your treatment with Vascepa, talk with the healthcare professional ordering the test.
There are currently no reports of Vascepa interacting with cannabis (commonly called marijuana) or cannabis products such as cannabidiol (CBD). But as with any drug or supplement, talk with your doctor before using cannabis with Vascepa.
Note: Cannabis is illegal at a federal level but is legal in many states to varying degrees.
Certain medical conditions or other health factors may raise the risk of interactions with Vascepa. Before taking Vascepa, talk with your doctor about your health history. They’ll determine whether Vascepa is right for you.
Health conditions or other factors that might interact with Vascepa include:
Atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter: In rare cases, atrial fibrillation (AFib) and atrial flutter have been reported as side effects in people taking Vascepa. If you already have AFib or atrial flutter, taking Vascepa could worsen your condition.
If your doctor prescribes Vascepa, they may closely monitor your heart health throughout treatment. Or they may recommend a treatment besides Vascepa for your condition.
Bleeding condition: Be sure to let your doctor know if you have a bleeding condition, such as hemophilia, before you start taking Vascepa. Treatment with Vascepa increases your risk of bleeding, and having a bleeding condition can further raise this risk. Due to this risk, your doctor may suggest a treatment besides Vascepa for your condition.
Liver problems: It’s not known whether Vascepa is safe to take if you have a liver condition. Studies of the drug didn’t include people with liver problems.
If you have a liver problem such as cirrhosis, your doctor may want to closely monitor your liver health if you take Vascepa. They may do this by ordering blood tests or other diagnostic tests throughout your treatment. 
Fish or shellfish allergy: Vascepa contains icosapent ethyl, which is made from omega-3 fatty acids found in fish oil. If you have a fish or shellfish allergy, you may have an allergic reaction if you take Vascepa. You can ask your doctor about other treatments that may be better choices for you.
Pregnancy: It’s not known whether Vascepa is safe to take during pregnancy. If you’re pregnant or planning a pregnancy, talk with your doctor before taking Vascepa. 
Breastfeeding: It’s not known whether it’s safe to take Vascepa while breastfeeding. The drug passes into breast milk, but it isn’t known whether the drug may cause side effects in a child who is breastfed. If you’re breastfeeding or planning to do so, talk with your doctor about your options.
Allergic reaction: If you’ve had an allergic reaction to Vascepa or any of its ingredients, your doctor will likely not prescribe Vascepa. This is because taking the drug could cause another allergic reaction. You can ask your doctor about other treatments that may be better choices for you.
Taking certain steps can help you avoid interactions with Vascepa. Before starting treatment, talk with your doctor and pharmacist. Things to discuss with them include:
It’s also important to understand Vascepa’s label and other paperwork that may come with the drug. Colored stickers that describe interactions may be on the label. And the paperwork (sometimes called the patient package insert or medication guide) may have other details about interactions. (If you did not get paperwork with Vascepa, ask your pharmacist to print a copy for you.)
If you have trouble reading or understanding this information, your doctor or pharmacist can help.
Taking Vascepa exactly as prescribed can also help prevent interactions.

title: What Types of Sleep Apnea Devices Are Available?
content:
Various medical devices are available to help treat sleep apnea. Choosing the right one comes down to the severity of your condition, your personal preferences, and your lifestyle. 
Sleep apnea is a sleep disorder marked by interruptions or pauses in breathing during sleep. Over time, this condition may decrease sleep quality and increase the risk of health complications like hypertension, diabetes, and heart disease. 
In addition to lifestyle changes and adjustments to sleeping positions, treatment involves using devices to help keep the airway open during sleep and prevent disruptions in oxygen flow to the body.
Learn more about what devices are available to treat sleep apnea, how each works, and how to decide which one may work best for you.
Sleep apnea is caused by either an inability of the brain to control breathing during sleep (central sleep apnea) or a physical blockage in the upper airway, like the tongue falling backward (obstructive sleep apnea). Both types can be treated with devices that work to ensure better oxygen flow to the body.
A sleep apnea device is a medical tool — machine, appliance, or implant — that helps people breathe more easily during sleep. 
Various devices are on the market, but they all share the goal of keeping the airway open and preventing pauses in breathing. These devices can improve sleep quality and reduce the health risks associated with sleep apnea.
PAP devices are the most common form of treatment for sleep apnea. These machines provide constant air pressure throughout your upper airways. This positive pressure keeps airways open and allows for unobstructed breathing while you sleep. 
Types of PAP devices include:
Side effects of PAP devices may include:
It is important to note that these side effects can be addressed with adjustments to your PAP equipment.
A doctor may prescribe an oral appliance to wear during sleep. This device fits like a mouth guard or retainer on both the upper and lower teeth. A dentist will take impressions of your teeth so it is custom to you. When you wear it, it holds the jaw forward to keep your airway open. 
A tongue-retaining device can also be made to prevent the tongue from falling backward into the airway. This device consists of a clear silicone cover that holds the tongue in a forward position during sleep, keeping the airway unobstructed. 
Side effects of oral appliances may include:
Inspire therapy involves surgically inserting a small device under the skin of the upper chest, just below the collarbone. 
The implant provides mild electrical stimulation to the tongue and nearby muscles, keeping the airway open. This device is controlled using a remote that allows it to be turned on for sleep and turned off during daytime hours.
Surgery to insert an implant is typically an outpatient procedure. Still, surgery is more invasive than other options and may carry certain risks.
While similar to PAP machines in purpose, an EPAP device does not require electricity or batteries to work. Instead, this device fits into or over the nostrils. It helps to maintain positive airway pressure and prevents airway collapse by creating resistance in a person’s exhalations (breaths out).
A pillow or other bed device may help people with sleep apnea caused by gravity and sleep position. Positional devices help guide the body to a side-sleeping position. When a person sleeps on their side, the tongue and throat are less likely to obstruct the airway.
Another option for positional sleep apnea is to wear a device on the body (chest or neck) that alerts the user to back sleeping. The accelerometer will vibrate with varying intensity to encourage repositioning to a side-sleeping position.
This device is worn in the mouth while you are awake for just 20 minutes each day. It works by delivering mild electrical currents to the tongue muscle, strengthening the muscle over time so it does not relax and block the airway during sleep. 
Choosing the right sleep apnea device depends on factors like the severity of your condition, your preferences, and your lifestyle. Working with a healthcare professional is key to finding the best treatment.

Ultimately, the best device is one that effectively manages your apnea while being comfortable enough that you’ll continue using it. A doctor can walk you through the pros and cons, plus suggest types to try based on your unique needs.
Sleep apnea devices can help treat sleep apnea when combined with other lifestyle changes. A doctor can help you find the most effective device that fits both your lifestyle and comfort preferences.

title: How Does Sensorimotor Psychotherapy Work?
content:
Sensorimotor psychotherapy is a type of movement therapy that can be used to treat trauma disorders. It works to strengthen the mind-body connection in an effort to relieve the physical symptoms of trauma. 
Sensorimotor psychotherapy is a type of somatic (physical-based) therapy. It was created to treat trauma and trauma-related disorders. 
It is considered a body-centered talk therapy. It combines movement and talk therapy to help heal and address deeper emotional issues. It is also known as body psychotherapy.
Sensorimotor psychotherapy can help address the physical symptoms of trauma, which traditional therapy can sometimes overlook. These physical symptoms can include stomach issues and nausea, sleep problems, severe headaches, muscle pains, or even changes in heart rate. 
Sensorimotor psychotherapy aims to address the mind, body, and spirit as a whole. Knowing how the body reacts to certain thoughts and feelings can help people address their experiences and eventually move forward.
Sensorimotor psychotherapy can benefit people who have tried more traditional talk therapy and found it triggering or unhelpful.

title: Mental Health and Suicide Risk in People with Multiple Sclerosis
content:
People with MS may be twice as likely to die by suicide as people in the larger population. But research suggests that coping strategies and social support can significantly reduce this risk.
A diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) can be daunting. Many people experience significant mental health challenges after diagnosis, including depression, anxiety, and stress. Related symptoms like sleep problems and fatigue can also affect quality of life.
For some people with MS, these challenges can lead to thoughts of suicide. However, research shows that recognizing the signs and offering the right kind of support can significantly reduce suicide risk among people with MS.
If you or someone you know is considering suicide, you’re not alone. Help is available right now:
Research has consistently found a higher suicide rate among people with multiple sclerosis than those in the broader population.
For example, a 2019 review of studies found that people with MS were 72% more likely to die by suicide than those in the broader population.
The review also found that the risk of suicide at diagnosis was higher than the risk at the onset of symptoms. Suicide risk was more than double that of the broader population at the time of diagnosis.
Earlier research from 2017 examined nine studies from across Europe and North America. Researchers in that review concluded that the suicide risk among people with MS was about twice that of the broader population.
A 2024 study found that 19.1% (about 1 in 5) of people with MS experienced suicidal ideation (suicidal thoughts) across their lifetime. That was more than double the rate in the broader population.
A 2023 review found that 4.1% of people (about 1 in 25) with MS attempted suicide. However, that study did not include a control group.
Depression is the most significant causal risk factor for suicide in people with MS. Up to 50% of people with MS experience depression at some point in their lives. Yet, some experts say it often goes unrecognized and untreated.
Even though MS is three times as common in females, a 2017 review noted that young males with MS may be at higher risk of suicide within the first 5 years of their diagnosis.
A 2019 review also noted that social isolation and reduced independence are key risk factors for suicidal ideation in people with MS.
A 2024 study identified additional risk factors, including:
Notably, the study researchers found that support strategies that allowed people with MS to feel more independent reduced the effect of all the risk factors except for household income.

Despite the mental health challenges that may accompany an MS diagnosis, several avenues of support are available. Recommended options include:
Joining an MS support group can be helpful, especially for people with a new diagnosis. In-person and online support groups are available. Some people benefit from a combination.
The following resources may be helpful:
If you’re looking to connect with other people with MS, resources like Healthline’s Bezzy MS also offer an online safe space for community, guidance from peers and experts, and support.
A 2020 study found a link between social support for people with MS and a lower likelihood of suicidal thoughts or risk factors for them. Social support can be:
If you notice signs of suicidal ideation in someone with MS, you may want to talk with them about it if you feel comfortable doing so. Some people worry that bringing up a sensitive topic like suicide may increase the risk, but experts note that this is not the case.
If you suspect that someone with MS may be thinking about suicide, try encouraging them to get help by contacting a mental health professional or a suicide hotline.
Mental health challenges, like depression and anxiety, are common among people with MS, especially soon after a diagnosis. This can cause people with MS to experience suicidal thoughts at rates twice as high as the larger population.

title: What Is I and A in Medicare?
content:
In Medicare, online tools such as the Provider Enrollment, Chain, and Ownership System (PECOS) help streamline the enrollment of doctors and healthcare organizations. This makes it easier for them to securely submit and manage their enrollment information electronically.
To access these tools all in one place, healthcare organizations and professionals can use the Identity and Access Management (I&A) system.
In the past, healthcare organizations had to register for several different systems from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to track Medicare enrollment and reimbursement.
I&A was created to simplify this process. With the I&A system, doctors and the healthcare organizations they work for can more easily complete Medicare enrollment tasks in one place, using just one online login.
Using I&A, healthcare organizations can access:
To create an I&A account, healthcare organizations need to register on the CMS website.
They will then need to print, sign, and mail any additional required materials to a CMS-contracted Medicare fee-for-service contractor or Medicare administrative contractor. This contractor will then process the materials and decide on enrollment status.
In general, “identify and access management” refers to the way organizations make sure that only the right people, organizations, or their representatives have access to their internal systems.
In Medicare billing, a surrogate is an organization that is working on behalf of a healthcare organization or individual doctor to access, view, and modify CMS information.
As part of the application to create an NPI with the NPPES, the person filling out the application has to indicate whether they represent the healthcare organization directly or are their surrogate.
Before, healthcare organizations had to register on multiple CMS systems to keep track of Medicare enrollment and reimbursements.

title: What Are the Symptoms of UC Outside the Intestines?
content:
Ulcerative colitis causes ulcers in your large intestine that can lead to gastrointestinal problems. Some people with ulcerative colitis develop symptoms in other body parts, such as their joints or skin.
Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis are collectively known as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Ulcerative colitis commonly causes symptoms like abdominal pain or diarrhea.
Up to 50% of people with IBD develop symptoms outside of their large intestines in places like their joints, eyes, or skin. The underlying cause of these extraintestinal manifestations isn’t well understood but is thought to be related to the gut’s inflammation response.
Read on to learn more about the symptoms of ulcerative colitis and IBD outside the intestines, collectively called “extraintestinal” manifestations.
Extraintestinal manifestations of ulcerative colitis can affect many parts of your body. Up to a quarter of people with IBD may experience them. These are some of the specific types you might develop.
Arthritis is the most frequent extraintestinal manifestation of IBD. It may occur in up to 40% of people. It may occur before, at the same time, or after the onset of gastrointestinal symptoms.

Eye symptoms seem to appear in about 4% to 12% of people with IBD with similar rates in people with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis.
Eye complications may include:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis and autoimmune hepatitis occur in almost 5% of people with IBD. Autoimmune hepatitis is when your immune system attacks healthy cells in your liver. 
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is another autoimmune condition where the bile ducts inside and outside of your liver become inflamed.
Some people may develop kidney stones or obstruction of the urinary tract. IBD may also be linked to some types of urinary tract cancers, such as bladder or kidney cancer.
The risk of venous blood clots in people with IBD is thought to be about double compared to people without IBD.

Joint pain is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease, followed by skin problems, liver and gallbladder problems, and eye problems.
Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis can cause similar extraintestinal symptoms. Some research suggests that thoracic symptoms like airway problems or lung problems might be more common in ulcerative colitis. 
Ulcerative colitis most often causes gastrointestinal symptoms, but some people develop symptoms affecting other parts of their body, such as the joints, skin, or eyes.

title: What Is Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome (CAPS)?
content:
Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS) is a rare and life threatening complication of antiphospholipid syndrome. Up to half of people with CAPS die, so timely treatment is essential.
Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune disease that increases your risk of blood clots. 
Fewer than 1% of people with APS can experience a complication of this disease called catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS), where symptoms become widespread suddenly and progress rapidly.
As CAPS can affect multiple organ systems, symptoms can vary, and treatment can be challenging. CAPS is potentially life threatening and requires immediate medical attention.
Read on to learn how to recognize the symptoms of CAPS, how doctors work to diagnose and treat it quickly, and what the outlook may be for people who experience this complication.
CAPS has a traditionally reported mortality rate of around 50%.
However, research over the past two decades suggests that survival rates have increased due to improvements in diagnosis and treatment. Some reports suggest that current mortality rates are closer to 25% to 30%.
CAPS causes blood clots to form throughout your body. Symptoms can vary significantly depending on which organs are affected.
Symptoms of CAPS may include:
CAPS symptoms come on suddenly and develop rapidly.
CAPS requires emergency medical care. If you or someone you know is experiencing sudden onset of the above symptoms, or has APS that suddenly gets worse, call 911 or your local emergency services right away.

Even though CAPS is a complication of APS, it may be the first presentation of the disease, especially in children and young adults. This can sometimes complicate diagnosis.
There’s no known optimal treatment for CAPS. However, treatment typically involves a type of combination treatment known as “triple therapy,” involving:
Doctors exercise caution when prescribing IVIG, as the risk of serious side effects, such as acute kidney failure and thrombosis, may be high for some people.
Your medical team may need to pause anticoagulation therapy if you’re about to undergo a medical procedure, such as a surgery, biopsy, or dental extraction.
If these treatments don’t work, a doctor may consider monoclonal antibodies like rituximab or eculizumab. These reduce the number of B cells, which help produce antiphospholipid antibodies.

Since CAPS is a rare disease, it’s challenging for researchers to identify other risk factors. However, there may be a genetic component.

Some of the most common complications of CAPS include:
CAPS occurs in fewer than 1% of people with antiphospholipid syndrome.
CAPS is a rare complication of APS. In some cases, it may be the first presentation of APS symptoms.

For a diagnosis of CAPS, symptoms typically progress within a week.
To prevent CAPS, experts recommend that people with APS keep taking anticoagulation therapy as prescribed by a doctor. They also recommend effective management and prevention of infections after operations.
Though rare, CAPS is a serious and potentially life threatening complication of APS. It can lead to blood clots in multiple organs and tissues, causing a wide range of symptoms. Even with treatment, many people experience fatal complications.
Still, timely treatment and diagnosis are essential to improving your chances of survival. If you have APS or another condition that puts you at risk of blood clots (like lupus), seek emergency help immediately if you experience rapidly progressing symptoms like blood in your urine or shortness of breath.
