Prescription medications for poison ivy are essential for managing severe cases, topical corticosteroids like clobetasol and triamcinolone can effectively reduce symptoms such as rash, itching, and inflammation.
For more extensive or unresponsive cases, a healthcare professional may prescribe an oral prescription medication for poison ivy, such as prednisone, to manage severe symptoms and prevent complications.

title: Pulmicort: Breastfeeding and Pregnancy Information
content:
Pulmicort (budesonide) is an asthma drug that’s considered safe to use while pregnant. The drug passes into breast milk but is also considered safe to use while breastfeeding.
Pulmicort is generally considered safe to use while pregnant. The drug hasn’t been found to raise the risk of complications if used during pregnancy. Doctors often prescribe budesonide (the active ingredient in Pulmicort) for pregnant people over other options due to its long safety record when used during pregnancy.
Pulmicort is used to treat asthma. It’s important to note that not treating this condition during pregnancy may also carry certain risks.
Because of this, you and your doctor should discuss the risks and benefits of taking Pulmicort while pregnant versus not treating your condition during pregnancy.
If you have questions about using Pulmicort while pregnant, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
If you’re currently breastfeeding or planning to do so, it’s important to understand the effects that Pulmicort could have on you or the child who is breastfed.
Pulmicort is considered safe to use while breastfeeding. Budesonide, the active ingredient in Pulmicort, passes into breast milk. But no side effects have been reported in children exposed to Pulmicort through breast milk.
If you have questions or concerns about using Pulmicort while breastfeeding, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.

title: Does Medicare Cover Cremation Costs?
content:
Medicare is a federal insurance program that provides healthcare coverage for people ages 65 years and older and younger people with disabilities. It does not cover funeral or burial expenses, including cremation.
While Medicare does not cover funeral benefits, the Social Security Administration (SSA) offers a $255 lump sum death benefit to a surviving spouse or child of the deceased. This benefit can help pay for cremation services, although it will not cover the entire amount.
Some states offer burial assistance programs that can also help pay for cremation expenses.
This article examines the cost of cremations, savings options to consider, and resources you can explore to help cover these costs.
According to the National Funeral Directors Association, the rate of cremation is rising in the United States, with a projected increase of 1.3% since 2023, leading to a rate of 61.9% for 2024. In comparison, burial rates for 2024 are expected to decrease by 1.3% to 33.2%.
The increased preference for cremation is thought to be influenced by environmental concerns, fewer religious requirements, and cost.
The cost of cremation in the United States ranges from $795 to $3,200, depending on your location, type of cremation, and the funeral home or cremation provider you choose.
Factors that affect the cost of cremation include:
You can use this online tool to find reference guides that include the different rules, regulations, and cost of cremations for each state.
While Medicare does not cover funeral and cremation costs, there are other financial assistance options worth pursuing. These include:
Medicare does not cover the cost of funeral and burial services, including cremation. 
The SSA provides a one-time lump payment of $255 that can be used towards cremation costs.

title: Can You Get the Bird Flu Virus by Drinking Dairy Milk?
content:
There’s been an ongoing outbreak of bird flu in dairy cows since March 2024. The pasteurization process ensures that milk is safe to drink by killing the virus. However, raw milk may still contain bird flu.
There are many different types, subtypes, and lineages of influenza (flu) virus. Avian influenza, or bird flu, is a type of flu virus that mainly affects birds. It can be either highly pathogenic (HPAI) or low pathogenic (LPAI).
In March 2024, HPAI was reported in dairy cows in several states, marking the first time this type of flu virus has been found in cows. Shortly afterward, scientists detected the virus in samples of raw, unpasteurized milk.
You may be wondering whether the milk that you buy from the store is safe to consume. The answer is yes.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza, or HPAI, is a type of bird flu that causes a severe, and often fatal, illness in birds.
Like other influenza A viruses, bird flu is characterized by two proteins found on its surface: hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA). In birds, there are 16 different types of HA and nine different types of NA.
HPAI viruses have one of two HA types, 5 or 7, and are called H5 and H7 viruses. While many H5 and H7 viruses are low pathogenic (LPAI), meaning they cause milder illness, viruses like H5N1, H5N8, and H7N9 are all HPAI.
H5N1 is the HPAI virus that was found in dairy cows.
It’s highly unlikely that you can catch bird flu from milk. Pasteurization is a big reason for this.
Pasteurization is the process through which raw milk or other milk-based products are heated to kill any germs that are in them, such as viruses and bacteria.
It involves heating milk to a high temperature, often 161°F (72°C), for at least 15 seconds before cooling it back down.
In a May 2024 study of bird flu virus in cow’s milk, scientists used lab equipment to heat milk samples to 161°F for 15 seconds. They found that this significantly reduced the amount of virus in the sample but didn’t completely inactivate it.
Another June 2024 study supported these findings. It reported a very significant drop in the amount of virus in milk after 5 seconds at 161°F.
However, there was still a very small amount of active virus at 20 seconds.
While these results are informative, they don’t reflect real-world conditions. The scientists in both studies stressed that they cannot replicate the commercial pasteurization process using their lab equipment.
That’s where a July 2024 study comes in. Researchers in this study analyzed a total of 297 samples of grade A pasteurized milk products. Samples included 132 milk processors from 38 states.
The scientists detected the virus’s genetic material in 20.2% of the samples. However, infectious virus was not found. That means that pasteurization was effective at killing bird flu virus in milk.
The bottom line: It’s safe to consume commercially available milk products. That’s because the pasteurization process can effectively kill bird flu virus and other germs present in milk.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there have been a total of 58 cases of bird flu in people in 2024 as of December 2024.
Of these, 31 of them were associated with exposure to cows. No person-to-person spread of bird flu has been reported.
The people who have contracted bird flu from cows have been workers on dairy or cattle farms. They got the virus through having close contact with cows, not by drinking milk.
The commercial milk supply remains safe, according to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). That’s because 99% of commercially available milk in the United States is pasteurized before entering the market, the organization says.
There still may be a risk of getting sick if you consume raw, unpasteurized milk. For example, the May 2024 study above found that mice became ill after consuming raw milk samples containing bird flu.
According to the FDA, there’s limited research on whether bird flu can be transmitted to humans through raw milk products.
However, the CDC recommends against consuming raw milk in general. That’s because consuming raw milk products can expose you to other harmful germs, such as:
While pasteurization can kill the bird flu virus in milk, further measures are in place to help prevent human illness.
The CDC, FDA, and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) continue to track and monitor the spread of bird flu in cows.
According to the USDA, milk from cows known to be sick with bird flu is being diverted out of the commercial milk supply and destroyed.
The best way to prevent getting ill from drinking dairy milk containing the bird flu virus is to only drink pasteurized milk.
Pretty much all milk in the United States that’s available to consumers is pasteurized. However, if you’re ever unsure, follow the tips below.
You may also be wondering if the flu vaccine can protect you from bird flu. The answer is no.
While the flu vaccine is safe and effective for preventing serious illness from the seasonal flu, it cannot protect against bird flu. Bird flu viruses are quite different from the flu strains included in the seasonal flu vaccine.
The overall risk to the general public from bird flu is low. The vast majority of the people who have contracted bird flu have had close contact with sick cows or birds.
If you’ve been exposed to an animal, either alive or dead, that may have had bird flu, contact your doctor if you have symptoms like:
Be sure to let them know that you had close contact with an animal that may have been sick with bird flu.
Consuming raw milk products can lead to illness in general, especially food poisoning. Contact a doctor if you’ve consumed raw milk and are having symptoms like:
A total of 15 states have had confirmed bird flu in dairy cows since March 2024. These are California, Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico, Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, South Dakota, Minnesota, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio, and North Carolina.
Yes, it’s safe to drink commercially available dairy milk. Pasteurization kills bird flu and other germs in the milk. Milk from sick cows is being removed from the commercial supply and destroyed.
Pasteurization can kill bird flu virus in milk. Similar to seasonal flu virus, cleaning and disinfecting can kill virus on surfaces, while handwashing can help to remove virus from your hands.
Since March 2024, there’s been an ongoing bird flu outbreak in dairy cows. Bird flu has also been detected in milk from these cows.

title: Aptiom and Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Birth Control
content:
Aptiom is a prescription drug that’s used to treat focal onset seizures (also called partial onset seizures). The drug comes as an oral tablet. It’s not known whether Aptiom is safe to take while pregnant or breastfeeding.
Keep reading to learn more about Aptiom and reproductive health. And for a detailed overview of this drug, check out this article.
If you can become pregnant, it’s important to consider whether Aptiom is a safe option for you. 
It’s not known whether Aptiom is safe to take during pregnancy. Animal studies have shown that Aptiom can raise the risk of developmental problems in a fetus (also known as birth defects). However, animal studies don’t always predict what may happen in humans.
More research is still needed, as there haven’t been enough human studies done to determine the risk to the fetus if Aptiom is taken during pregnancy.
It’s possible that Aptiom may affect fertility (the ability to conceive a child). But more research is still required.
In animal studies, Aptiom affected the embryo’s development and decreased fertility. But animal studies don’t always predict what may happen in humans. Human studies have not yet looked at whether fertility may be affected by Aptiom.
If you’re planning to conceive, talk with your doctor about Aptiom and fertility. They may recommend a different medication for you.
If you’re currently breastfeeding or planning to do so, it’s important to understand the effects that Aptiom could have on you or the child who is breastfed.

title: Is Provigil a Controlled Substance?
content:
Provigil (modafinil) is considered a Schedule IV controlled substance due to its small risk of potential abuse, dependence, or addiction. The drug is taken to treat excessive sleepiness caused by certain sleep disorders. 
All known medications that have a risk of abuse or dependence are classified into one of five categories. The United States Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classify these categories as controlled substances.
Within these categories, Schedule I drugs have the highest risk of abuse and have no known medical use. On the other hand, Schedule V drugs have the lowest potential for abuse.
Provigil is a Schedule IV drug. This means that the risk of abuse with the drug is low. But a few cases have been reported in medical literature.
Note: While “misuse,” rather than “abuse,” is now commonly used, this article uses “abuse” to match the sources. Abuse is taking a drug in a way other than how a doctor prescribes it.
Controlled substances are medications, illegal drugs, or recreational drugs that primarily act on your central nervous system (CNS). (The CNS includes your brain and spinal cord.) These drugs can lead to a physical or mental dependence or addiction. They also may have the potential for serious complications at high doses. (With dependence, your body needs the drug to function as usual. With addiction, a drug is used even if it’s causing harmful outcomes.)
The United States government oversees the distribution of controlled substances to restrict their usage. All controlled substances require a prescription, but all prescription medications are not controlled substances. 
The table below explains the categories of controlled substances, including information from the DEA and a 2023 published source.
Provigil is a Schedule IV controlled substance, which is defined as having a low risk of physical or mental dependence and a low risk of abuse. Despite Provigil having a low risk of abuse, rare cases of addiction have been recorded in medical literature. (Remember, with addiction, a drug is used even if it’s causing harmful outcomes.) It’s important to note that these cases involved the use of modafinil, which is a generic version of Provigil.
A 2018 publication notes that a 24-year-old person from Turkey developed dependence with the use of modafinil. This person had been taking high doses of modafinil to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). When not taking the drug, they developed:
A 2015 publication also notes dependence in a 44-year-old person from India, which was also with the use of modafinil. This person also took antipsychotics to treat psychiatric symptoms that developed following the death of their parent.
Provigil is a type of stimulant known as a nonamphetamine. Stimulants are medications that increase CNS activity in your body and increase alertness. (The CNS includes your brain and spinal cord.) 
The way Provigil works in your brain isn’t well understood.
Modafinil is not a narcotic. Narcotics are drugs that affect your mood or behavior. People take them for nonmedical reasons, and often they’re sold illegally. The best-known example might be heroin, including products made from it. 
Provigil is a Schedule IV controlled substance. As such, healthcare professionals consider it to have a low risk of abuse and a low risk of physical or mental dependence. While Provigil has a low risk of abuse, rare cases of addiction have been recorded in medical literature. But these cases involved the use of modafinil, which is a generic version of Provigil.
Before taking Provigil, it’s a good idea to talk with your doctor about potential side effects and risks. They can best advise you about these and the benefits of Provigil to treat your condition.

title: Understanding the Connection Between Menopause and Heart Rate Changes
content:
Menopause causes a drop in estrogen, which can lead to changes in heart rate, such as palpitations or fluctuations in heart rhythm.
Menopause marks a significant transition in a person’s life, bringing about various physical and hormonal changes. 
One key aspect of this transition is the effect on heart rate, which can fluctuate due to hormonal shifts, particularly a decrease in estrogen levels.
Menopause can lead to heart rate changes, including symptoms like palpitations and shifts in heart rate variability.
These symptoms are often linked to hormonal fluctuations, particularly the drop in estrogen levels, which can affect the autonomic nervous system that controls heart rate and blood pressure. 
Heart palpitations, or feelings of rapid or irregular heartbeats, are common during menopause, affecting up to 42% of perimenopausal and 54% of postmenopausal women. 
Palpitations are associated with worse sleep, stress, depression, and reduced quality of life.
One study categorized women into three groups based on the frequency of heart palpitations during menopause:
The study found no connection between palpitations and early indicators of heart disease, such as arterial stiffness or hardened arteries.
You’ll notice that the language used to share stats and other data points is pretty binary, fluctuating between the use of “male” and “female” or “men” and “women.”
Although we typically avoid language like this, specificity is key when reporting on research participants and clinical findings.The studies and surveys referenced in this article didn’t report data on, or include, participants who were transgender, nonbinary, gender nonconforming, genderqueer, agender, or genderless.
Heart rate variability (HRV) measures the time between heartbeats, reflecting how well the body adapts to stress and physical changes. A higher HRV indicates a healthier heart and better stress response, while a lower HRV may signal health issues.
Menopause, particularly postmenopause, can affect heart health by lowering HRV.
One study found that postmenopausal women had lower HRV at rest compared to premenopausal women. 
While the difference wasn’t significant after adjusting for age and body weight, postmenopausal women experienced a greater drop in HRV when exposed to stress, suggesting a reduced ability to handle stress.
Another study showed that women with severe menopause symptoms, like hot flashes, had lower HRV, indicating less balance between the heart and nervous system, which could raise heart-related risks during menopause.
Symptoms of heart rate changes can include:
Estrogen helps regulate heart rate and supports cardiovascular health by balancing the autonomic nervous system. It increases parasympathetic activity (slowing heart rate) and reduces sympathetic activity (speeding heart rate), leading to a steadier, lower resting heart rate. 
Estrogen also enhances HRV, a marker of good cardiovascular health.
During high estrogen phases of the menstrual cycle, heart rate often decreases slightly, while postmenopause, declining estrogen levels can lead to higher resting heart rates and lower HRV, increasing cardiovascular risks. 
Overall, estrogen promotes heart health by improving nervous system balance and blood flow.
Changes in heart rate can indicate how well the heart and nervous system are functioning. A consistently high resting heart rate or low HRV may signal difficulties with cardiovascular health, increased stress, or hormonal imbalances. 
These changes are linked to a higher risk of heart disease, high blood pressure, and other conditions. Monitoring heart rate changes can help detect potential health issues early and guide interventions to reduce risks.
Menopause brings various changes to the body, including fluctuations in heart rate and heart rate variability. These changes may affect heart health, with lower HRV indicating potential cardiovascular risks.

When the biologic drug’s patent expires, other drugmakers can create biosimilar versions. This competition in the market may lead to lower costs for biosimilars. And because biosimilars are very similar to biologic drugs, they don’t need to be studied again. This can also lead to lower costs for biosimilars.

title: Which Neurological Conditions Affect Vision?
content:
Visual changes can often be a symptom of a neurological condition, such as stroke, migraine, or an infection. In some cases, changes may be permanent or progressive, but in many cases, prompt diagnosis and treatment can help.
You may not think about it, but your nervous system plays an essential role in your vision. Visual information from your eyes travels to your brain through the optic nerve. The part of your brain that interprets visual information from your optic nerve is your visual cortex.
Any neurological condition that causes problems with your optic nerve, visual cortex, or the parts of your brain that relay information between these structures can cause visual changes.
Read on to learn more about some of the neurological conditions that can cause vision loss.
Symptoms of neurological vision problems vary depending on the underlying cause. They might onset quickly or develop slowly over weeks to years. 
Potential symptoms include:
Migraine is a neurological condition that often causes severe headaches, especially on one side. Some people have migraine aura, which are sensory symptoms that occur before migraine headaches. Nearly everyone who experiences migraine aura has symptoms such as:
Some people experience ocular migraine, also called retinal migraine. These episodes often cause:
Retinal migraine causes symptoms in one eye. Migraine with aura will typically affect both eyes.
Traumatic brain injury is characterized by brain damage from an external force such as those caused by:
If you have damage to parts of your brain that control vision, you may have symptoms such as:
Optic neuritis is swelling in your optic nerve that might cause:
The cause of optic neuritis isn’t known, but it may be due to an autoimmune reaction where your body attacks your optic nerve. It’s more common in people with some conditions, such as:
In a 2023 study, researchers estimated optic neuritis occurred in 8.1 people per 100,00 in the United States from 2006 to 2018. Females seem to develop it more than males.
A stroke occurs due to a blocked or bleeding blood vessel in your brain. Experts estimate strokes occur in nearly 800,000 people per year in the United States.
Strokes commonly cause visual changes such as:
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a neurological condition in which your immune system attacks a protective layer around your nerves called myelin. Damage to myelin can lead to slowed nerve conduction. Experts estimate it affects 2.8 million people worldwide.
In addition to other symptoms, MS can cause vision loss in one eye and symptoms of optic neuritis. Up to 70% of people with MS develop an episode of optic neuritis.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive neurological condition that affects neurons in your brain that produce the neurotransmitter dopamine. It commonly causes symptoms such as tremors, slowed movement, and balance problems. 
The World Health Organization estimates that Parkinson’s disease affects more than 8.5 million people globally.
Many people with Parkinson’s disease experience visual problems such as:
Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune condition in which your immune system attacks neuromuscular junctions, where your nerves send information to your muscles to contract.
Some people develop eye symptoms such as:
Most people develop problems with other muscles within a couple of years.
An infection in your brain is called encephalitis. The most common causes include:
Brain infections can cause many neurological symptoms, including changes to your vision.
Chronically high blood sugar levels in people with diabetes can damage nerves. Diabetic retinopathy occurs when these blood sugar levels damage the retina at the back of your eye. Symptoms can include:
Brain tumors can be cancerous or benign (noncancerous). Even tumors that aren’t cancer can cause problems if they grow large and press on healthy brain tissue.
If a tumor presses on your optic nerve, visual cortex, or other important visual structures, you may develop symptoms such as:
Most people think of glaucoma as an eye condition, but it’s also a neurological condition. Glaucoma affects the eye by causing optic nerve degeneration, often as a complication of high eye pressure.
Glaucoma usually doesn’t cause symptoms in the early stages, but it can eventually lead to blindness. Some people are at an increased risk of glaucoma, including people who:
Eye movement disorders are a group of conditions that cause problems with the muscles and nerves that control your eyes. They may cause:
Eye movement disorders can develop due to genetic diseases or injury to your eye muscles or nerves.
It’s important to visit an eye doctor if you notice new changes to your vision, especially if these symptoms develop quickly or are severe. Many eye conditions have the best outlook when you initiate treatment promptly.
Many neurological conditions cause visual problems. Some may be temporary, while others might be permanent or progressive.

title: Neurological Symptoms of Mold Exposure
content:
Problems with memory, balance, and other thinking and motor skills are among the potential health consequences of inhaling mold spores.
Mold is a type of fungus that can grow in damp places, like basements, bathrooms, or even on old food. If you breathe in mold spores or come into contact with mold, you can experience various health problems, including neurological symptoms.
Symptoms affecting the brain and nervous system can range from mild headaches to more serious problems like memory loss or difficulty walking. Children, older adults, and people who are pregnant or have weakened immune systems are especially vulnerable to complications from mold exposure.
This article will explain the potential neurological effects of mold exposure, what symptoms to watch for, and when you should contact a doctor.
A 2020 study suggested that mold exposure can cause neurological symptoms in two main ways:
One example of a mold that can cause infection is Cladophialophora bantiana, which can invade the brain and spinal cord. This can lead to a serious condition called central nervous system (CNS) infection. While CNS infections are rare, they can be very dangerous.
More commonly, mold exposure doesn’t cause direct infections but triggers an immune response in the body that affects the nervous system. 
A 2021 animal study found that mold inhalation caused an innate immune response that led to problems with memory, anxiety symptoms, and other consequences.
Mycotoxins are toxic substances produced by certain types of mold. When mold grows inside buildings, it can release these mycotoxins into the air, which people can breathe in.
Mycotoxins can also harm the brain directly. Some research has shown that mold toxins may affect brain function by interfering with the nervous system’s communication pathways. This may lead to symptoms like headaches, memory problems, and sudden changes in mood.
Several neurological symptoms can result from mold exposure, and there’s often no way to tell who will be affected or what health complications might occur. 
Symptoms can vary greatly depending on the person’s overall health, whether they have any underlying medical conditions, and the degree of mold exposure.
Some of the most common neurological symptoms are:
Headaches are a common symptom of mold exposure and can range from mild to severe. Experts think mold-related headaches are due to the body’s immune response to mold spores or mycotoxins.
People often describe mold-triggered headaches as dull, constant, or pressure-like. They can sometimes feel like a migraine, and you may experience nausea or sensitivity to light and sound.
Mold, especially when it leads to CNS infections, can trigger seizures in some people. The mycotoxins produced by certain types of mold may affect the brain’s electrical activity, leading to seizures.
Though much less common than headaches, seizures are a more serious neurological symptom. If someone experiences a seizure after mold exposure, it is important to get medical help immediately.
Mold exposure can also affect a range of thinking skills problems, such as difficulty with focus, concentration, and memory — a set of symptoms often referred to as “brain fog.” People with brain fog may feel mentally slow, distracted, or confused.
A 2023 study suggested that mycotoxins might disrupt typical brain function, making it harder for the brain to process information and think clearly.
Mold exposure can also affect your emotions, causing you to experience:
The exact reason for this is still under examination, but one theory is that mold toxins may interfere with the chemicals in the brain that control mood and emotions.
Mold exposure can cause inflammation, leading to painful joints and muscle aches. It may also be a factor in developing fibromyalgia, a condition in which you feel pain throughout your body for no clear reason.
A 2020 study also suggested a link between mold exposure and the onset or worsening of complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), a condition that tends to follow severe health concerns, such as infection, heart attack, or surgery.
CRPS can produce pain that seems disproportionate to the injury or illness that caused it. Like fibromyalgia, CRPS is a chronic condition without a cure. Symptom management is usually the goal of treatment.
Some people exposed to mold may experience difficulty with movement. This can include:
Movement disorders related to mold exposure may be due to mycotoxins causing brain or nervous system damage.
In addition to movement and muscle control problems, mold exposure may also affect your balance and coordination, making it harder to walk or stand without falling. You may feel unsteady on your feet or have trouble performing tasks that require fine motor skills, like writing or using a computer or phone.
These problems may arise due to how mold toxins can affect the parts of the brain responsible for movement and balance.
Delirium is a state of confusion or disorientation that can occur due to mold exposure. A 2021 report indicated that this may be due in part to the abnormal response of the immune system to mold exposure.
People who experience delirium may be unable to focus, think clearly, or understand what’s happening around them. This is a more severe symptom and usually requires immediate medical attention.
If you suspect that mold is affecting your brain or nervous system, it’s important to contact a doctor as soon as possible. Seek medical help if you experience persistent headaches, memory problems, seizures, or other unusual neurological symptoms.
Even if you’re unsure if mold is causing your symptoms, a doctor may be able to test for mold exposure and other potential triggers and recommend treatments to help manage them.
A 2017 Finnish study of mold in homes, hospitals, schools, and other locations found that, though it rarely occurs, peripheral neuropathy is one of many neurological conditions associated with mold exposure. Peripheral neuropathy can lead to pain or numbness, often in the hands or feet.
Testing for mold toxicity typically involves a combination of blood tests and urine tests. These tests look for markers of mold exposure, such as mycotoxins in the body. 
Sometimes, more involved testing is required to make a diagnosis, which is why it’s always best to see a doctor if you think you’ve been exposed to mold.
Detoxifying from mold exposure involves:
Always consult a doctor for advice on the best way to detox rather than purchase over-the-counter products that may not be proven effective in detoxing your body from mold.
Mold exposure can cause a range of neurological symptoms, including headaches, memory problems, seizures, and mood changes. These symptoms are often due to the mycotoxins produced by mold, which can affect the brain and nervous system.
If you’re experiencing any of these symptoms, as well as respiratory difficulties or other unexplained health problems, and you suspect mold exposure, contact a doctor for help.
The best way to prevent mold-related health problems is to reduce mold in your home by managing moisture levels and addressing water damage quickly.

Gaining weight during Vraylar treatment is possible in some people. Exercise can be helpful in managing your weight, but be careful not to overheat, become dehydrated, or overexert. title: When Does Medicare Cover Lapiplasty (Bunion Correction Surgery)?
content:
Medicare covers lapiplasty if it’s medically necessary. Medicare will cover 80% of the approved amount after you’ve met your Part B deductible. You’ll pay the remaining 20%.
Lapiplasty is a newer and less invasive surgical treatment for correcting bunions. It focuses on correcting the root cause of bunions: a misaligned toe bone.
The procedure uses small medical instruments to push your metatarsal bone back into proper alignment. A surgeon then inserts a titanium plate to secure the alignment. This method permanently corrects the protrusion and straightens the toe.
Benefits include small surgical wounds, less pain after surgery, and faster recovery time. Most insurance companies, including Medicare, cover lapiplasty if it’s deemed medically necessary.
This article reviews the criteria Medicare uses for what’s considered medically necessary, along with what you’ll pay for the cost of the procedure.
Medicare Part B (medical insurance) and Medicare Advantage (Part C) cover foot exams by a podiatrist (foot specialist) and bunion treatment, including lapiplasty, if that treatment is medically necessary.
Medicare considers bunion treatment medically necessary if a podiatrist or doctor finds that your bunion deformities are severe enough to cause pain and limit your mobility.

title: Learning to Thrive: One Nurse’s Journey with HIV
content:
Bridgette Picou, a licensed vocational nurse (LVN), shares her journey with HIV — from diagnosis and treatment to caring and supporting others with the condition.
Editor’s note: This story has been edited for brevity, length, and clarity.
A certified AIDS Care Nurse in Palm Springs, California, Bridgette works as the stakeholder liaison for The Well Project, a nonprofit organization that provides information and support to women living with HIV.
Bridgette was 40 years old when she learned she had HIV. She had gone in for a routine women’s health checkup and was surprised by the diagnosis. 
“I went in to have a Pap smear done, and the clinician asked if I needed STI testing,” she told Healthline. “I told her, ‘Not really, but we can go ahead and do it while I’m here,’ and lo and behold, I got an HIV diagnosis.”
Bridgette knew enough about HIV to know that treatment was available. 
Today’s antiretroviral therapies can reduce HIV to undetectable levels in the blood, which helps prevent complications and stops the virus from passing from one person to another. Some people need to take only a single pill per day or a long-acting injection every month or every other month to treat HIV, while others may be prescribed multiple pills a day.
Even with advancements in treatment, adjusting to life with HIV can be challenging. 
“There was still a process of letting go of old stigmas, like the idea that I’m going to get sick and I’m going to die. My brain knew better, but my spirit needed the lesson,” Bridgette said. 
“I had to figure out how to navigate what felt like a new life while re-evaluating who I was and who I thought I was.”
One of the first challenges that Bridgette faced was finding treatment and support that fit her needs as a Black woman with HIV. She didn’t feel supported by the first doctor she saw for treatment and switched to another clinic.
“Even after I started going to a clinic where I felt like I was getting the care I needed, it was still a predominantly white gay space,” she said. “There was nobody that looks like me, that walks like me, that talks like me, that has my experiences. You know that saying, you can be lonely in a room full of people? That’s what it felt like.”
Bridgette knew there were other Black women living with HIV, but she had to go online to find them through social media and The Well Project. Finding women with similar life experiences was important for creating a sense of trust and mutual understanding.
“Because of all of the structural, institutional racial systems that Black women face, there’s a core that we recognize in each other,” she explained. “When you use that as a foundation to build on, it opens up trust, and it opens up the kinds of tough conversations that you can’t have with other people.”
Bridgette also found a growing sense of connection with other people who were getting care at her HIV clinic. She found that despite their different life histories, they could relate over the shared challenges and frustrations of adapting to life with HIV.
“My built community is not just Black women. It’s also gay Black men, gay white men, the clinicians that take care of me, the people that I’m able to educate,” she said. “That community has expanded my world tremendously and expanded my ability to cope and feel seen.”
“The onus is always on the person living with HIV to explain and educate, and it’s exhausting. Folks who are not living with HIV could take some of the responsibility off of us.”
Bridgette is an Air Force veteran who later worked for years in customer service.
After learning she had HIV, she went back to school to become a licensed vocational nurse. She originally hoped to work in hospice care but soon found herself employed at the same HIV clinic where she was getting treatment.
“When the opportunity came up to work at the clinic, I took it thinking, ‘OK, I’ll do 6 months and get this experience,’” she recalled, “and that’s an example of how God, fate, or the universe works — because that’s where I got planted, that’s where I grew, and that’s where I continue to grow from.”
Bridgette worked at the HIV clinic for almost 8 years and is now employed as the stakeholder liaison for The Well Project. She described her role there as “standing in the gap between clinicians and people living with HIV,” particularly women with HIV. 
“I understand a little bit about both sides, and I try to make sure that they understand each other. That’s the piece of my job that I love the most.”
Gaining knowledge about HIV has helped Bridgette live well with this condition, and sharing knowledge with others has been a meaningful part of her journey, too.
She said that people without HIV also have a responsibility to educate themselves about the condition and help fight the stigma that surrounds it.
“The onus is always on the person living with HIV to explain and educate, and it’s exhausting,” she said. “Folks who are not living with HIV could take some of the responsibility off of us.”
Bridgette recently passed her twelfth “seroversary,” or the anniversary of the day on which she received her HIV diagnosis. It’s the first year that the day has passed her by unnoticed. 
“I was so busy living that I didn’t realize it had happened until 2 days later,” she said.
Bridgette said that she still finds the challenges of managing HIV feel “exhausting” some days.
“A lot of times, HIV is not the first time that I think of when I wake up in the morning,” she explained. “I have bills to pay, I have a job, I have a son, I have a grandson. I have all the things that everyone has.”
“I just have HIV on top of it, which is another little layer,” she continued. “Sometimes that layer is pancake thin, and sometimes it’s a king-size mattress.”
Finding an outlet to vent negative feelings about HIV is important, she said. She’s a “fan of therapy,” but she also believes that talking with a trusted friend, journaling, or doing other things to release pent-up emotions can help people move forward when they’re feeling stuck.
She also emphasized the value of making time for things that have nothing to do with HIV. For example, she paints, makes jewelry, roller skates, and continues to find joy in the hobbies that she loves.
“Sometimes you forget there are spaces where you were happy before you got the diagnosis, but if you can find your way back to those spaces, it makes the rest of it so much easier to deal with,” she said.
“People tell you you’re not going to die, they tell you to take your pills, but they don’t tell you how to live with HIV,” she added. “And I’ve realized that you just do. I’ve gone from being terrified and feeling othered to knowing that I just need to put one foot in front of the other. Stop worrying about what the steps are — and just live.”

title: Dosage Details for Novoseven
content:
Novoseven (coagulation factor VIIa, recombinant) is a prescription drug that’s used to treat hemophilia and certain other bleeding disorders. The drug comes as a powder that’s mixed to make a liquid for intravenous (IV) infusion. It’s usually given every few hours until bleeding stops.
Novoseven is used to treat bleeding episodes and prevent them during surgery in:
The active ingredient in Novoseven is recombinant coagulation factor VIIa. Novoseven belongs to a group of drugs called recombinant clotting factors.
This article describes the dosages of Novoseven, as well as its strengths and how to take it. For a detailed overview of this drug, check out this in-depth Novoseven article. 
This section describes the usual dosages of Novoseven. Keep reading to learn more.
Novoseven is available as a powder in a vial that’s mixed into a liquid solution. It comes with a prefilled syringe or vial of diluent (a liquid that’s mixed with a powder to form a solution). It’s given as an intravenous (IV) infusion (an injection into your vein over a period of time) or an IV injection over a few minutes.
Novoseven comes in single-dose vials in four strengths:

Your doctor will use a Novoseven dosage calculator to determine your dosage. It will depend on several factors, including:
The typical Novoseven dosage for adults with hemophilia A or B to treat bleeding episodes is 90 mcg/kg every 2 hours until the bleeding stops. Your doctor may recommend continuing Novoseven for a period of time after the bleeding stops if the bleeding was severe. This dosage is typically 90 mcg/kg every 3 to 6 hours.
The typical Novoseven dosage to prevent bleeding related to surgery is 90 mcg/kg right before surgery and every 2 hours during surgery. Your doctor will continue Novoseven after surgery. The dosage depends on the type of surgery:
An example of a major surgery is cardiac (heart) surgery.
For adults with congenital factor VII deficiency, the typical dosage of Novoseven to treat bleeding episodes is 15 to 30 mcg/kg every 4 to 6 hours until the bleeding stops. 
The typical Novoseven dosage to prevent bleeding related to surgery is 15 to 30 mcg/kg right before surgery and every 4 to 6 hours during surgery. Your doctor may continue this dosage until any bleeding stops.
The typical Novoseven dosage for adults with Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia to treat bleeding episodes is 90 mcg/kg every 2 to 6 hours until the bleeding stops.
The typical Novoseven dosage to prevent bleeding related to surgery is 90 mcg/kg right before surgery and every 2 hours during surgery. Your doctor will likely continue Novoseven after surgery to prevent bleeding. The typical dosage is 90 mcg/kg every 2 to 6 hours.
For adults with acquired hemophilia, the typical dosage of Novoseven to treat bleeding episodes is 70 to 90 mcg/kg every 2 to 3 hours until the bleeding stops.
To prevent bleeding related to surgery, the typical dosage is 70 to 90 mcg/kg right before surgery and every 2 to 3 hours during surgery. Your doctor may continue this dosage until any bleeding stops.
Novoseven is used to help treat bleeding episodes and prevent bleeding related to surgery in children with:
The pediatric dose is the same as the dosage for adults. To learn more, see the “What are the usual dosages of Novoseven?” section.
Novoseven is given by IV injection into a vein over a few minutes. In some cases, it’s given as a continuous IV infusion.
If you’re in the hospital or having surgery, a healthcare professional (HCP) will give you the doses of Novoseven. 
If you’ll be taking Novoseven at home, your doctor or another HCP will teach you how to mix and inject the drug yourself. You’ll receive a patient instruction sheet with detailed administration guidelines. The manufacturer also provides step-by-step instructions explaining how to use the drug.
No, Novoseven is usually used as a short-term treatment to treat or prevent bleeding episodes.
Do not use more Novoseven than your doctor prescribes, as this can lead to harmful effects. 
Call your doctor right away if you think you’ve used too much Novoseven. You can also call 800-222-1222 to reach America’s Poison Centers or use its online resource. But if you have severe symptoms, immediately call 911 (or your local emergency number) or go to the nearest emergency room.

Brief eclectic psychotherapy (BEP) is a type of eclectic therapy treatment that is often suggested for treating post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
Eclectic therapies aim to adapt to a person’s individual needs while using several treatment approaches.

When applied over a limited number of sessions to address a specific problem, BEP can help some people find meaning in their traumatic experiences and develop coping strategies.
Brief eclectic psychotherapy (BEP) is a therapy that’s intended to treat PTSD for a short period of time. Emergency personnel and others may use it to manage the effects of a single event that led to symptoms of PTSD.

title: What Is the Difference Between Guillain-Barré Syndrome and Multiple Sclerosis?
content:
Both Guillain-Barré syndrome and multiple sclerosis involve an autoimmune attack on the nervous system. Guillain-Barré syndrome affects the peripheral nervous system, while multiple sclerosis impacts the central nervous system.
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and multiple sclerosis (MS) are considered neurological disorders because they affect the function of the nervous system. They’re also autoimmune conditions.
In both GBS and MS, the immune system damages healthy tissue in your nervous system. GBS progresses quickly and causes paralysis, which in some cases may jeopardize your life. On the other hand, MS has a slower progression, gradually causing stiffness that often leads to mobility challenges and disability.
GBS is a rare neurological condition in which the immune system attacks the fatty protective covering (myelin) on nerve cells of the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The PNS is a vast network of nerves that carries signals between the body’s tissues and the brain and spinal cord.
In MS, the immune system targets nerve cells in the central nervous system (CNS). The CNS is made up of your brain and spinal cord.
When the immune system attacks myelin in healthy tissues of your nervous system, it can lead to symptoms that involve your senses, movement, and coordination, among other functions.
It’s possible that symptoms of GBS and MS overlap. However, there are also differences to be aware of.
The two main symptoms of GBS are muscle weakness and sensory changes. 
Muscle weakness often impacts the legs first, but within days, it may affect the upper parts of the body, including the chest, arms, and face. 
Sometimes, the condition severely affects the muscles in the chest that control breathing, which may lead to someone not being able to breathe on their own.
Sensory changes related to GBS may include:
In severe cases, GBS may also lead to other symptoms like:
The symptoms of MS can depend on the location and extent of CNS damage. They may change or intensify as the condition progresses and may include:
Despite some overlap in symptoms, GBS and MS are two distinct conditions with different outlooks.
GBS is a rare condition. It’s estimated to affect between 3,000 and 6,000 people in the United States each year.
The exact cause of GBS isn’t well understood, but some known risk factors include:
In some cases, certain vaccines, like the flu or COVID-19 shots, may cause an exaggerated immune response. This immune response could become an autoimmune reaction that triggers GBS. Surgery may also rarely lead to the same immune response.
GBS symptoms come on suddenly and affect both sides of the body. They can increase in intensity over hours or days. Symptoms typically peak by 4 weeks before starting to ease.
MS is more common than GBS. According to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society, almost one million people in the United States are living with MS.
The exact cause of MS isn’t known. Some experts have theorized that a combination of genetic and environmental factors contribute to MS onset. 
Some factors that may increase the chance of MS include:
MS develops over time and can progress in different ways, depending on the individual. The different types of MS include:
In addition to getting your medical history, a healthcare professional may use similar exams and tests to diagnose GBS or MS. These include:
No cure has been found yet for GBS. However, treatments can shorten recovery time and reduce the severity of symptoms.
Many people with GBS need to be hospitalized. Interventions like mechanical support for breathing and medications for heart rate and blood pressure can help.
Plasma exchange therapy and intravenous immunoglobulin therapy (IVIG) are two treatments that can help stop the immune system from attacking the PNS. Researchers have found that these two treatments are equally effective.
Symptoms of GBS typically ease a few weeks after the onset. Recovery may vary by individual, taking from a few weeks for some to years for others. During this time, rehabilitative care, such as physical or occupational therapy, may be helpful.
About 20% of people who’ve had GBS develop some form of disability for over a year. GBS can be fatal in around 3% to 7% of people.
As with GBS, no cure has been found for MS. 
The first line of treatment for MS involves medications to prevent the immune system from attacking myelin. Some medications may help reduce the severity and impact of symptoms. Other medications, like disease-modifying treatments (DMTs), will help to reduce the frequency of symptom recurrence and slow the progression of the disease.
Healthcare professionals may use a variety of strategies to manage MS symptoms. These can depend on the specific symptoms and may include:
The outlook for MS depends on factors like the type of MS you have. Overall, the majority of people with MS have a typical life expectancy. However, about 10 to 15 years after onset, some people with MS develop long-term disability.
It’s possible that people with MS also develop GBS. However, this is very rare.
According to a 2021 case study, only nine people with both GBS and MS have been described in case studies, in addition to another seven cases reported in a survey study.
GBS and MS are neurological and autoimmune conditions where your immune system mistakenly attacks myelin in your nervous system. GBS affects the peripheral nervous system, while MS affects the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord).
Some overlap in symptoms and potential factors exists between GBS and MS. However, these two conditions each have different progression patterns, treatments, and outlooks.

title: What Is a Vitreous Hemorrhage?
content:
Vitreous hemorrhage is bleeding in the inner chamber of your eye that contains a colorless gel called vitreous humor. It’s a complication of many eye conditions like retinal tears or eye injury.
Vitreous hemorrhage is also known as vitreous bleeding. An eye doctor might be able to see blood in your vitreous humor during an eye exam, or if bleeding is more severe, you might develop symptoms like floaters or hazy vision.
Blood from a vitreous hemorrhage sometimes gets reabsorbed by your body without specific treatment. However, serious causes might need eye surgery or other treatments like injections.
Some of the conditions that can cause a vitreous hemorrhage can be vision-threatening if not promptly treated, so it’s always best to see an eye doctor if you develop sudden changes to your vision.
Read on to learn more about vitreous hemorrhages, including the causes, symptoms, and treatment options.
Symptoms of vitreous hemorrhage vary depending on the extent of bleeding. Minor cases might not cause any symptoms but might be detectable on a visual exam.
Potential symptoms include:
The most frequent cause of vitreous hemorrhage is posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) with or without:
PVD is when the vitreous humor pulls away from the back of your retina. 
Other potential causes include:
Blood in your vitreous humor can end up in several anatomical spaces in your eye. Doctors sometimes subdivide it into:
Many of the conditions associated with vitreous hemorrhage, such as PVD, become more common with age. Other people at risk include those who have a high risk of eye disease or injury, such as those:
Some conditions that cause vitreous hemorrhage have a high risk of turning into vision-threatening conditions, such as retinal detachment and glaucoma.
Delayed surgery for people who need it might have an increased risk of complications like:
It’s important to get immediate medical attention any time you notice sudden changes to your vision. Sudden visual changes can be a sign of a serious medical condition. 
Many of these conditions are treatable if identified and treated early.
Doctors will run tests to help identify the underlying cause of your bleeding. Some of the tests you might receive include:
Treatment for vitreous hemorrhage might involve conservative options, injections, laser treatment, or surgery.
A doctor may recommend observation alone if it’s expected that your condition will heal by itself. They may also recommend observation for a certain period if they can’t adequately visualize your retina. 
Maintaining an elevated head posture and getting plenty of rest may help support your recovery.
Anti-VEGF injections are used to treat new blood vessel formation, which can impair your vision. These injections may be used to treat vitreous hemorrhage caused by some conditions like diabetic retinopathy.
Laser photocoagulation involves using a laser to seal leaking blood vessels. It may be used to treat proliferative retinopathies as soon as your retina is visible.
If your doctor doesn’t think your blood will reabsorb by itself without causing complications, they may recommend a vitrectomy. This surgery involves removing vitreous humor from your eye and replacing it with a saline solution.
A vitrectomy might need to be performed urgently for some causes like a detached retina.
Your recovery largely depends on the underlying cause of vitreous hemorrhage. In mild cases, blood might be reabsorbed in 2 to 3 months.
If you receive a vitrectomy, you may have to wear an eye shield every night for 4 weeks to make sure you don’t accidentally rub your eye while you’re sleeping. You may also need a few weeks of rest from intensive activities. 
Some of the causes of vitreous hemorrhage can be prevented. For example, you can take precautions to protect your eyes from blunt injuries or degenerative changes by:
Vitreous hemorrhage requires immediate medical attention to identify the underlying cause. Some of the underlying causes can cause permanent vision loss if not treated promptly. 
Some conditions that cause vitreous hemorrhage, such as diabetic retinopathy or a detached retina, can cause permanent vision loss.
Retinal detachment is when a layer of cells at the back of your eye that allows you to sense light becomes detached. It is a potential cause of vitreous hemorrhage.
Blood inside your eye from vitreous hemorrhage can cause pressure inside your eye and glaucoma.
The recovery time for vitreous hemorrhage can depend on the underlying cause. In some cases, blood might reabsorb within 2 to 3 months.
Vitreous hemorrhage is bleeding inside the chamber of your eye that contains a supportive gel called the vitreous humor. Depending on the underlying cause, you might need eye surgery to treat it, or it might be manageable with conservative treatment alone.

title: How Long Does It Take for Calquence to Start Working?
content:
Calquence starts working as soon as you start taking it. But it can take time to see results on laboratory or imaging tests. You’ll likely continue taking Calquence for as long as it’s effective against your cancer.
Calquence (acalabrutinib) is a targeted therapy drug used to treat certain blood cancers. 
Calquence is approved to treat mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) in adults who have tried at least one other treatment. It’s also approved to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) in adults.
Note: Both CLL and SLL refer to the same disease. The name depends on where the cancer cells are concentrated. With CLL, most cancer cells are found in your blood and bone marrow. With SLL, most cancer cells are found in your lymph nodes.
If you’ve recently been prescribed Calquence, you may be wondering how long it takes for it to start working. Keep reading below as we answer this question and more.
Calquence works by blocking an enzyme called Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK). Because BTK signals cancer cells to divide, blocking it can help stop the growth of the cancer.
Calquence comes in the form of a tablet that you take once every 12 hours. The recommended dose is 100 milligrams (mg).
Generally speaking, Calquence starts working shortly after you take it.
The drug’s prescribing information notes that one dose of Calquence blocks 95% or more of the BTK enzymes in your body over 12 hours. That means that after one dose, most BTK enzymes are no longer actively telling the cancer to grow and divide.
However, while Calquence begins working immediately, it may take a few weeks to see results on lab or imaging tests.
Clinical trials of Calquence for MCL and CLL found that inflammation decreased significantly after 28 days of treatment. And Calquence worked to gradually shrink lymph nodes over time in most participants.
Calquence is meant to be taken on a long-term basis. Because of this, you’ll likely take it as long as it continues to effectively treat your cancer.
A 2019 clinical trial report detailed how long Calquence was effective in treating MCL that had relapsed (come back after treatment) or was refractory (didn’t respond to other treatments).
It found that the median duration of response to Calquence was 26 months. That means that Calquence was effective at treating many people’s MCL for a little over 2 years.
A 2021 clinical trial report estimated that 97% of CLL cancers would respond to Calquence for at least 4 years (48 months).
Similar to how you’d take Calquence for MCL, you’ll continue to take Calquence for CLL as long as it’s effective.
Overall, Calquence is an effective treatment for MCL. A 2019 report noted that clinical trials found that 81% of MCLs respond to treatment with Calquence.
The report further details that 40% of people experienced complete remission with Calquence treatment. It also notes that 72% of people taking Calquence are alive after two years (24 months).
For CLL, the 2021 clinical trial report discussed earlier found an overall response rate of 97% for Calquence. The researchers observed that 90% of CLLs had a partial response to Calquence. Seven percent of people had a complete remission.
Calquence is a targeted therapy drug approved for MCL, CLL, and SLL. It works by blocking an enzyme that signals these cancers to grow and divide.
Generally speaking, Calquence starts working as soon as you begin taking it. However, it may take several weeks to see results on lab or imaging tests.
If you’re prescribed Calquence, you’ll likely continue to take it as long as it’s effective. If there are signs that your cancer is no longer responding to Calquence, your doctor will recommend another treatment.

title: Lumryz Interactions: Alcohol, Medications, and Others
content:
Lumryz (sodium oxybate) is a prescription drug used to treat certain narcolepsy symptoms. This drug can interact with alcohol, other medications, and some supplements. A few examples include cetirizine (Zyrtec) and gabapentin (Horizant, Neurontin, others).
Lumryz is used in adults to treat excessive daytime sleepiness or cataplexy related to narcolepsy.
An interaction can occur because one substance causes another substance to have a different effect than expected. Interactions can also occur if you have certain health conditions.
Keep reading to learn about Lumryz’s possible interactions. And for more information about the drug, including details about its uses, see this in-depth Lumryz article.

Before you start taking Lumryz, tell your doctor and pharmacist about any prescription, over-the-counter, or other drugs you take. Sharing this information with them may help prevent possible interactions. (To learn whether Lumryz interacts with herbs, vitamins, or supplements, see the “Are there other interactions with Lumryz?” section.)
If you have questions about drug interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
The table below lists drugs that may interact with Lumryz. Keep in mind that this table does not include all drugs that may interact with Lumryz. For more information about some of these interactions, see the “Drug interactions explained” section.
Note: Lumryz has a boxed warning for the risk of CNS depression. A boxed warning is the most serious warning from the FDA. To learn more, see the “Boxed warnings” section at the top of this article.
Certain health conditions or other factors could increase your risk of harm if you take Lumryz. These are known as contraindications. In such cases, your doctor may not prescribe this medication for you. The list below includes contraindications of Lumryz.
If you have succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency: Doctors typically will not prescribe Lumryz for people with this condition. SSADH is a rare genetic (inherited) condition that could cause Lumryz to build up in your system. As a result, your risk of side effects from this medication may be higher.
If you have SSADH deficiency, talk with your doctor before taking Lumryz. They can recommend other treatment options for your condition.
If you consume alcohol or take sedative hypnotics: Doctors typically will not prescribe Lumryz for people who consume alcohol or take sedative hypnotics. Examples include zolpidem (Ambien, Edluar), zaleplon (Sonata), and eszopiclone (Lunesta).
This is because Lumryz, alcohol, and sedative hypnotics can all cause CNS depression. This means they can slow down the activity of your brain, spinal cord, and nerves. Taking Lumryz with alcohol, sedative hypnotics, or both increases this risk.
In fact, Lumryz has a boxed warning about the risk of CNS depression. A boxed warning is the most serious warning from the FDA. To learn more, see the “Boxed warnings” section at the top of this article.
If you consume alcohol or take sedative hypnotics, talk with your doctor before starting Lumryz. They can recommend other treatment options for your condition.
You should not consume alcohol during your Lumryz treatment. For details about this, see the “When should I avoid Lumryz?” section.
Learn more about certain drug interactions that can occur with Lumryz.
Lumryz can interact with muscle relaxers, which are used to treat muscle spasm. 
Examples of muscle relaxers include:
Lumryz and muscle relaxers can cause CNS depression. So taking these drugs together can increase your risk of this side effect.
With CNS depression, the activity of your brain, spinal cord, and nerves is slowed. This may affect many bodily functions, including awareness, movement, and thinking.
Lumryz has a boxed warning about the risk of CNS depression. This is the most serious warning from the FDA. To learn more, see the “Boxed warnings” section at the top of this article.
Before starting Lumryz, tell your doctor about any muscle relaxers you take. In most cases, they’ll avoid prescribing muscle relaxers with Lumryz and can recommend other options for your condition.
In some cases, such as after an injury, you may need to take a muscle relaxer. If so, your doctor may temporarily stop your Lumryz treatment. This will help lower your risk of severe CNS depression while you’re taking the muscle relaxer.
If you have questions about taking Lumryz with muscle relaxers, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Lumryz can interact with certain antihistamines, which are medications used to manage allergic conditions, nausea, and more. Some antihistamines are available over the counter (OTC), which means you don’t need a prescription to purchase them.
Examples of antihistamine medications include:
Lumryz and certain antihistamines can cause CNS depression. Taking them together can further increase your risk of this side effect. (You can learn more about the risk of CNS depression with Lumryz in the “Boxed warnings” section at the top of this article.)
Before taking an antihistamine or any OTC allergy drug with Lumryz, talk with your doctor or pharmacist. They can recommend antihistamine products that may be safe to take with Lumryz.
Lumryz can interact with gabapentin (Horizant, Neurontin, others). This drug is used to treat certain types of seizure or pain.
Lumryz and gabapentin can both cause CNS depression, so taking them together can increase your risk of this side effect. (To learn more about the risk of CNS depression with Lumryz, see the “Boxed warnings” section at the top of this article.)
Before starting Lumryz, tell your doctor if you take gabapentin. They can tell you whether it’s safe to take with Lumryz.
If you do take these drugs together, tell your doctor right away if you have symptoms of CNS depression. These may include excessive sleepiness and respiratory depression (slowed or shallow breathing). If your symptoms seem severe or life threatening, you or a bystander should call 911 or a local emergency number.
If you have questions about taking Lumryz with gabapentin, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Lumryz may have other interactions. They could occur with supplements, foods, vaccines, or even lab tests. See below for details. Note that this information does not include all other possible interactions with Lumryz.
Lumryz may interact with caffeine supplements, which are often taken to help people stay awake. Taking Lumryz with caffeine supplements could increase your risk of certain side effects from caffeine, such as insomnia, nervousness, and irritability.
Before you start taking Lumryz, talk with your doctor and pharmacist about any herbs or vitamins and supplements you take. Sharing this information with them may help you avoid possible interactions.
If you have questions about interactions that may affect you, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
Lumryz can interact with St. John’s wort, which is used to ease symptoms of depression and other conditions.
Taking Lumryz with this supplement may enhance the effects of Lumryz. This can lead to excessive sleepiness or a higher risk of side effects from the drug.
Talk with your doctor before taking Lumryz with St. John’s wort.
There are currently no reports of Lumryz interacting with vitamins. But this doesn’t mean that vitamin interactions won’t be recognized in the future.
For this reason, it’s still important to check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any of these products while taking Lumryz.
Lumryz may interact with caffeine, which can be found in many foods and drinks. Examples include certain soft drinks, green tea, coffee, and chocolate.
Taking Lumryz with caffeinated foods or drinks could increase your risk of certain side effects from caffeine, like insomnia, nervousness, and irritability.
It’s also important to note that you should take Lumryz at least 2 hours after eating. Taking Lumryz with food could decrease the level of the drug in your body, making it less effective.
To learn more about Lumryz and food, talk with your doctor or pharmacist.
There are currently no reports of Lumryz interacting with vaccines. If you have questions about getting certain vaccines during treatment with Lumryz, talk with your doctor.
There are currently no reports of Lumryz interacting with lab tests. If you have questions about having certain lab tests during treatment with Lumryz, talk with the healthcare professional ordering the test.
Cannabis (commonly called marijuana) and cannabis products, such as cannabidiol (CBD), have been specifically reported to interact with Lumryz.
When taken individually, Lumryz and cannabis products may cause CNS depression. This means they can slow down the activity of your brain, spinal cord, and nerves. Taking them together increases this risk. 
Lumryz has a boxed warning about the risk of CNS depression. A boxed warning is the most serious warning from the FDA. To learn more, see the “Boxed warnings” section at the top of this article.
Before you start treatment with Lumryz, tell your doctor and pharmacist if you use cannabis. By sharing this information with them, you may help prevent possible interactions.
Note: Cannabis is illegal at a federal level but is legal in many states to varying degrees.
Certain medical conditions or other health factors may increase the risk of interactions with Lumryz. Before starting this medication, talk with your doctor about your health history. They’ll determine whether Lumryz is right for you.
Health conditions or other factors that might interact with Lumryz include:
SSADH deficiency: Doctors typically will not prescribe Lumryz for people with a rare genetic condition called SSADH deficiency. To learn more, see the “When should I avoid Lumryz?” section above.
Low sodium diet: Before taking Lumryz, tell your doctor if you’re following a low sodium diet. This may include a low sodium diet for kidney problems, high blood pressure, or heart failure.
This is because Lumryz contains a high amount of sodium, which you’ll likely want to factor into your daily intake. To learn about the sodium content in each dose of Lumryz, see the drug’s prescribing information.
Mental health conditions: In rare cases, taking Lumryz may lead to depression or suicidal thoughts and behavior. This risk may be higher for people who’ve ever had suicidal thoughts or mental health conditions, including depression. Your doctor can recommend whether Lumryz is right for you.
Liver problems: Before starting Lumryz treatment, tell your doctor if you have a liver problem, such as liver failure. Liver problems could cause Lumryz to build up in your body, increasing your risk of side effects from the drug. Due to this risk, doctors may prescribe a different treatment for your condition.
Breathing problems: Before taking Lumryz, tell your doctor if you have a breathing problem such as sleep apnea. Lumryz may cause slowed or shallow breathing, which could worsen any breathing problems you already have.
If you have a breathing problem, your doctor can recommend whether Lumryz is a safe treatment option for you.
Pregnancy: It’s not known whether Lumryz is safe to take during pregnancy. If you’re pregnant or planning a pregnancy, talk with your doctor before starting this medication. 
Breastfeeding: It’s not known whether it’s safe to take Lumryz while breastfeeding. The drug passes into breast milk, but it isn’t known whether it may cause side effects in a child who’s breastfed. If you’re breastfeeding or considering it, talk with your doctor about your options.
Allergic reaction: If you’ve had an allergic reaction to Lumryz or any of its ingredients, your doctor will likely not prescribe this drug for you. Ask your doctor about other treatments that may be better choices for you.
If you or someone you know is in crisis and considering suicide or self-harm, please seek support:
If you’re calling on behalf of someone else, stay with them until help arrives. You may remove weapons or substances that can cause harm if you can do so safely.
If you’re not in the same household, stay on the phone with them until help arrives.
Taking certain steps can help you avoid interactions with Lumryz. Before starting treatment, talk with your doctor and pharmacist. Things to discuss with them include:
It’s also important to understand Lumryz’s label and other paperwork that may come with it. Colored stickers that describe interactions may be on the label. And the paperwork (sometimes called the patient package insert or medication guide) may have other details about interactions. (If you did not get paperwork with Lumryz, ask your pharmacist to print a copy for you.)
If you have trouble reading or understanding this information, your doctor or pharmacist can help.
Taking Lumryz exactly as prescribed can also help prevent interactions.

title: Do Gallbladder Diseases Run in Families?
content:
Your gallbladder is a small pear-shaped organ near your liver that stores bile, a substance that helps break down fat so your body can absorb it. Gallbladder disease refers to anything that can affect the function of your gallbladder, including:
Experts think some people may be at greater risk than others due to their genetics. Having a family history of gallbladder problems may put you at increased risk of any type of gallbladder disease.
While you may inherit genes that increase your risk, that doesn’t mean you’ll develop gallbladder disease. Many people also develop gallbladder problems without a family history.

title: Does Medicare Cover Hoyer Lifts?
content:
Hoyer lifts use a sling to lift and move a person who has mobility challenges with minimal physical effort. They come in manual or battery-powered options. The word “Hoyer” refers to a well-known brand of these lifts, but other manufacturers make similar models as well.
Medicare covers lifts under the durable medical equipment (DME) benefit of Original Medicare’s Part B. Here’s what you need to know if you or a family member want to get a Hoyer lift through Medicare.
Part B covers either the purchase or the rental of lifts, including Hoyer lifts, as long as the supplier is enrolled in Medicare and accepts the assignment. If so, you’ll have to pay only the coinsurance and deductible.
To qualify, you’ll need to meet face to face with your doctor and have them fill out and sign an order for the supplier. This order must include:
Whether Medicare will require you to rent or buy the lift and whether it will cover a manual or powered lift may depend on your specific case. 
That said, if you rent the lift and make payments on it for at least 13 months, the supplier will consider you the owner of the lift.
Hoyer lifts can cost somewhere between a few hundred and a few thousand dollars. This depends on the brand and whether it’s manual or powered. Rental will cost less per month, but you’ll have to make continuous payments.
Whether Medicare covers your purchase or rental, it should pay 80% of the cost if you’ve met the 2025 deductible for Part B ($257) and you make your monthly premium payments ($185 or higher, depending on your income).
Aside from Hoyer lifts, which use a sling, other types of lifts use belts, straps, and vests. Some lifts are portable, while others are mounted to the ceiling or a wall. Search Medicare-approved DME suppliers in your area to see what they have to offer.

Generally, Medicare should pay for most medical equipment if it’s medically necessary. Exceptions include devices you can’t use at home, disposable items, eyeglasses, hearing aids, and orthopedic shoes.

title: Dosage Details for Soliris
content:
Soliris (eculizumab) is a prescription drug used to treat certain rare autoimmune conditions. It comes as a liquid solution for intravenous infusion by a healthcare professional. The dosage depends on the condition Soliris is being used to treat.
Soliris is used to treat several types of autoimmune conditions in adults. These include:
Note: Soliris is also used to treat aHUS in children ages 2 months and older. Soliris isn’t used to treat HUS triggered byE. coli infection.
The active ingredient in Soliris is eculizumab. Soliris belongs to a group of drugs called complement inhibitors. It’s a biologic medication made from living cells.
This article describes the dosages of Soliris, as well as its strength and how it’s given. To learn more about this drug, see this in-depth Soliris article.
The table below highlights the basics of Soliris’s dosage. All doses are listed in milligrams (mg). 
For more details about the dosages of Soliris, see the information below.
Soliris comes as a liquid solution that’s given as an intravenous (IV) infusion (an injection into a vein over a period of time) by a healthcare professional.
Soliris comes in one strength of 300 mg per 30 milliliters (mL) — or 10 mg/mL — in single-dose vials.
Your doctor will start you on the recommended dosage of Soliris based on the condition the drug is being used to treat.
The Soliris infusion protocol involves two different treatment phases. The first phase of treatment is the induction phase when you’ll receive Soliris each week. This is followed by the maintenance phase when you’ll typically receive Soliris every 2 weeks.
The information below describes dosages that are commonly used or recommended. In some cases, doctors may adjust your dosage from those shown below. For example, if you’re also receiving plasmapheresis, plasma exchange, or fresh frozen plasma treatments, you’ll likely need additional doses of Soliris to maintain effective levels of the drug in your body.
The typical starting Soliris dosage for adults with PNH is 600 mg every week for 4 weeks. This is the induction phase of treatment.
Then, you’ll receive one 900-mg dose on week 5 of treatment. After this, you’ll receive 900 mg every 2 weeks as the maintenance phase of your treatment.
Talk with your doctor if you have questions about your dosage or dosing schedule.
For adults with aHUS, the typical dosage of Soliris is 900 mg per week for 4 weeks. This is the induction phase of treatment.
After this, you’ll receive 1,200 mg on week 5 of treatment. Then, your dose is 1,200 mg every 2 weeks as the maintenance phase of treatment.
If you have questions about your dosage, talk with your doctor to learn more.
The Soliris dosing for generalized MG is 900 mg each week for the first 4 weeks. This is the induction phase of treatment.
Then, you’ll receive 1,200 mg of Soliris at week 5 of treatment. After this, you’ll receive 1,200 mg every 2 weeks as the maintenance phase of treatment.
For adults with NMOSD, the typical starting dosage of Soliris is 900 mg per week for 4 weeks. This is the induction phase of treatment. 
Then, you’ll receive a dose of 1,200 mg on week 5 of treatment. After this, you’ll receive 1,200 mg of Soliris every 2 weeks as the maintenance phase of treatment.
Soliris is used to help treat aHUS in children ages 2 months and older.

A typical Soliris infusion lasts around 35 minutes.

The Soliris package insert contains detailed information from the manufacturer about the drug’s uses, dosage, and how it’s given.
Talk with your doctor if you have questions about how Soliris is administered.
